case_name: Posluns v. Toronto Stock Exchange and Gardiner

Posluns v. Toronto Stock Exchange and Gardiner

[1964] 2 O.R. 547-684

ONTARIO

[HIGH COURT OF JUSTICE]

GALE, J.

28th APRIL 1964.

Torts -- Inducing breach of contract -- Stock Exchange withdrawing approval of customers' man employed by member -- Discharge of customers' man -- Whether lawful termination of employment or procurement of breach of contract -- Implied term of employment that customers' man subject to proper control of Exchange -- Whether Exchange acted within its powers and according to rules of natural justice -- Illegal means as vitiating defence of justification where otherwise established.
Unless there is a privilege or justification so to act, a person is liable in tort if, knowing of an employment contract, although unaware of its precise terms, he procures a breach thereof by direct and deliberate interference through his power over the employer's business operations, resulting in dismissal of the employee, and it is immaterial that he acted without malice or spite, and its is also immaterial that the employer might have lawfully brought the contract to an end. A wish to do harm is not a prerequisite of the cause of action if the purpose was to bring an end to the employment contract and if damage resulted accordingly. A breach of contract knowingly induced by a stranger thereto will also be actionable if illegal means are used, and these may consist of acts which are not otherwise actionable or may involve conduct by the stranger, being a corporate or statutory body, which is beyond its lawful power or authority.  The use of illegal means will vitiate the defence of privilege or justification which might otherwise exist by reason of the object or purpose pursued by the defendant, as, for example, if being a corporate body it acts beyond its powers when it procures plaintiff's dismissal or fails to apply (where this is found to be required) the principles of natural justice in the dealings which result in the dismissal.
An action for procuring a breach of an employment contract will not lie if it is shown that the parties thereto have explicitly or implicitly agreed that the employer may act upon any valid withdrawal of approval to the continued employment of the employee manifested by a third party, so that a lawful termination of the contract results rather than an actionable interference for which the third party would otherwise be liable.
The Toronto Stock Exchange, a corporate body, gave approval to one of its members, in pursuance of its by-laws, to plaintiff becoming a shareholder and director, and the member thereupon also employed plaintiff as a customers' man (as the Court found, rather than as a mere salesman) to the knowledge of the Exchange.  Subsequently, and after certain hearings, the Exchange fined the member for having acted improperly in connection with certain "put and call" option transactions on behalf of a customer in respect of which the member took improper "spreads" and was guilty of a conflict of interest. At the same time, the Exchange withdrew all consents to plaintiff acting as a shareholder, officer (which he never was), director or employee of the member because plaintiff had an interest in a firm which was at the other end of the "put and call" option dealings carried out on behalf of the aforementioned customer.  The Exchange intended that plaintiff be discharged as an employee and he was.  In an action for damages for wrongfully procuring a breach of plaintiff's contract of employment, held, although the Exchange had knowingly and intentionally interfered with the contract with resulting damage, it was justified in so doing and, moreover, there was a lawful termination rather than a breach since the parties to the contract must be taken to have agreed that the member could act upon any valid withdrawal of approval by the Exchange.  The Exchange could not excuse its interference with the employment contract on the ground that it was acting in the public interest or to protect the public welfare, since it was primarily concerned to discipline the offending member and the plaintiff.  However, it could invoke as justification the right impliedly given by the agreement between the member and plaintiff to exercise control over the latter in accordance with its powers and by proper means, so long as plaintiff continued under its aegis.  Justification was proved as to purpose since there was evidence on which the Exchange could find that plaintiff continued under its aegis.  Justification was proved as to purpose since there was evidence on which the Exchange could find that plaintiff's conduct was incompatible with the ethical behaviour it deemed necessary to protect public investors.  Further, no illegal means were involved since the Exchange acted within its by-laws in withdrawing its approval (which extended to a customers' man) and there was no denial of natural justice.

Administrative law -- Boards and tribunals -- Application of rules of natural justice -- Stock Exchange withdrawing approval of customers' man employed by member -- Failure to give notice of charges -- Defective proceeding cured by rehearing.
Associations -- Application of rules of natural justice in disciplinary proceedings -- Toronto Stock Exchange -- Withdrawal of approval of customers' man employed by member.
Provided a domestic tribunal, e.g., the governors of the Toronto Stock Exchange, has acted honestly and bona fide, the Court will not act as an appellate Court from its decision on a question of fact nor probe the decision to see if they would have reached a similar verdict.  However, the Court may review a domestic tribunal's decision which involves a question of law such as the construction or the interpretation of the rules of the organization.  Held, also, whether a Court is limited to seeing if there is no evidence at all to support a domestic tribunal's finding or whether the true test be that a Court can scrutinize the decision to see whether the evidence, taken as a whole, is reasonably capable of supporting the finding, there was no ground for impugning the decision of the governors of the Toronto Stock Exchange that a customers' man, employed by a member of the Exchange and approved as a shareholder and director, was guilty of unbecoming conduct and that in consequence, approval of his association with the member as shareholder, director or employee should be withdrawn.  Held, further, although the governors were entitled to terminate an approval at their discretion without assigning a reason and hence there would be nothing to review, yet where a reason was given, the Court was entitled to look at it, at least to see whether there was any evidence to support the conclusion. Held, too, the Exchange was entitled to withdraw its approval of the customers' man because it acted within its own rules in so doing and under the conventions of natural justice. Although a domestic tribunal, the governors of the Toronto Stock Exchange were bound by the rules of natural justice in the same way as domestic tribunals whose constitution of rules provide for expulsion of a member for a stipulated cause; and notice and hearing (as required by the rules of natural justice) must be given even where the power of dismissal is exercisable in the discretion of a domestic tribunal, and this is expecially so where misconduct is the alleged ground for exercise of the discretion. It matters not, so far as concerns the applicability of these rules, whether the Exchange imposes its penalty directly or whether it procures the dismissal of a person indirectly, e.g., by withdrawing approval of his employment as a customers' man by a member of the Exchange.  In so acting within its powers and in accordance with the rules of natural justice, the Exchange has a valid defence to what would otherwise be liability for procuring breach of contract. Although the Exchange was in violation of the rules of natural justice in the first hearing that it held on certain alleged improprieties in stock dealings, in that it failed to give the customers' man, whose conduct it reproved, notice of charges against him in his personal capacity (although a formal charge was not necessary), nor was he given any opportunity to speak to the matter of the penalty, nevertheless the situation was remedied by a subsequent hearing at which the affected person was given full opportunity to adduce evidence and make representations.  He was then aware of the nature of the allegations against him, and, on the evidence, the governors of the Exchange (who were not required literally to annul their previous decision) met the applicable test of holding the rehearing under a resolve conscientiously and honestly to reconsider the matter without being influenced by the effect or terms of their earlier decision.  There was no evidence of any prior decision by them as to what they would do at the rehearing, and, indeed, they varied the previous disposition of the case by offering the customers' man the opportunity resign.
Administrative law -- Whether rules of association may exclude rules of natural justice.
Association -- Domestic tribunal -- Whether rules may exclude rules of natural justice.
In the absence of an express prohibition the Courts will not construe the rules of an association or of a body having disciplinary authority over its members as impliedly excluding the rules of natural justice when they would otherwise be applicable.  The question whether these rules have been applied in any one case is an issue of law but nonetheless it rests in each instance on the particular facts.  Shortly stated, the rules of natural justice require that a person know the nature of an accusation against him, that he be given an opportunity to state his case (including an opportunity to speak to a proposed penalty), and that the tribunal should act in good faith.
Torts -- Inducing breach of contract -- Justification -- When defence operative.
Although justification as a defence to an action for inducing a breach of contract has never been precisely defined, and although the defence rarely succeeds (since it does not include self interest or fulfilment of an undertaking to protect others in the same interest, nor an honest belief in a duty to act, nor inducement of a breach of contract because the other party thereto has broken another contract with the intervenor), yet it has been admitted where the interference has been promoted by impersonal or disinterested motives and also where it was effected in the public interest.  Beyond these cases, a person may be justified in inducing a breach of contract because of statutory or contractual privilege.  Thus, where the Toronto Stock Exchange, a corporate body, gave approval to a member to have plaintiff as a shareholder and director and plaintiff, who was also employed by the member, acted as such and subsequently the Exchange withdrew its approval because of plaintiff's improper conduct and in consequence he was dismissed, held, plaintiff's relationship to the member involved an agreement to submit to the proper of the Exchange which, therefore, was justified in procuring his dismissal when it acted in accordance with its by-laws and in accordance with the principles of natural justice in withdrawing its approval of plaintiff.
Torts -- Conspiracy -- Officers of association voting same way to detriment of plaintiff -- No previous agreement to injure -- Whether conjoint vote supports claim for actionable conspiracy.
Officers or directors of an association who, without any previous agreement on the matter, vote withdrawal of approval previously given to a person being a shareholder and director of a member company, with the result that such person is dismissed from his employment with the member, do not become liable for actionable conspiracy merely because they voted the same way, especially where no malice or improper motive was shown.
Damages -- Inducing breach of contract of employment -- Loss of earnings as element in damages -- Reduction by amount of income tax payable thereon.
A plaintiff who succeds in an action for inducing breach of contract is not limited to recovery of his actual pecuniary loss but may also have a sum appropriate to the circumstance of the wrong inflicted, once financial loss is shown.  Semble, such portion of the damages awarded as represent loss of earnings would have to be reduced by the amount of income tax payable on such earnings.

GALE, J., delivered judgment as follows:--

I
THE NATURE OF THE ACTION

In this action, which resulted in a very long trial, the
plaintiff seeks judgment against the Toronto Stock Exchange
(hereafter to be designated by the abbreviations "the Stock
Exchange" or "the Exchange") for substantial damages for the
alleged inducement by the defendant of a breach of a contract
of employment which existed between the plaintiff and R. A.
Daly and Company Limited (which from this point on I will call
"Dalys" or "the Daly company" or "the Daly firm"), and a
declaration that an order of the Board of Governors of the
Exchange withdrawing its approval of the plaintiff as a
director, shareholder and employee of the Daly company was made
illegally and without power or authority.  As against both
defendants Mr. Posluns claims large damages said to have been
suffered by him as a result of a wrongful conspiracy between
them and with the other members of the Board to terminate his
association with Dalys, to prevent him from obtaining
employment with any other member or member firms or
corporations of the Exchange, and wilfully to cause injury to
his reputation and good name.  Punitive damages are also
claimed in respect of the conspiracy.

Originally, Mr. Eric Scott, who was president of the Exchange
in 1961, was a party to the action as an alleged co-
conspirator, but when the trial opened on May 14, 1963, and
at the request of counsel for all parties, I dismissed the
action as against that defendant without costs.

Until the case came to be argued, the plaintiff also asked
triple damages under the Statute of Monopolies, 21 Jac. I, c.
3, but at that time I was informed by his counsel that such
claim was being abandoned.  It will not, therefore, be
considered further.

II THE PUT AND CALL OPTION BUSINESS

After his graduation from the University of Toronto with a
Bachelor of Commerce degree, Mr. Posluns commenced to work with
the Toronto brokerage firm of Burns Bros. and Company Limited
(hereafter to be referred to as "Burns") as a sales trainee.
By May of 1957 he had been approved by the Exchange as a
shareholder and customers' man of that firm.  Such approval as
a shareholder of a member firm was required by Exchange By-law
67, s. 2, and that as a customers' man who is a person employed
"primarily for the solicitation of commission business in
securities listed on this Exchange", by s. 1 of By-law 49.  In
his application to be a customers' man and in consideration of
the Exchange approving the application, Mr. Posluns submitted
himself to the jurisdiction of the Exchange and agreed, inter
alia, that he would not, directly or indirectly, take or
receive a share in the profits of any customer's account.

About that time, a Dr. Morton Shulman, who had been active in
the securities business in general, became interested in what
is called the put and call option aspect of it.  Although
trading in stock options had been, and still is, carried on in
the United States, Dr. Shulman was probably the first to enter
the field in Canada.  Early in 1958, while still with Burns,
Mr. Posluns met Dr. Shulman who introduced him to the put and
call business.  The plaintiff commenced to study this activity
and soon visted New York in an endeavour to learn more about it
from the put and call dealers there.

Perhaps at this point it might be well to explain briefly the
stock option business which is not only complicated but calls
for great experience, acumen and capital to operate
successfully.  Basically, those options which take the form of
negotiable bearer contracts are simply bought and sold like any
other commodity for the trading of which there is no exchange.
There are six types of stock options:  a call; a put; a
straddle; a strap; a strip; and a spread.

The "call" option is the most popular form.  It is a contract
purchased for an agreed premium entitling the holder, at his
option, to buy from the vendor on or before a fixed date a
specified number of shares at a pre-determined price.  On the
other hand, a "put" option is one to sell a specific quantity
of stock at a fixed price for a stipulated period of time.  A
"straddle" consists of two options, one "call" and the other
"put", either of which may be exercised independently of the
other at any time during the life of the straddle.  "Strips"
and "straps" are more intricate combinations of puts and calls.
The former includes two puts and one call whereas the latter is
composed of one put and two calls.  Lastly, a "spread" is an
extremely uncommon type of option consisting of a put and a
call exercisable at different prices.

A discussion here of the supposed advantages and
disadvantages of dealing in stock options would not serve any
useful purpose.  They are a very speculative type of investment
and ordinarily the man on the street is interested only in
simple call options; the other types are traded, with few
exceptions, only by the professional put and call brokers.
Perhaps it should be emphasized, however, that the person who
is willing to sell options in the first instance is the
essential factor in the whole business.  The buyers are made up
of the members of the general public who respond to the
advertisements and promotions of the put and call brokers
possessing options for sale.  But the options do not originate
with those brokers who act merely as middlemen, making their
profit in the difference between the acquisition price paid to
the vendor for the option, and the price at which the broker
disposes of it to the public or to another dealer.  Thus, as I
have already stressed, they key man is the original seller of
the option -- the individual who creates it.

That man requires a vast amount of capital for he must either
have the stock with which to meet calls which may be made
against him upon the exercise of call options, or,
alternatively, have the capital to go into the market to
purchase the stock for that purpose.  Similarly, he requires
capital in the event that a put option which he has sold is
exercised against him.  In his testimony, Dr. Shulman stated
that for every one hundred dollars that a seller of options
receives in premiums, he must be prepared to put up
approximately $1,000 in capital.

It must be borne in mind, too, that these options are not
traded on an exchange, such as the Toronto Stock Exchange or
the New York Stock Exchange, but are traded through members of
a recognized Exchange.  The Toronto members act as the put and
call brokers in respect of any transaction, purchasing the
option from a seller and re-selling it to the members of the
public or in some instances to another broker.

Because of the option-seller's potential liability, the
broker who purchases the option from him (in Ontario, usually a
member of the Toronto Stock Exchange) insists upon some form of
security that the option-seller will be able to fulfil his
contract in the event that the option is exercised against him.
In this Province, a member of the Exchange, through whom an
option-seller was selling an option, exacted, as security,
either the stock on which the option had been sold, any where
from 30% to 50% of the capital value of the stock (being the
usual margin requirement), a bank guarantee, or the guarantee
of another Exchange member. On the other hand, if an option
were to be sold in New York to a put and call broker, there had
to be endorsed on the back of the option contract a guarantee
by a member of the New York Stock Exchange.  That guarantor,
being a member of that Exchange, itself required as security
the stock, or 30% of capital, or the guarantee of another
member of the New York Exchange.  Thus, a New York Exchange
member would not accept as security the guarantee of a bank or
the guarantee of a member of the Toronto Exchange.

In 1958, Dr. Shulman and the plaintiff formed a partnership
named Lido Investments. It was comprised of three limited
companies in each of which the doctor had a one-half share
interest and the plaintiff, or one of his two brothers, a 50%
interest.  In essence, therefore, Dr. Shulman owned 50% of Lido
and the three Posluns brothers the other 50%.  The total
capital invested in Lido was $190,000.  Dr. Shulman supplied
$95,00 and each of the three Posluns advanced one third of the
other $95,000.

From its formation in 1958 until January, 1960, Lido Traded
in stocks and sold options.  In other words, it acted as an
originator of options in the manner already described.  The few
options it purchased were held by it and not resold.  It was
agreed between Dr. Shulman and the plaintiff that generally the
former would look after the day to day business of selling
options and any trading of stocks required, and that the
plaintiff would arrange the financing needed by Lido for
margining its account.  Lido did not possess an office of its
own but the facilities of the medical office of Dr. Shulman
were employed for its purposes.  An extremely efficient lady,
Mrs. Kathleen Jones, worked in the same building and assisted
in certain administrative and other duties for Lido.  At the
beginning of their association, the plaintiff visited the
doctor's office on Lido affairs about once a week.  Thereafter,
he visited less often.  In addition, while Mr. Posluns was at
Burns, he received from Dr. Shulman each day a sheet showing
the Lido transactions of the day before, and while he did
little of the day to day trading, on one or two occasions he
may have conducted a few sales of options.

The plaintiff caused the Burns firm to enter the put and call
business in 1958 and for about a year it purchased Lido share
options which were guaranteed by Lido's bank.  Lido did not
confine the sale of its options to Burns but also, according to
the evidence of Dr. Shulman, sold options even more extensively
to Doherty Roadhouse & Co., another member firm of the Toronto
Stock Exchange. During 1958 and the first half of 1959 the
options sold by Lido were with respect to Canadian stocks only.
However, in the spring of 1959, the doctor visited New York
City and established contact with the two leading American put
and call brokers of the day, Thomas Habbs and Botts and Filer
Schmidt & Co., as a result of which Lido commenced thereafter
to do business with those two firms.  The options that Dr.
Shulman, on behalf of Lido, sold to those two New York brokers
were largely on inter-listed stocks, that is, stocks that were
listed on both the Toronto Stock Exchange and either the
American Stock Exchange or the New York Stock Exchange.  A few
of the stocks were not inter-listed but listed exclusively on
either the New York Stock Exchange or the American Stock
Exchange.

In order for an option contract to be sold in the United
States, a document which constituted the option contract had to
be guaranteed by a member of the New York Stock Exchange who
would endorse his signature on the back of the option contract.
Accordingly, before either of the aforementioned New York
brokers would purchase an option from Lido they had to be
satisfied that a member of the New York Stock Exchange would be
endorsing those options.  To take care of that situation the
plaintiff made arrangements with Oppenheimer & Company, a New
York member house, to endorse all options sold in the United
States by Lido.  Before the Oppenheimer company would guarantee
or endorse the Lido options, it had to have deposited with it
securities or margin, since it was the party liable on the
actual contract.  Because the Oppenheimer company would satisfy
its liability by looking to Lido, the actual seller of the
option, Lido or Burns, was required to place margin on deposit
with the New York firm.  The margin was 30% or 25%, depending
on whether or not the option was a put or a call.  In fact, it
was the Burns company which put up the margin with Oppenheimer
company.  Burns in turn required margin from Lido and the
plaintiff looked after the margin arrangements at Burns.  He
stated in his testimony that he did not check the demands for
margin made upon him against the daily sheets of Burns to see
whether the transactions had in fact occurred which
necessitated the deposit of margin.  He accepted the demands
made upon him in that respect.  The margin took the form either
of securities deposited by Lido or of cash deposited by certain
companies with which Mr. Posluns was associated.  One other
point is of significance in connection with the period of the
plaintiff's employment with the Burns company.  When the put
and call option buisness began at Burns, the firm employed
contract froms apparently identical to those of exs. 5 and 6,
hereafter described in greater detail.  The treasurer of Burns
testified that the form adopted by his firm was submitted to it
by the plaintiff.  It was the same as that being issued by J.A.
Kennedy Limited, a company company also dealing in puts and
calls.  The plaintiff in his examination-in-chief testified
that while at Burns he had nothing to do with the drafting of
the document, but under cross-examination in response to the
question, "Did you have anything to do with the settling of the
forms that Burns were going to use?" he replied, "I may have,
Sir, I don't recall."

The financial statement for the first year of operations of
the Lido partnership ending May 31, 1959, revealed that it had
a net profit of $27,725.46.

III THE PLAINTIFF AT THE DAILY COMPANY

The plaintiff left Burns as of January 6, 1960 because he was
informed that the firm was unable to continue paying him one-
third of the commissions earned by it on transactions
effected by his customers in respect of the sale of United
States securities.  He went over to the Daly company.  On
January 5, 1960, the Burns firm advised the Toronto Stock
Exchange that the plaintiff had ceased to be one of its
customers' men, and by letter dated January 6, 1960 (ex. 48),
the Ontario Securities Commission informed the plaintiff that
it had consented to the transfer of his registration as a
salesman from Burns to the Daly company.

At a meeting of the Board of Directors of the Daly company
held on January 6th (see ex. 145), one hundred shares of the
common stock of the company, representing approximately a 5%
interest, were transferred to the plaintiff and he was
appointed as one of its directors, subject to the approval of
the Exchange.  On the same day, a shareholders' agreement was
executed by all of the shareholders of the company, which inter
alia, required Mr. Posluns to sell his shares to the other
shareholders in the event of his "death, retirement or
dismissal ... from active participation in the business of R.A.
Daly & Company Limited ..." The plaintiff stated in his
evidence that at the time of the signing of this agreement
there was an arrangement with the senior directors of Dalys
that if things worked out well in the future, he would be able
at least to double his interest in the company in the next few
years.  This statement is somewhat borne out by the contents of
the minutes of a meeting of the Baord of Directors of the Daly
firm held on November 25, 1959 (ex. 143) prior to the
commencement of the plaintiff's association with that company.
A further eight treasury shares were issued to Mr. Posluns on
May 27, 1960.

By letter dated January 13, 1960 (ex. 45) the Stock Exchange
informed the Daly firm that its Board of Governors had approved
the admission of the plaintiff as a new shareholder and
director of the Daly firm, but there was never any specific
approval by the Exchange of his employment by Dalys as a
customers' man.

The plaintiff served as commission salesman at Dalys and also
commenced to work on underwriting.  His rate of commission on
transactions effected by his customers was one-third of the
commission paid on United States listed stock traded on the New
York Stock Exchange and 50% in the case of over-the-counter
stocks.  Because he was a director of the Daly firm he received
50% of the commission on Canadian stock trades as opposed to
the usual customers'-man rate of 33 1/3%.

Once the plaintiff commenced his employment with Dalys, Lido
ceased selling its options to Burns and, following a short
transitional period, began to employ the Daly company in
connection with the sale of Lido options in New York.  For that
purpose Dalys completed arrangements with Alfred F. Vanden
Broeck and Company, a member of the New York Stock Exchange, to
have the Vaden Broeck firm endorse all options that were sold
in New York by Lido and other customers of Dalys.

IV THE LYNCH-DALY-LIDO OPERATIONS

Prior to the commencement of 1960, while Lido sold options in
inter-listed stocks, the options were those which it, itself,
originated; it did not act as a middleman. In 1960 an important
change in its operations took place for Lido then commenced
buying on a heavy scale options on U.S. stock, that is, stocks
exclusively listed on U.S. exchanges.  The business of Lido
accordingly became one of trading options, the buying of
options on U.S. stocks in Canada and the selling of identical
options in the U.S.  A report compiled by the Stock Exchange
examiner in April 1961 (ex. 181) and a schedule drawn by the
defendant Exchange for the purposes of the trial (ex. 72),
disclosed certain facts with respect to the source from which
Lido acquired the options which it resold in the U.S., the
number of options purchased from that source, and the number of
options sold by Lido in the U.S. In the period from January,
1960 to January, 1961, Lido sold 917 U.S. stock options in the
U.S., employing in each case the Daly firm as its intermediary
to effect the sale.

During this relevant period the only other major seller of
U.S. stock options was one John Lynch, a Peterborough druggist.
In addition to having other outside activities, Mr. Lynch
became interested in securities in 1947 from which time until
the collapse of his operations in that field in February, 1961,
he dealt with many brokers.  Without relying on any particular
person for advice, he apparently made substantial profits and
at one time had a credit of $250,000 with his bank.

Mr. Lynch testified that he first met the plaintiff in 1959
when the latter was employed at Burns at which time Mr. Lynch
was dealing with Mr. Curry, a customers' man of that firm.  He
said that Mr. Curry told him that the plaintiff was an expert
in puts and calls and that he thereupon had a conversation with
Mr. Posluns concerning the option business and informed him
that he owned shares in Provo Gas.  The plaintiff stated,
according to Mr. Lynch, that he would see what price he could
pay for an option on Provo and eventually Mr. Lynch did sell a
straight call option on Provo to Burns which in turn resold the
same option to Lido for the same premium.  During that year,
Mr. Lynch sold three additional options to Burns.

During 1960, Mr. Lynch employed both the Daly firm and
Doherty Roadhouse as his brokers to effect the sales of his
U.S. stock options.  The following figures, while perhaps not
completely accurate, are sufficiently correct to indicate the
scope of the sales transactions put through by both Mr. Lynch
and Lido:

Of 917 options sold by Lido in New York, 499 originated with
Mr. Lynch, and as to the balance, a number were acquired from
other sellers, and the remainder apparently originated with
Lido. One of the major issues in this case concerns the fact
that the plaintiff, while a director of Dalys, participated in
the profits earned by Lido, on options purchased by Lido from
Mr. Lynch, a client of Dalys, which options were subsequently
resold by Lido in New York at a greater price than was paid to
Mr. Lynch.  That being so, the Board of Governors of the
Exchange felt obliged to decide whether the plaintiff, as a
director of Dalys, violated any duty that he owed to Mr. Lynch
for whom the Daly firm acted as agent in selling his options to
Lido.  In order to fully determine whether the plaintiff was in
fact guilty of any improper conduct with respect to Mr. Lynch,
it is necessary to examine closely the mechanics of the
transactions conducted by the Daly firm.

The two major put and call brokers in New York to whom Dr.
Shulman sold the Lido options were the same dealers with whom
transactions had been conducted while the plaintiff was at
Burns, namely, Mr. Kleinberg at Thomas Habbs & Botts, and Mr.
Bergman at Filer Schmidt.  In order that a U.S. stock option
could be sold in New York, the reverse side of the contract
document embodying the option had to be endorsed by a member
firm of the New York Exchange.  An option written or guaranteed
or endorsed by a member of our Exchange would not suffice. It
was the custom in the put and call trade in New York for the
member firm which endorsed the option to receive from the
purchasing put and call dealer, as a consideration for so
doing, a "signatory fee" of $6.25 or multiples thereof,
depending upon how many options were involved.  For example, a
signatory fee of $12.50 was payable on straddles (which
consisted of two options) and $18.75 on strips and straps.  The
arrangement made by Mr. Robb, the vice-president and director
of the Daly company, who handled its stock trading, with Vaden
Broeck, was as follows:  An arbitrage account already in
existence for use of the two firms was to be employed as a
joint account for purposes of option sales in New York.  The
general principle in the operation of the joint account was
that the Daly firm, acting as agent for the Toronto option
seller (either Mr. Lynch or Lido) would complete a sale of the
option to a New York put and call dealer such as Thomas Habbs
& Botts or Filer Schmidt, for a certain price.  The New York
put and call dealer would pay into the joint account the price
plus the $6.25 signatory fee for each option included in the
transaction.  The joint account would then credit its Toronto
seller with the equivalent of the price only, the signatory fee
remaining in the joint account to be divided between Dalys and
Vanden Broeck.  In order for Vanden Broeck to guarantee these
options, the joint account required a considerable amount of
margin as security for the performance of the obligations of
the seller of the option.  The Daly firm accordingly put up
funds or security in New York with Vanden Broeck, as its share
of the margin in the joint account.  The remainder apparently
was furnished by Vaden Broeck itself. Dalys in turn obtained
the funs via loan from either Lido or one of two corporations,
Cross Country Investments Limited or Irving Posluns Sportswear,
with which the plaintiff was associated.  Lido, in addition to
putting up cash with the Daly firm, would also place securities
as part of its margin requirements with the latter which would
pay interest to Lido, and the two hereinbefore-mentioned
associated corporations of Mr. Posluns, on the amount of the
loans outstanding. The cost of this interest was not charged
back to Lido but was borne by the Daly firm itself.  Mr.
Posluns stated in evidence, probably correctly, that the funds
enabled the Daly firm to operate a put and call business in New
York; not just Lido's business with respect thereto, but also
the transactions concerning the Lynch options sold by Dalys,
acting as agent for Mr. Lynch in New York.

The vast majority of the Lido options sold in New York to the
put and call brokers in New York were negotiated directly by
Dr. Shulman with the particular broker. There is some evidence
which would lead me to think that in only 37 of the 917 sales
of Lido options in New York, did the Daly firm itself negotiate
the sale of the Lido option to the New York put and call
broker.  (See ex. 181, p. 2, third last paragraph.)  However,
in all cases of Lido option sales in New York, the transaction
was handled through the joint account.  Mr. Kleinberg of Thomas
Habbs & Botts testified that in the majority of his dealings
with Dr. Shulman, the initiating telephone call was made by Mr.
Kleinberg in order to purchase an option from Lido.  He would
ask Dr. Shulman for prices on options on certain stock and
generally the transaction would be completed on the one call.
On occasion, Mr. Kleinberg would quote a price that he would be
willing to pay for an option on a particular U.S. stock and Dr.
Shulman would ask him to keep the price firm for a short period
of time.  Dr. Shulman would subsequently return the telephone
call to Mr. Kleinberg, either accepting the offer or refusing
it.

After receiving a call from a New York put and call dealer
wherein a sale of a Lido option was completed, or wherein a
firm offer had been submitted to Lido by the New York put and
call dealer, Dr. Shulman would telephone either a Mr. Gordon
Wiley (the customers' man at Dalys who dealt with Mr. Lynch) or
one of two men at Doherty Roadhouse, Mr. Low or Mr. O'Connor.
Taking the Daly transactions first, Dr. Shulman would quote to
Mr. Wiley a lesser price than the agreed sale price of the
option to the New York put and call broker, or the price quoted
to him by the New York put and call broker, in the event of an
offer and not a completed sale in New York.  The quotation made
by Dr. Shulman would, of course, be on the same U.S. stock and
on the same terms.  A transaction would subsequently be
consummated with Mr. Wiley whereby an option was sold by the
Daly firm acting as an agent for a seller, to Lido.  In those
instances where Dr. Shulman had received a firm bid from New
York but no transaction had been completed, he would thereupon
call New York to accept the offer previously made to him.

Dr. Shulman stated that on a number of occasions he would
quote to Dalys (or to Doherty Roadhouse if he were dealing with
them on the particular occasion) a higher price than had been
submitted to him by the New York broker.  This might occur if
the New York broker gave Dr. Shulman a price which the latter
considered to be too low, and knowing that the New York dealer
wished such an option, he would call Dalys (or Doherty
Roadhouse) and quote a higher price in order to get a firm
offer.  Once a firm offer was received at the higher price, Dr.
Shulman would telephone New York and state that Lido could not
sell at the lower price first submitted but would sell at a
price which was equal to the price to be paid to the Toronto
broker, plus the price of two brokerage commissions, plus a 10%
profit for Lido.  A deal would then be negotiated.

When a New York put and call broker purchased an option from
Lido, the following would occur:  The put and call broker would
telephone Vanden Broeck to inform the latter that for the
account of the Daly company, the latter were selling to the
broker a particular option at a particular price.  Vanden
Broeck would then advise Dalys of the transaction, whereupon
Dalys would communicate with Dr. Shulman to ascertain if Dr.
Shulman had in fact sold such an option to a put and call
broker in New York.  He or his secretary, Mrs. Jones, would
confirm to Dalys the fact that such a transaction had been
consummated and Dalys would in turn confirm the transaction
over the teletype wire to Vaden Broeck in New York, which would
then endorse the option and put the contract document through
to the put and call broker. Mr. Lynch was charged a commission
by Dalys on his sales to Lido, at the rate of 50% of the rate
applicable to the stock involved for each option included in
the contract.  In the case of Lido, commissions were charged to
it by the Daly firm on purchases at a nominal rate (generally
$5 to $20) except for a few trades at the commencement of
operations when commissions were taken at the same rate as for
Mr. Lynch.  On the 313 transactions at the Daly firm between
Mr. Lynch and Lido, the fomer was charged 5.5% commission on
the sales, and Lido paid 1.1% commission on the purchases.  On
a subsequent sale of the option to a New York broker, or in
fact on any sale by Lido of an option in New York, Lido was not
charged any commission whatever.

On each transaction involving the acquisition of an option,
Lido would receive a contract confirmation slip showing that
the Daly firm had purchased that particular option as an agent
for Lido.  When that option was sold in New York by Lido, a
different contract document was guaranteed by the New York
Stock Exchange member, Vaden Broeck & Co.

Exhibit 181 would indicate that with two exceptions all the
Lido stock options that were acquired through the Doherty
Roadhouse firm, were in fact purchased from Mr. Lynch as
seller.

The manner in which those options were acquired through that
firm and subsequently disposed of in New York City, did not
differ substantially from that employed when the Daly firm
acted for Mr. Lynch.  However, there were two important
differences. In the first place, Doherty Roadhouse, rather than
acting as agent for Mr. Lynch, purchased the options from him
as principal and resold them as such to Lido, the differential
between what was paid by Doherty Roadhouse for those options
and the price at which they were resold being that firm's
profit in the transactions.

A second dissimilarity arose because of Mr. Lynch's
unwillingness to furnish security other than in the form of
bank guarantees which were unacceptable to the put and call
brokers in New York City.  Because of that, Doherty Roadhouse,
feeling that the Lynch U.S. options could only be sold to Lido,
did not endeavour to obtain a price for them elsewhere.  Mr.
Lavender, the Toronto Stock Exchange examiner, stated that in
his examination of the Doherty Roadhouse books, in only two
cases did he find that Mr. Lynch had put up cash as security so
that the options could be sold in the United States.
Presumably all of the other Lynch U.S. options were sold to
Lido. On the other hand, of the total 569 options which it
disposed of on behalf of Mr. Lynch, the Daly firm sold 256 of
them to New York put and call brokers.  The balance of 313 was,
of course, sold by it directly to Lido.  The 256 Lynch options
sold by Dalys to New York put and call brokers, were all
endorsed by Vaden Broeck & Company and were transacted through
the medium of the joint account, and, later, to a lesser
extent, also through another account known as the Toronto
Office Option Account, opened by Mr. Robb and operated much in
the same way as the arbitrage account.  The evidence would
appear to indicate that Mr. Lynch did not put up any additional
security with Dalys for the sale of those options in New York
and certainly he had no direct contact with the New York put
and call brokers.  The sales of his options in New York were
negotiated on his behalf by Dalys or Vanden Broeck.  However,
Mr. Lavender pointed out that since the Daly firm kept credits
in U.S. dollars with Vanden Broeck in New York, if Mr. Lynch
had any credits in U.S. funds they would help to margin the
joint account in New York.

Mr. Posluns testified that he assumed on those occasions when
the Daly firm sold options in New York directly, they must have
done so because they were obtaining better prices in New York
than from Dr. Shulman.  He further stated that Mr. Wiley always
checked New York City before asking Dr. Shulman for his prices,
but, of course, his evidence in that regard as well as that of
R. Bredin Stapells, Esq., Q.C., the Daly firm solicitor, and of
Dr. Shulman, was hearsay since Mr.Wiley, who was the only
individual who could have stated what he did in the matter of
checking prices in New York or elsewhere, did not testify.
However, Mr. Wiley did give that information to the Board of
Governors on February 28, 1961, as will be explained later.

On sales of Lynch options in New York by Dalys, the joint
account received the signatory fee of $6.25 per option and in
addition the Daly firm charged Lynch with a commission on the
sales effected by Dalys on his behalf.

In addition to the commissions payable to brokers on the
purchase and sale of options in the manner described above,
there were also commissions payable on the exercise of an
option.  For example, if the New York purchaser of a call sold
by Lido through Dalys exercised that call against Lido, Lido
would be required to sell the stock at the option price to the
New York purchaser.  Since this would amount to a sale of
stock, Lido was obliged to pay commissions to Dalys for the
sale of stock consummated on the exercise of the option.  If
Lido had purchased that call from Mr. Lynch via Dalys acting as
agent. Lido in turn would exercise the call against Mr. Lynch,
and, accordingly, Lido would purchase the stock at the
particular option price.  Lido would again pay commission to
Dalys for the purchase of stock upon the exercise of its option
against Mr. Lynch as the seller.  On such a transaction the
latter in turn would be required to pay brokerage commission to
Dalys upon the sale of the stock to Lido when Lido exercised
its option against Mr. Lynch.  In the case of an option
acquired by Lido from Doherty Roadhouse, the evidence was not
very clear as to whether Lido was required to pay brokerage
commission to Doherty Roadhouse when Lido exercised an option
against Mr. Lynch.

V THE WITNESSES

I propose to discuss briefly the probable extent of the
knowledge of the operations possessed by the persons who were
involved, but before doing so I should comment generally upon
my appraisal of the various persons who appeared as witnesses.

With several possible exceptions, all were persons of deep
probity who were honestly endeavouring to recall at the trial
what had occurred and to pass on their information accurately.
Leaving aside for the moment the plaintiff, Dr. Shulman and Mr.
Lynch, that description would apply to all of the witnesses who
testified, however unimportant their respective roles.  While
there were small discrepancies in some of their answers, I came
to feel that in the main I could trust what they said.  That
observation extends, of course, to the members of the Board of
Governors of the Exchange and its officers, each of whom
appeared to me to have acted in good faith with reasonable
care, fairly, and with a sincere desire to do what was
fundamentally, right, not only for the public but also for the
plaintiff.  They may have made mistakes in judgment, but they
cannot otherwise be criticized.

During the course of the trial, there were some things said
which could only be interpreted as suggesting that the minds of
the Governors and those officers had been infected by a wish to
discriminate against the plaintiff for racial reasons (he is a
Jew, I believe) or simply to hurt him.  Let me say that so far
as I am concerned those imputations were utterly groundless.

Except in several respects the plaintiff himself was, in my
mind, a reasonably reliable witness.  He is an extremely able
man who bears a fine reputation.  As a witness he can be
disparaged only on the issues as to the depth of his knowledge
of the Lido operations and the extent of his contacts with Mr.
Lynch, already discussed.  That Dr. Shulman was the principal
actor in Lido's daily operations is not to be denied; but I
could not at the trial, and do not now, as will be shortly
explained, believe that Mr. Posluns, with his education, his
familiarity with the brokerage business generally, and his
special training and interest in the put and call phase of it,
his association with the Daly company, and with a huge personal
and representative financial stake in the partnership, would be
as ignorant about the Lido operations as he would have had me
think.  Nor was he as removed from Mr. Lynch as he pretended.

The testimony of the other two witnesses who have been
singled out is not easy to evaluate.  Unquestionably, Dr.
Shulman is blessed with a brilliant and facile mind.  However,
his performance as a witness probably suffered because of being
so endowed, for at times he responded so quickly as to invite
the notion that he was too glib to be entirely truthful.  On
occasions he certainly contradicted himself, perhaps for that
very reason, or perhaps he did not stop to consider his answers
before making them, and I came to the conclusion that where his
evidence was found to be in conflict with that of a calm but
reflecting witness, I should accept that of the latter.

Mr. Lynch was, in my opinion, the witness who most frequently
strayed from the path of truth.  He is an able, cheerful
extrovert with a large measure of irresponsibility in his
system.  On the stand he showed a superficial inclination to
agree with anything suggested to him unless he sensed danger in
doing so and then he became inordinately cautious.  His
evidence was so riddled with changes and small contradictions
that in the end I decided that I should put very little faith
in those parts of it which were incompatible with the testimony
of other witnesses.

This much can certainly be said:  There is little doubt that
when testifying those three named persons were more likely to
be motivated by self-interest or a desire for self-
justification than any of the other witnesses.

VI THE KNOWLEDGE OF THE PARTIES INVOLVED

By the middle of 1960, Dr. Shulman knew all that was being
done.  He testified that in the period of January to May 1960
the plaintiff told him that Mr. Lynch was a seller of many of
the options bought by Lido.  At that point of time Lido had not
yet commenced to acquire U.S. options from Doherty Roadhouse.
Dr. Shulman further admitted that he had been informed by Mr.
Wiley and the plaintiff that most of the American options
purchased by Lido from Dalys in the year 1960 were being sold
by Mr. Lynch.  With respect to the options acquired by Lido
from Doherty Roadhouse, a subsequent quirk of fate put Dr.
Shulman on notice that Mr. Lynch was at least one of the
sellers, if not the only seller, of options via Doherty
Roadhouse, although prior to that time that firm had been very
careful to conceal the identity of the seller. Dr. Shulman
further admitted that by September, 1960, he knew that a great
many of the options that he was buying from Dalys and Doherty
Roadhouse were being sold by Mr. Lynch.  Indeed, I would be
inclined to think that he knew in the summer that virtually all
of the options being acquired from those two firms were
originating with Mr. Lynch.

By early fall of 1960, Dr. Shulman had completed the purchase
of some options directly from Mr. Lynch.  He said that the
transactions were few in number and were usually initiated by
Mr. Lynch, adding, however, that all the trades were put
through a broker.  Mr. Lynch, on the other hand, swore that Dr.
Shulman called him with respect to option transactions at a
rate of about 20 or 25 times a month for several months, and
that invariably it was the doctor who made the telephone call.
I am inclined to think, however, that Mr. Lynch launched more
trades than he was prepared to admit and that the number of
transactions which the two men negotiated directly was
somewhere between Dr. Shulman's figure and Mr. Lynch's figure.

It was on the question of how much Mr. Lynch knew and in
particular whether he was aware of the fact that Lido was
reselling the options it acquired from him at a profit in New
York that the major conflict in the testimony arose.  Dr.
Shulman testified that the druggist had knowledge of the fact
that Dr. Shulman acquired those options on behalf of Lido for
the purpose of reselling at a greater price in New York and
that Mr. Lynch appreciated that many of those options were sold
off in New York prior to having been acquired by Lido from Mr.
Lynch.  The latter denied such knowledge, his evidence being to
the effect that while he knew Lido was making a profit upon the
disposition of his options in New York, he always believed that
Dr. Shulman was acting as an agent for a New York put and call
broker and accordingly obtained his profit by way of
commissions from those New York brokers.  He swore that he had
no idea that Lido were reselling the options at an increased
price in New York.  Once again, I think that the truth lies
somewhere in the middle.  I cannot accept the idea that Dr.
Shulman was as explicit with Mr. Lynch as he indicated at the
trial, nor do I believe that Mr. Lynch was as much in the dark
about the machinations of Lido as he purported to be.  His
statements contained in ex. 192 would suggest the contrary, as
would the evidence of Mr. O'Connor who, though not recalling a
specific converstion, said:  "I am sure Lynch was made aware of
this by me", namely, that some of the options were being sold
in New York.  However, I am bound to add that there can be no
question but that Mr. Lynch was quite confused as to some of
the particulars of the way in which the transactions were being
handled.

Unquestionably, Mr. Lynch knew from the outset that Mr.
Posluns was a partner in the Lido business and was a director
of the Daly company.  Nor can there be any doubt that he was
perfectly satisfied with Mr. Wiley's services to him and that
he was aware that Mr. Wiley had checked option prices in New
York before dealing with Dr. Shulman.

I turn now to the plaintiff's state of knowledge.  The
evidence is rather unsatisfactory as to the date in the year
1960 when he realized that Dalys were selling options on behalf
of Mr. Lynch and the date when he came to know that the options
sold by Doherty Roadhouse to Lido were coming from the same
source.

Dr. Shulman told us that some time in the period from January
to May, 1960, the plaintiff informed him that Mr. Lynch was the
seller of the options being bought by Lido through Dalys and on
his examination for discovery Mr. Posluns fixed the time as
being in February of that year.  However, he also swore that it
was not until August 5th that he came to know that Mr. Lynch
was also selling options directly to New York through the Daly
company, and that about the same time he was told by Dr.
Shulman that the doctor had dealt directly with Mr. Mr. Lynch
with respect to options.

From the time that he commenced at Dalys until shortly after
April, 1960, the plaintiff obtained day sheets from Lido
showing the transactions conducted by Lido.  Those sheets
disclosed, for example, the sale of an option in New York, the
purchase in Toronto and the spread taken.  However, by looking
at them the plaintiff would not have been able to know who the
seller was, or it it was Mr. Lynch.  He said he never ccecked
the Lido margin requirements against the daily sheets of the
Daly firm and that he did not know that Dr. Shulman was
immediately selling off options in New York.  In the light of
the other information placed at his disposal by Dr. Shulman, I
would decline to believe that statement.

Mr. Posluns also swore that he was aware that Mr. Wiley
always checked New York before dealing with Dr. Shulman to make
sure that he obtained the best price for Mr. Lynch and that he
assumed that when Dalys sold options in New York it did so
because they could get better prices there than from Dr.
Shulman.

He admitted that in 1960 he knew that Mr. Lynch was operating
through the Daly company by means of bank guarantees and that
Mr. Robb had disclosed to him that Lido was buying Lynch
options and had described the manner in which they were being
traded or sold.  He knew, for example, about the joint
arbitrage account of Dalys and Vaden Broeck, of the
differential in premiums paid and received by Lido, and that
options were bought from Doherty Roadhouse and through Dalys
and that similar options were resold in New York.

At the trial, the plaintiff stated that while at the Daly
firm he had nothing to do with any of the Lynch transactions
although conceding that during 1960 he may have spoken to that
gentleman once or twice.  Mr. Lynch countered by saying that
during the course of the transactions conducted by him through
the Daly firm he had many communications with the plaintiff,
although those communications with the plaintiff, althougn
those communications were not as numerous as the ones he had
with Dr. Shulman.  Once again, Mr. Lynch's evidence was tainted
by his propensity to exaggerate but I believe that there is
some truth in what he said on this point, particularly as the
plaintiff conceded at one stage that while once or twice Mr.
Lynch did attempt to quote him a premium, in those instances he
always put Mr. Lynch on to somebody else at the Daly firm.

In the light of all the evidence I am entirely satisfied that
Mr. Posluns knew nearly as much, if not as much, as Dr. Shulman
about the nature of the Lynch-Daly-Lido dealings and their
consequences to all those who were involved in them. Turning
now to the others at the Daly firm, it would be my view that,
with the exception of Mr. Robb, the plaintiff would certainly
know more about those transactions than any other director or
officer.  Indeed, those gentlemen had scant appreciation of
what was really being done.  On the other hand, Mr. Robb
probably was as informed as Mr. Posluns about that end of the
business and in one respect possessed more knowledge.  I have
in mind, of course, that Mr. Robb must have realized that
spreads were being improperly taken against the clients by the
Daly firm in the New York option account and subsequently in
the Toronto office option account which he caused to be opened.
I think that Mr. Posluns was ignorant of that.

Whatever other knowlege the Daly directors had, they must, of
course, be assumed to have been familiar with the
correspondence with the Audit Committee of the Exchange in
February and March of 1960 (exs. 1,2, 3 and 4).  Further
reference to that correspondence will be made later on.

Similarly, the officers of the Exchange had whatever
information is contained in the exhibits to which I have just
alluded.  The Audit Committee consisted of three governors and
at the relevant time was composed of Messrs. Lailey, Scott and
Gardiner.  In addition, the executive vice-president of the
Exchange.  Mr. Somerville, testified that about the time that
Mr. Posluns went to the Daly firm, he, Mr. Somerville, became
aware of Lido and that the plaintiff had an interest in it.
However, he said that he did not know at that time that Dalys
were transacting business for Lido.

During the second fiscal period of Lido, running from June 1,
1959 to May 31, 1960, a net loss was incurred by it of
$33,693.81.  This period included the last eight months of the
plaintiff's employment at Burns and the first four months of
his association with the Daly firm.

Exhibit 71, being a schedule prepared by the Stock Exchange,
discloses the amount of premiums paid out monthly by Lido upon
the acquisition of options sold by Mr. Lynch through both
Doherty and Daly.  Those figures show a decided increase each
month from June, 1960 to the end of the calendar year. For
example, according to that exhibit, Lido paid $20,302.12 for
Lynch options in the month of June and increasing amounts until
December when it paid $118,965.  In January, 1961, that which
was paid out came to about $98,000. For the fiscal year, June
1, 1960, to May 31, 1961, Lido Investments earned a net profit
of $103,761.87, but it is to be remembered that it traded in
stocks as well as in stock options, and as to the latter, it
bought and sold not only options pertaining to American stocks
but also those with respect to Canadian stocks.  Thus, the
profit earned in the year just referred to may have been
attributable to any or a combination of two or more of the
partnerships' activities.

It was given in evidence that in his capacity as a customers'
man of the Daly company, the plaintiff earned, by way of
commissions in 1960, the sum of $60,844.17, and in that part of
1961, while still with that company, the sum of $19,892.26. He
stated that he believed that he received 50% of the commissions
earned by the Daly firm on options exercised in New York
against Lido and that approximately one-half of all of his
commissions while at Dalys were attributable to the Lido
business.

VII EVENTS LEADING UP TO FEBRUARY 28, 1961

The options which Mr. Lynch sold through Doherty Roadhouse
and Dalys had been secured with those firms by means of bank
guarantees executed by the local branches of two banks at
Peterborough.  In January of 1961 the head offices of both
banks decided to stop the practice.  Because there were a
number of options sold by Mr. Lynch which, owing to a time
interval between the moment of sale and the time of submission
of the guarantees to his local bank branches had not yet been
guaranteed by the two banks, the Daly and Doherty Roadhouse
firms having sold the options on behalf of Mr. Lynch would have
been liable to the purchasers thereof in the event that Mr.
Lynch could not perform his obligations in respect of those
options.

The first inkling that the Toronto Stock Exchange received of
any difficulties concerning the put and call option  business
arose when Mr. Somerville received telephone calls first from
John Rogers of the Doherty Roadhouse firm and then from Mr.
Robb of the Daly company early in February, 1961, at which time
he was informed that if the two banks did not honour the
guarantees given to Mr. Lynch, their respective firms would
suffer serious financial losses.  General Graham, the president
of the Exchange, and Mr. Somerville, met with Messrs. R.A.
Daly, Jr., and Mr. Robb on February 9th, following which Mr.
Lavender was instructed to examine the records of both Dalys
and Doherty Roadhouse to check their respective capital
positions.  Mr. Lavender proceeded to do that with respect to
the Daly company on either February 9th or 10th.  On February
13th, General Graham and W.M. Wismer, an Exchange vice-
president, met with representatives of the two banks to
discuss the question of the liabilities of the banks with
respect to the Lynch guarantees.  In passing, perhaps I should
add that while there was some doubt at first whether the banks
would honour the guarantees, they soon agreed to do so.

On the morning of February 14th, Mr. Lavender returned to the
Daly offices to look at its records of some Lynch and Lido
option transactions.  He decided to examine the relevant
records for the first part of December, 1960, and in doing so
observed that there appeared to be identical options being
bought and sold on the same day by Lido which options seemed to
be the same as those sold by Mr. Lynch.  Copies of the records
of those transactions were obtained from the Daly firm by Mr.
Lavender who thereupon reported on the same day to the Board of
Governors who were then in the midst of a meeting.  It was
there decided that the vice-chairman of the Board, Mr.
Gardiner, the secretary, Mr. Stearns, who was also another
governor, and General Graham, should meet with representatives
of the Daly company on the following day.  At his meeting of
the Board apparently no mention was made of the plaintiff.

On February 15th, the following day, Mr. R.A. Daly, Jr.,
Colonel Christie, the president of the Daly firm, Mr. Robb and
the plaintiff were interviewed by General Graham, Mr. Gardiner
and Mr. Stearns.  Mr. Gardiner asked a number of questions of
Mr. Robb and the plaintiff as to the put and call operations of
both Dalys and Doherty Roadhouse and in his evidence at the
trial Mr. Stearns stated that the plaintiff was questioned on
the manner in which Lido operated. He further gave in evidence
that it was apparent that Mr. Lynch, a client of Dalys, was
selling the major part, if not all, of his options to Lido
which Lido subsequently resold and generally that the Daly firm
had been acting for Mr. Lynch in connection with the sale of
many of his options.  Most of these transactions had been
guaranteed by one bank.  The guarantees were obtained in the
following manner:  Dalys, after selling an option on behalf of
Mr. Lynch, would forward to him a letter (see for example exs.
5 and 6) employing in the case of the sale of a put the
following words:

For value received, you have agreed to buy from us 200 shares
American Motors at $23 3/4 per share U.S. Funds at any time
within 96 days, expiring November 21, 1960.

Such language, of course, indicated that the Daly firm was
acting as a principal in its dealings with Mr. Lynch in that it
refers to a purchase and sale of a put option between them.
The letter further requested Mr. Lynch to sign an enclosed copy
of the letter to signify that the particulars of the agreement
were correct, and also stated:

As the regulations of the Toronto Stock Exchange require us
to have the delivery of a transaction of this nature
guaranteed by the vendor's bank, we would appreciate it if
you would also have your bankers endorse the statement on the
enclosed copy.

At the bottom of the letter there was space for Mr. Lynch's
signature confirming the particulars, and for a guarantee to be
executed by the bank at Peterborough in the following form:

In the event that the option referred to herein is exercised
by R.A. Daly and Company Limited we hereby guarantee to
accept delivery of 200 shares American Motors against payment
of $4750.00 U.S. funds less any contract price adjustment.

As already noted, although the form of the letter referred to
implied that the Daly firm was acting as a principal, the
confirmations subsequently sent out by it to Mr. Lynch were in
the usual brokerage form and indicated that the firm was acting
as an agent and was charging Mr. Lynch commissions on the
transactions.

At that meeting the representatives of the Exchange also
learned of the particulars of the plaintiff's association with
the Daly company, that he had a one-sixth interest in Lido and
that it was to Lido that a great number of Lynch options were
sold. On his examination for discovery Mr. Somerville, through
his counsel, related that General Graham stated that it was
also learned that Lido "laid-off", meaning that it immediately
sold, the whole or part of those options or, alternatively,
retained and exercised them, in each case profiting form the
transactions, that plaintiff know of the Lido-Daly-Lynch
operation and stated at the meeting that he received statements
regularly from Lido indicating that those operations were
profitable.

After the conclusion of the meeting General Graham prepared a
memorandum concerning that which had occurred (ex. 9) which
contained a paragraph, number 9, suggesting that "... it was
the custom for R.A. Daly to sell most, if not all, of the said
option contracts to Lido ..." On his examination for discovery,
Mr. Somerville conceded that that paragraph was inaccurate in
its suggestion that "all" of the Lynch option contracts were
sold to Lido.

Paragraph 11 of the memorandum stated:

It is probable that at least in some of the Daly-Lynch
transactions Lynch knew that "Shulman" was a purchaser, but
there is not evidence to indicate that he knew that Posluns
was interested in the sale of options.

In his evidence at trial, General Graham stated that while that
paragraph was accurate when it was written, subsequent
information revealed that Mr. Lynch was aware that the
plaintiff had an interest in Lido.

The memorandum went on to set out a possible course of action
for the Board of Governors to adopt.

On the following day, February 16th, a meeting of the Board
was convened and was presided over by the vice-chairman, Mr.
Gardiner.  At it, those present were either handed copies of
ex. 9, or it was read out to them.  In any event, the Board
decided that another meeting should be held on Tuesday,
February 28th, to decide whether or not R.A. Daly, Jr., the
member of the Exchange for the Daly company, was guilty of any
offence under the by-laws or rulings of the Exchange.

On the morning of February 20th, Colonel Christie, the
president of the Daly firm, telephoned General Graham to advise
him that his firm would like an "airing" as soon as possible
before the Board.  He was then told that a hearing would be
held on February 28th.  Colonel Christie informed the General
that the plaintiff had mentioned that he wished to leave on a
holiday in Mexico on February 27th.  General Graham advised
Colonel Christie that Mr. Posluns would be expected to be at
the Board meeting on February 28th and the Colonel said that he
would inform Mr. Posluns that he had to remain in Toronto for
that purpose.  He did so.

About the same time, General Graham, with the assistance of
Allan Graydon, Esq., Q.C., who was and is counsel for the
Exchange, prepared a notice of the hearing to be held on
February 28th which set forth the charges of improper conduct
alleged against the Daly firm. The notice was given pursuant to
By-law 11, s. 1, which read as follows:

Sec. 1.  If any member shall be adjudged by the Board of
Governors guilty of a violation of any of the By-Laws or
Rules or Regulations of the Corporation, or of failure to
obey or conform to any decision of the Corporation of the
Board, or of any conduct, proceeding or method of business
which the Board in their absolute discretion deem unbecoming
a member of the Exchange, or inconsistent with just and
equitable principles of trade, or detrimental to the
interests of the Exchange; -- the Board may impose any one or
more of the following penalties, viz.:  (1) a fine not
exceeding $5,000, (2) suspension for such period or periods
and upon such conditions if any as the Board may determine,
and (3) expulsion; and, in addition thereto, may declare
forfeit the seat and membership of any member expelled.

The notice was addressed to R.A. Daly, Jr., c/o R.A. Daly
& Co. Limited, 44 King Street West, Toronto, Ontario, rather
than to the firm itself, because Mr. Daly is the actual member
of the Exchange.  By-law No. 11, s. 2 provided:

Sec. 2.  A member shall be fully responsible for the acts and
omissions of his employees, and if he carries on business as
a member firm for the acts and omissions of his partners and
the employees of such member firm, and if he carries on
business as a member corporation for the acts and omissions
of the directors, officers and employees of such member
corporation...

Accordingly, Mr. Daly would be responsible for any acts of his
firm that might be held to be improper and any penalty would
likewise be imposed upon him personally.

The notice served upon Mr. Daly (ex. 12) is so important to
the issues involved in this case that I here reproduce the body
of it in full:

The notice was delivered to R.A. Daly, Jr. and Colonel Christie
on the afternoon of February 22nd.

Prior to the actual hearing on February 28th, General Graham
prepared a memorandum for the use of the chairman of the Board
of Governors, Mr. Scott, as to the procedure to be followed at
the hearing (ex. 14).  It was as follows:
