Another memorandum (ex. 16) was drawn up for the use of Mr.
Gardiner setting forth the fact that the meeting had been held
on February 15th and outlining the information gained at such
meeting.  It read in this way:

On February 15th, in response to a request of the Board of
Governors, Mr. R.A. Daly, Jr., Col. Christie, Mr. Robb and
Mr. Posluns of R.A. Daly & Co. Limited, came here and were
interviewed by the President, myself and Marshal Stearns.  As
a result of this interview, we learned a number of things:

First, that R.A. Daly & Co. Limited had been acting for Mr.
John T. Lynch of Peterborough in connection with a large
number of "put" and "call" transactions.

Second, that most, if not all, of these transactions had
been guaranteed by the Imperial Bank of Canada at
Peterborough. The guarantee was not under seal and was in the
form of a note at the foot of a letter.

Third, from the form of letters which had been sent by Daly
to Lynch, it appeared to us that Daly was acting as a
principal; however, we learned that confirmations were sent
by Daly to Lynch which indicated that Daly was actually
acting as Lynch's agent and was charging Lynch commissions on
these transactions.

Fourth, we learned that, on and after about January 14th,
Lynch had not received this form of guarantee from the bank,
although Daly had, in fact, put through a considerable number
of transactions between January 14th and about January 24th.
It could not be said, therefore, that these transactions were
margined, and we learned that, with regard to these, Daly
could be expected to take a very considerable loss.

Fifth, we learned that Mr. Posluns was a director of Daly,
and, at the same time, he had a one-sixth interest in a
partnership known as Lido Investments; it was to Lido
Investments that a great number of the Lynch options, which
included "puts", "calls", "strips", "straps" and "straddles",
were sold.

All the above came to our knowledge as a result of
voluntary statements made at the meeting I have referred to.
Copies of the form of letter which Daly had been in the habit
of sending to Lynch, with the signature of Lynch and the
signature of the bank manager, were given to us.

Mr. Stapells had been exposed to the Daly problems concerning
the Lynch options in January and February when he conducted
negotiations with one of the banks involved concerning the
guarantees.  On the evening of February 27th, Mr. Posluns
communicated with Mr. Stapells as to whether or not he should
have his own counsel at the hearing on the following day.  Mr.
Stapells gave in evidence that he believed that the plaintiff
probably also got in touch with him again on the morning of
February 28th.  In any event, Mr. Stapells called Mr.
Somerville of the Exchange and informed him that he had had the
telephone call asking if he, Mr. Stapells, thought that the
plaintiff should be separately represented at the hearing as an
individual and as a director of Dalys.  Mr. Somerville did not
give Mr. Stapells any advice one way or the other on this
point.  However, the latter then advised the plaintiff and his
solicitor, Edwin A. Goodman, Esq., Q.C., that it was to be a
hearing with respect ot the Daly company and that he did not
think that the position of Mr. Posluns was particularly
different from the other directors who, in varying degrees,
bore responsibility for the charges that were facing the firm.

In his preparation for the hearing of February 28th, Mr.
Stapells had instructed the appropriate officers of Dalys to
prepare material reflecting the Lynch-Lido transactions in the
period of December 1st to 15th, that being the period selected
by and known to Mr. Lavender. On the evening of February 27th,
Mr. Stapells examined the schedule prepared for him and noticed
that on transactions put through the New York joint account by
Dalys on behalf of both Lido and Mr. Lynch, the Daly firm had
retained for the benefit of the joint account, a spread, in
addition to the signatory fee to which it was entitled.  In
other words, on a great many of the options that the Daly firm
sold in New York on behalf of both Mr. Lynch and Lido, the
amount of the premium received by the New York joint account on
account of the sale in New York, exceeded the amount credited
to Mr. Lynch and Lido by more than the signatory fee of $6.25
per option.  Neither Mr. Lynch nor Lido, of course, had been
aware that the Daly firm had been retaining for itself a
differential in excess of the signatory fee.  It was
ascertained that Mr. Robb had been in charge of the joint
account and he took responsibility for the spread.  Indeed, he
was the only person who could explain the account to Mr.
Stapells.  At that time the latter concluded that the spread
had arisen because of inadvertence and through an innocent
error by Mr. Robb.  That was the impression given by Mr. Robb
and Mr. Stapells accepted it.

Being men of integrity, the other senior directors of the
Daly company were extremely disturbed.

On the following morning Messrs. R.A. Daly, Jr., Colonel
Christie, Robb and Stapells had an early meeting with General
Graham and Mr. Somerville to explain what they had found, to
ask what should be done about it and to suggest a postponement
of the hearing.  General Graham's reaction was that the fact
should be revealed to the Board of Governors and that there was
no reason to delay the hearing.

VIII

THE HEARING ON FEBRUARY 28, 1961

The hearing conducted on the afternoon of February 28th in
the Board room of the Exchange was far more informal than
ordinary proceedings in a court of law.  For one thing, the
evidence was not under oath, and secondly (and unfortunately),
no shorthand reporter was present to take a verbatim account of
the proceedings. The only notes available are those written by
Mr. Somerville which are somewhat sketchy.

Seven governors were at the hearing -- Messrs. Gardiner,
Lailey, Stearns, Heavenor, Deacon, Funston and Scott, who acted
as chairman.  General Graham, Mr. Somerville, Mr. Graydon and
Mr. Lavender were also present.  On the other side for the Daly
company were its president Colonel Christie, R.A. Daly, Jr.,
Mr. Robb, Mr. Wiley, the plaintiff and Mr. Stapells.

After the meeting was called to order, the memorandum of
procedure (ex. 14) was followed substantially.  As to item
number 4 on that agenda, Mr. Gardiner read the statement, ex.
16, which set out the situation generally as it was then
understood by the officers of the Exchange, and mentioned the
circumstances that, despite indications to the contrary.  Dalys
had in fact been acting as Mr. Lynch's agent in respect to the
option business and charging him a commission, and that Mr.
Posluns had an interest not only in the Daly company but also
in Lido to which a great number of Lynch options were sold by
Dalys.

Mr. Lavender then outlined what had been disclosed by his
investigation at the Daly company and produced certain relevant
documents.  Certainly exs. 6 and 7 were tabled and ex. 5 may
have been.  Exhibit 7 consisted of three confirmation slips
sent out by the Daly firm to Lido in two instances and to Lynch
in the other.

Mr. Lavender explained that the three confirmation slips
indicated that on November 30, 1960, Dalys had acted as agent
for Mr. Lynch in the sale of an option; on the same day they
acted as agent for Lido in the purchase of that particular
option and that on the same day they had again sold the option
for Lido.  Lido received $300 U.S. funds on the sale of the
option after having paid $240 plus $10 commission for it,
making a net profit on the differential in premiums of %50.
Mr. Lavender stated that this was only one of a large number of
transactions of a similar nature which he had noted in the
relevent period under examination.  One of the governors asked
Mr. Lavender as to whether or not a new paper was required for
the sale of the option to New York or whether the exact same
document was employed on the sale in New York.  Mr. Lavender
was unable to furnish the governor with an answer to his
question.

After Mr. Lavender had completed his evidence, the Governors
directed questions to the various members of the Daly group in
order to obtain information from them. The questions were
largely asked of Mr. Wiley and of the plaintiff.  Some were
also directed to Mr. Robb. Since several of the issues in this
action depend, in part at least, upon what occurred at that
meeting, it will be appropriate to set out some of the
statements which, according to the evidence at trial, were made
there.

Mr. Wiley, who had most of the contact with Mr. Lynch stated
that Mr. Lynch always sold options, that it had been his
practice (Wiley's) to check with the New York dealers for
prices for the Lynch options and thereafter compare those
prices with the prices offered by Lido so as to be sure to
obtain the best possible prices for Mr. Lynch, that Mr. Lynch
knew of the existence of Lido and that he, Wiley, was dealing
with Lido, and that Mr. Posluns was a part of or had an
interest in Lido.  Mr. Wiley is also purported to have said
that he always discussed the Lido business with Dr. Shulman and
never had any contact with the plaintiff in that respect and
that he always cautioned Mr. Lynch against accepting any offer
if the price was not right.  Mr. Wiley also indicated that
initially he sold nearly all of the Lynch options to Lido but
thereafter a number were sold directly to New York clients.  He
was unable to explain the reason why Dr. Shulman obtained
better prices than he personally could obtain in New York.  He
also said that it was his impression that Mr. Lynch was a most
sophisticated investor with a background in the option business
before commencing to deal with the Daly firm.

Mr. Stapells explained generally the operations and place of
the Daly firm in the put and call business saying that in all
cases it had acted as a middleman and admitting that there was
a conflict between the letters which had been sent out to Mr.
Lynch (exs. 5 and 6) and the confirmation notes subsequently
received by Mr. Lynch (ex. 7); that in the former the Daly firm
purported to act as principal and in the latter as agent.  Mr.
Stapells then discussed in detail the operation of the joint
account carried on by the Daly firm with Vanden Broeck and
admitted that improper spreads had been taken by his client.
While he was speaking, Mr. Graydon as counsel for the Board
observed that one could not divorce Lido from Mr. Posluns and
that the latter as a director of the Daly firm should have
applied his knowledge for the benefit of Mr. Lynch.  Mr.
Stapells countered by stating that the Daly organization had
not really looked sufficiently closely at the accouht to see
the manner in which it was being operated and that while the
plaintiff had an interest in Lido, all of the Lido tradings
were carried on by Dr. Mr. Stapells also brought to the
attention of the Board that in the spring of 1960 the auditor
of the Exchange had been informed of Lido and its operations
and apparently had been satisfied that they were in order.  In
making that submission he had reference to the letters which
has passed between Dalys and the Exchange, filed at the trial
as exs. 1, 2, 3 and 4, and which were as follows:

Bay Street, TORONTO, Ontario

Dear Mr. Pettit:--

We have a client Lido Investments Limited which is a

Mr. Wilfred M. Posluns owns a 50% interest in Wilmos

Since none of the other Directors or shareholders of R.A.

we would like to receive your comments as to the status of

Yours very truly,
Vice-President

Mr. R.F. Robb, R.A. Daly & Company Limited, 44 King Street
West, Toronto, Ontario.

Dear Sir:

Your letter of February 4, 1960 was put before the Audit
Commitee without names.  Before ruling on this we would
appreciate your telling us in more detail just what the
operations and purposes of this company Lido Investments

The plaintiff, Mr. Posluns, then spoke and stated that he had
formed his association with Dr. Shulman when the doctor had
required capital for his operations and that for such purpose
he or his family had furnished the business with capital of
$900,000 to $1,000,000.  He emphasized that the operations were
run by Dr. Shulman and that he was informed only the next day
of the Lido transactions.  He explained that Lido was a trader
of options, that is, that it bought and sold them, and further
that he knew that it was dealing with Mr. Lynch but said that
he was not aware of the joint account in New York.

Mr. Robb conceded that he was the only one who knew of the
profit made by the joint account, but took the position that
such profit had been gained by inadvertence on his part.
Colonel Christie and Mr. Daly stated that they were completely
in the dark about improper spreads having been taken.

With respect to the charges that had been made against the
Daly firm and set out in the notice, ex. 12, Mr. Stapells made
the following submissions:

Re charge (a) -- (whether Dalys while acting as agent for Mr.
Lynch on one side of the transaction, had acted on the other
side in such transaction for or with Lido in which Mr. Posluns,
a Daly director, had an interest.)  Mr. Stapells conceded that
the Daly firm had not been judicious and might have considered
the potential conflict of interest but he argued that as Mr.
Lynch was aware of the interest of the plaintiff, such interest
in itself did not mean that the trading conducted by Dalys for
Mr. Lynch was improper. He contended that the relations of Mr.
Wiley with Mr. Lynch were such that the former had acted to the
best of his ability for the customer and that Mr. Wiley and the
plaintiff had never acted together with respect to Lynch
trades.

Re charge (b) -- (whether the Daly firm failed in any way to
perform or fulfil its duty to Mr. Lynch as a customer).  Again
Mr. Stapells pointed out that Mr. Lynch was Mr. Wiley's
customer and had never been the plaintiff's.

Re charge (c) -- As this charge really did not directly
involve the plaintiff and as the Board of Governors did not
give effect to it, I do not propose to discuss it.

Re charge (d) -- (whether Dalys carried on business
carelessly and improperly in that letters addressed to Mr.
Lynch indicated that it acted as principal, whereas subsequent
confirmations indicated that Daly acted as his agent). Mr.
Stapells admitted that the letters and the subsequent
confirmation slips were in conflict so that technically Dalys
had been negligent.  However, he stated that the form of the
letter adopted by the Daly firm was taken from a similar one
employed earlier by the Burns firm and that in any event the
letter was largely employed for the sole purpose of obtaining
the bank guarantee. Mr. Stapells also took the position that as
Mr. Lynch was aware of the nature of the transactions, he could
not have been misled by the documents.

Re charge (e) -- (whether misrepresentations had been made by
or on behalf of the Daly firm with respect to the requirements
of the Exchange with reference to guarantees by the bank).  Mr.
Stapells admitted that in fact there was no regulation of the
Stock Exchange requiring Mr. Lynch to obtain bank guarantees
but explained that Mr. Robb held the belief such a requirement
was going to be incorporated in the forthcoming regulations of
the Exchange as to put and call transactions.

Re charge (f) -- (whether the conduct or method of business
of Dalys was unbecoming a member of the Exchange or
inconsistent with just and equitable principles of trade or
detrimental to the interests of the Exchange).  Mr. Stapells
conceded that the trading practices of the Daly firm in
connection with their methods of confirmation, the
misrepresentation it had made, the practice in connection with
the New York trades, and the taking spreads were all improper,
but said they were clearly unintentional and in any event that
the trades with Mr. Lynch were just.  He stressed that the
directors generally were not aware of the improper spreads in
the New York account and that the director who was aware of
them did not see their significance.

A short but spirited argument on a point of law broke out at
the close of Mr. Stapells' remarks when he made some statement
to the effect that the disclosure to Mr. Lynch that the
plaintiff had an interest in Lido was sufficient. Mr. Graydon,
counsel for the Exchange, disagreed and said something to the
effect that when one acts as agent on one side and principal on
the other side, all material facts must be disclosed, not just
the mere circumstance that the agent has an interest as
principal, and further that the onus was on the agent to prove
he had given all relevant disclosures of all the material
details. He also took the position that the plaintiff had a
duty of disclosure ot Mr. Mr. Lynch.  At the trial, Mr. Graydon
testified that the only disclosure he could remember having
been discussed on February 28th was the fact that the plaintiff
had an interest in Lido; he could not recall any suggestion
that Mr. Lynch knew that Lido was reselling in New York.  He
added, however, that it was his opinion that whatever
disclosure was pleaded at the hearing was insufficient.

When Mr. Stapells had concluded his submissions, the Daly
group, along with Mr. Lavender, retired, and there followed a
discussion amongst the seven governors as to the facts that had
been adduced.  At the trial, there was evidence to the effect
that the Board looked somewhat to Mr. Gardiner for an
explanation of the mechanics of the put and call transactions
inasmuch as he was thought to be the most knowledgeable in that
respect.  On his examination for discovery, Mr. Gardiner, when
asked as to his understanding at the time of the hearing of the
sales of options conducted through the New York joint account
in New York, stated:  "At that particular time I was rather
confused as to what was happening.  I really didn't understand
what was going on in New York."  And yet at the trial he
admitted that of all the governors present he probably had the
most experience with the put and call business.  The others
must have been even more confused.

The evidence is clear that there was no discussion amongst
the governors concerning the evidence that Mr. Lynch had known
that the plaintiff had an interest in Lido or on the question
as to whether Mr. Lynch knew that the Daly company was also
acting for Lido. At the end of the discussion, the chairman,
Mr. Scott, polled the members with respect ot each charge.  On
each, save for charge (c), the governors (Mr. Scott abstaining)
voted unanimously that the Daly firm had in fact been guilty as
charged.

The Daly people were invited to return to the room and the
chairman, Mr. Scott, advised them of the fact that they had
been found guilty on all charges with the exception of (c).
They were asked whether they or their counsel wished to make
any representations as to the penalty which might be imposed
whereupon Mr. Stapells stated that the parties involved had not
been seriously hurt, that the put and call transactions were of
an unusual nature, and that the Daly firm had acted as guinea
pigs in this type of business.  R.A. Daly Jr. pointed out that
the firm had not intended any wrongdoing in this new form of
business which was without regulation on the part of the
Exchange.

Mr. Daly and his associates again retired from the room and
the Board then deliberated as to the penalty to be imposed upon
him as the member of the Stock Exchange who held the seat.  It
was pointed out that pursuant to By-law 11, s. 1 of the
Exchange by-laws, the maximum penalty, short of suspension or
expulsion of a member, that could be imposed was fine not
exceeding $5,000. After some observations that such maximum was
far too low, the Board agreed that it should be assessed
against Mr. Daly.

At that point an unfortunate error was made.  Instead of
recognizing and accepting the fact that it had completed the
inquiry with respect to the Daly company upon which it had
properly embarked the Board went on to deal independently and
additionally with the plaintiff, notwithstanding that he could
not have realized that he was in personal jeopardy and had had
no reason to think that he was being called upon to defend his
approval as a customers' man or otherwise because of alleged
personal misconduct.  It is a great pity that those present,
while acting honestly and in good faith, did not appreciate the
grave implications of what was next proposed.

This new issue was introduced when the chairman, Mr. Scott,
said something to the effect, "What about the directors of Daly
individually?"  Another governor then referred to Mr. Posluns
as being the one who had caused all the trouble since he was on
one side a member of the Daly firm which acted as agent for Mr.
Lynch, and on the other was a partner with his brothers and Dr.
Shulman as a principal.  With relatively little discussion, it
was decided that the penalty imposed upon the Daly firm was not
sufficient so far as the plaintiff personally was concerned and
accordingly a resolution was unanimously passed (see ex. 17,
the minutes of that meeting) that all prior consents given to
him as a director, officer and sharholder of the Daly company
be terminated forthwith.  Although no reference was made in the
actual resolution framed by the governors to the status of the
plaintiff as an employee with the Daly firm, it was generally
understood by them that his association with the Daly firm was
to be severed in all respects.

There were two provisions in the by-laws under which the
Board could withdraw approvals.  By-law 49, s. 4 read as
follows:

Sec. 4. The approval of a customers' man may be terminated at
any time by the Board of Governors, whereupon the member,
member firm or member corporation shall, within a reasonable
period, discontinue the employment of the customers' man
concerned.

By-law 67, s. 16, was in this language:

Sec. 16. The Board of Governors may, in its discretion, at
any time terminate any approval which it may have given with
respect to a member corporation and the member or members
affected shall conform to such direction as the Board of
Governors may make with respect thereto.

IX THE EVENTS PRECEDING THE HEARING OF MARCH 2, 1961

Shortly after, General Graham informed Colonel Christie by
telephone of the punishment inflicted not only upon Mr. Daly
but also upon Mr. Posluns.  When Mr. Stapells heard of the
result he called Mr. Somerville at once and expressed strong
feelings that there should be a hearing with respect to the
plaintiff's personal position.  The plaintiff immediately
conferred with his solicitor, Mr. Goodman, who asked Mr.
Somerville to refrain from making an immediate announcement of
the decision and also requested an opportunity to discuss the
matter with Exchange officals.

On the afternoon of the following day, March 1st, Mr. Goodman
and his associate, Mr. Solway, met General Graham and Mr.
Somerville at which time it was reiterated that the plaintiff
had made full disclosure to the Exchange, to the Daly directors
and to Mr. Lynch and that if anyone were guilty of wrongdoing
it was Mr. Robb who had been in charge of the account in which
the improper spread had been discovered.  Mr. Goodman argued
that the plaintiff had not been given a fair hearing, that he
could not understand why his client had been singled out from
all the directors and sought an opportunity to make
representations to the entire Board.  General Graham acceded to
that request and a meeting with the Board of Governors was
arranged for the following day.

By letter dated and despatched on March 1st, General Graham
notified Mr. Daly that his company had been adjudged guilty of
conduct deemed unbecoming a member of the Exchange and
inconsistent with just and equitable principles of trade and
detrimental to the interests of the Exchange and that the Board
had imposed upon him a fine of $5,000.  The fine was paid on
the same day.

In order to assist Mr. Goodman for his presentation to the
Board, the plaintiff visited the Daly offices and obtained
photostats of the following documents:

1. Exhibit 98A (the original was filed as ex. 98) being a
schedule of options for the period ending December 19, 1960
setting out a number of options together with the price at
which they had been sold through the joint account at New York
and the price at which they had been credited in the Toronto
option account to the seller of the options, either Mr. Lynch
or Lido.

2. Exhibit 99, being sheets 5 and 6 from the account known as
the Toronto Option Account found in the Daly clients' ledger.

3. A sales sheet that formed part of the Daly firm daily
blotter of August 22nd wherein are shown the sales made on that
day by the firm on behalf of clients.  A single sheet taken
from that blotter is ex. 121.

4. Exhibit 124, being a summary sheet headed "Quantity and
Origin of Transactions Effected" dated August 23, 1960 which
would ordinarily be attached to the daily sales blotter for
August 22nd.  When obtained by the plaintiff the summary sheet
was not attached to the blotter.

5. The daily summary sheet for August 24th which was
subsequently filed at the trial as ex. 125.

6. Exhibit 126, being a confirmation sheet from Dalys dated
December 1, 1960, recording the sale of a Mead Johnson put for
Lido for a premium of $1,900.

All of those photostats were taken to Mr. Goodman on March
1st in addition to the correspondence (exs. 1 to 4) between the
Daly firm and the Exchange in February and March 1960
concerning the audit status of Lido.

X
THE HEARING OF MARCH 2, 1961

The hearing held on the afternoon of Thursday, March 2nd, at
the Exchange offices, was attended by those governors who had
been present two days earlier and by General Graham, Mr.
Somerville and Mr. Graydon.  The plaintiff was accompanied by
his solicitors, Mr. Goodman and Mr. Solway.

Mr. Scott, acting as chairman, opened the meeting by reading
a statement which had been prepared by General Graham with the
assistance of Mr. Graydon.  A copy of this was filed as
Schedule A to ex. 24 and is as follows:

OPENING STATEMENT BY ERIC SCOTT

This meeting of the Board of Governors has been convened at
the request of Mr. Goodman, counsel for Mr. Wilfred M.
Posluns, a shareholder and director of R.A. Daly & Co.
Limited.

At a meeting held last Tuesday, February 28th, the Board
investigated and considered transactions in put and call
options conducted between January 1st, 1960 and January 31st,
1961, by R.A. Daly & Co. Limited with its customer John T.
Lynch, and heard and considered all evidence presented to it
and all representations which were made to it.  At that
meeting there were present the following directors of R.A.
Daly & Co. Limited, namely:  Col. Christie, Mr. R.A. Daly,
Jr., Mr. R.F. Robb, Mr. Posluns and Mr. G.A. Wylie, as well
as Mr. Stapells, who appeared as counsel.  The hearing was a
very complete one and all present were given the opportunity
to present all evidence and to make all representations which
they wished to make.  In particular, Mr. Posluns gave
evidence freely on his own behalf.

At the conclusion of the hearing the Board unanimously
passed a resolution "that any and all prior consents given of
Mr. Wilfred M. Posluns as a director, officer or shareholder
of R.A. Daly & Co. Limited be terminated, and that Mr. R.A.
Daly, Jr. be instructed to take any and all actions that may
be required to conform to such termination of approval."

Following the meeting, Mr. Goodman, as counsel for Mr.
Posluns, requested to be heard by the Board, and he was
advised that a meeting of the Board would be held today at
this hour at which he and Mr. Posluns and any other persons
they wished could attend and adduce such evidence or make
such representations as they might see fit as to why the
resolutions passed by the Board last Tuesday should not
stand.  At this time, I would like to point out that Mr.
Posluns was entitled to have counsel present at the meeting
of the Board held last Tuesday, but I understand that there
was some misunderstanding as to the necessity for this ...

I think it would be well for me to review the evidence
adduced at the meeting of the Board on Tuesday last in so far
as Mr. Posluns is concerned.

Mr. Posluns is a director and shareholder of R.A. Daly
& Co. Limited, and it was admitted that R.A. Daly & Co.
Limited, while acting as agent for John T. Lynch on one side
of the transactions in question, acted on the other side in
such transactions, or some of them, for or with a partnership
known as Lido Investments in which Mr. Posluns, a director of
Daly, on his own admission, had, through a company, a one-
sixth interest.  Mr. Posluns also admitted that, apart
from what might be called his share interest in Lido
Investments, he had advanced to it, or made available to it,
very substantial sums of money.

The Board also had before it copies made from the records
of R.A. Daly & Co. Limited of certain confirmations given to
Mr. Lynch and to Lido Investments Limited in connection with
transactions in put and call options.

After the reading of that statement Mr. Somerville presented
to the meeting certain confirmation slips as to transactions on
behalf of Mr. Lynch and Lido.  These were apparently the same
slips that had been explained to the Board at the previous
hearing by Mr. Lavender.  When asked whether he proposed to
call any additional evidence, Mr. Goodman indicated that as he
understood there was no dispute as to the evidence but that he
would proceed to review it and then deal with the
interpretation placed by the Board upon that evidence.

Mr. Goodman commenced by stating that Mr. Stapells had
informed him that at the previous hearing Mr. Stapells had
proceeded on the assumption that the interests of all the
directors in the Daly firm were identical. Mr. Goodman then
argued that the Board's decision as it affected the plaintiff
was discriminatory against him and was not substantiated by the
facts nor justified as to law and that no authority was to be
found in any act or in any enabling legislation is permit the
Board to indulge in such discrimination.

Mr. Goodman then proceeded to outline the facts as he
understood them and to make his argument with respect to the
interpretation of those facts. The evidence adduced at the
trial was not clear as to the point at which Mr. Goodman's
account of the facts ended and his argument commenced.  Subject
to the foregoing, it appears that he made the following address
to the governors:  that Mr. Posluns, upon his entry into the
Daly firm, had informed that firm of his interest in Lido and
had obtained the approval of the Daly firm to his holding, and
that the Daly firm had made disclosure of the plaintiff's
interest in Lido to the auditor of the Exchange.  Mr. Goodman
then produced for filing the four letters, exs. 1 to 4.
Although there was some suggestion made in the evidence of the
plaintiff at the trial, that Mr. Goodman also referred to a
telephone conversation between Mr. Robb and an individual at
the Exchange, presumably Mr. Lavender, concerning Lido's
position with the public, and the fact that the Daly firm would
act on transactions between its client and Lido, I am quite
satisfied that no such reference was made. Mr. Goodman went on
to point out that the plaintiff was not actively interested in
the operation of Lido, other than for the purpose of raising
money for it, but that the day to day management was in the
hands of Dr. Shulman.  He said that his instructions were that
Mr. Lynch knew that Mr. Posluns was a director of Dalys and had
a substantial interest in Lido.  He further stated that Mr.
Lynch did not suffer in his dealings with the Daly firm on the
sales of his options to Lido, and in fact that he realized more
money with the Daly firm in those transactions than he did when
his options were sold through the firm of Doherty Roadhouse.
He also mentioned the fact that a director of the Daly firm,
Mr. Robb, had been in charge of an account at the Daly firm
which had retained for itself on the sales of options in New
York an improper spread against both Mr. Lynch and Lido, and
that while this fact was not known to the plaintiff, he had
documents which would indicate that the other directors of the
Daly firm had had an opportunity to be aware of these improper
spreads.

After outlining those facts, Mr. Goodman asked the Board to
indicate to him whether they were the facts upon which the
Board had acted, and whether there were any other material
facts which the Board had taken into consideration in reaching
its decision.  The evidence is not very clear as to what the
chairman, Mr. Scott, replied to this question of Mr. Goodman's,
but apparently he gave him some reason to think that the facts
he had mentioned were those which had been before the Board and
he asked Mr. Goodman to continue.  Mr. Goodman then declared
that as a matter of normal business practice, the position of
the Daly company as agent and Lido as principal on the one
side, and Lynch on the other side as principal, was not illegal
or immoral.  Mr. Graydon took issue with him at this point and
stated that Mr. Goodman was wrong in that respect.  Mr. Goodman
went on to suggest that if the Exchange had wished a higher
standard of morality from the plaintiff who had made complete
disclosure, then he should have been notified of what was
required of him.  Mr. Goodman then referred to the position of
Mr. Robb who he alleged was the only director who had acted
improperly in the Daly firm, and stressed that the acts of Mr.
Robb had been committed without the knowledge of the plaintiff,
but in a manner which could have been known to the other
directors since they had circulated to them at the Daly firm
certain documents setting out the transactions conducted on
each day.  Mr. Goodman testified that at this point he held
before him, or in his hand, the documents which Mr. Posluns had
obtained for him the day before, from the Daly firm, being exs.
98A, 99, 121, 124, 125 and 126.  There is some dispute in the
evidence as to whether Mr. Goodman had all or some of those
documents, and, if so, what was done with them.  I believe that
some of them at least were in Mr. Goodman's possession there
and that he stated that they proved that the Daly firm had
taken a spread not only against Mr. Lynch but also against the
Lido firm.  Certainly he referred to two specific documents,
exs. 124 and 125, and argued that they established that the
senior directors, but not. Mr. Posluns, had had an opportunity
of examining daily transaction sheets of the Daly firm, which
would have revealed the spreads being taken in the account
operated by Mr. Robb.  It would seem that at this point he
handed these two mimeographed sheets containing the initials of
the senior Daly directors, to Mr. Somerville, who apparently
looked at them and returned them immediately to Mr. Goodman.
Some of the governors saw the mimeographed summary sheets
containing the initials in the brief interval during which they
were passed back and forth between Messrs. Goodman and
Somerville.  A number of the governors swore that they did not
see the documents at all.  In any event, it is abundantly clear
that none of them could understand the sheets or their
relevancy to the proceedings before them.  As Mr. Deacon
testified, at the time he could not grasp the significance of
the sheets because they were merely an analysis of the origin
of trades in the Daly firm.  The only bearing that he could see
in the production of the documents was that the plaintiff had
not initialled them and accordingly may not have been cognizant
of all that occurred in the firm.

Mr. Goodman continued by contending that since the wrongdoer
in the Daly firm was Mr. Robb, the director in charge of the
joint account, it was pure discrimination on the part of the
Board to take no action against Mr. Robb, but to act against
Mr. Posluns, who, in fact, had committed no wrong and whose
position could not be distinguished from that of the remaining
directors. Mr. Goodman concluded by explaining why action such
as the publication of the resolution that was proposed would do
irreparable damage to the plaintiff, his family and the
reputation of the family.

The chairman asked Mr. Posluns if he had anything to say and
the plaintiff repeated a number of the things that his counsel
had already presented.  The plaintiff, and Messrs. Goodman and
Solway, then left the room.

It might also be mentioned that Mr. Williston asked General
Graham at the trial whether anyone at the hearing said to Mr.
Goodman words to the effect, "There is evidence that Mr.
Posluns and Dr. Shulman were purchasing options from Lynch and
reselling them on the same day."  The General replied that
while he could not say who said those exact words, he knew that
it was understood by all those present that that was one of the
things to which the Board took such strong exception on the
part of Mr. Posluns; that if Mr. Goodman was not confronted in
so many words by that fact, it was clearly appreciated by him.

After the retirement from the room of Mr. Posluns and his two
solicitors, the Board discussed the matter again but not at
great length.  They were unanimously of the opinion that the
facts remained the same and that Mr. Posluns' approval should
be recalled.  However, they considered the plea that Mr.
Goodman had made that the publication of the withdrawal of his
client's connection with the Daly firm might cause damage to
his reputation and that of the Posluns family and decided that
the object of the Exchange would be served if he were allowed
to resign.  General Graham and Mr. Somerville were instructed
to discuss that possibility with Mr. Goodman.

XI THE EVENTS FOLLOWING MARCH 2, 1961

On the following afternoon Messrs. Posluns, Goodman and
Solway were advised that if the plaintiff resigned from the
Daly firm and disposed of his interest in it, the resolution of
the governors terminating the prior approval would become
inoperative but otherwise it would be effective.  Eventually
the plaintiff was given until Friday, March 10th, at 1 p.m. for
the purposes of making his election.

On March 8th the president of the Exchange wrote to Mr. O.E.
Lennox, the chairman of the Ontario Securities Commission, the
following letter (ex. 32): Mr. Wilfred Posluns is a director
and shareholder of R.A. Daly & Co. Limited:  the Board of
Governors of the Toronto Stock Exchange approved his
association with Daly & Co. about a year ago.

For several months ending in January 1961, the Daly firm
had been acting as agents for a man named Lynch at
Peterborough in the sale of stock options known as "puts" and
"calls".  Whilst acting as agents for Lynch and charging
him a commission for their service, the Daly firm were also
acting in most cases for the purchaser of the Lynch options,
namely Lido Investments; Wilfred Posluns has a one-sixth
interest in Lido Investments.

Daly & Co. and Posluns knew, or should have known, that
Lido Investments in many cases were immediately reselling the
Lynch options in New York at a profit. There is some evidence
that some of the Lynch options were sold by Daly to New York
purchasers and that Daly profited from these sales in that
they sold at a price higher than they actually credited to
Lynch.

As I advised you orally last week, the Toronto Stock Exchange
has found Daly & Co. guilty of conducting business in a manner
unbecoming a member of the Exchange, inconsistent with just and
equitable principles of trade and detrimental to the interests
of the Exchange, and fined the firm $5,000.

At the same time, because Posluns had profited in the Lynch
transactions both as a partner of the Daly firm and through the
sale of the Lynch options by Lido Investments, the Board
considered his actions were such as to justify the Board in
terminating the prior approval which had been given for Posluns
to be a director and shareholder of the Daly firm, and the
Board passed a resolution accordingly.  However, since there is
a possibility that Mr. Posluns may voluntarily sever his
connection with the Daly firm in the very near future, no
action has been taken by the Board to put the terms of the
resolution into effect.

Although I think I gave you most or all of the above facts
last week, I felt that you might like to have the information
put in writing.

On his discovery, Mr. Somerville explained that the letter had
been sent since it was the practice of the Exchange to keep the
Securities Commission informed of all Exchange actions,
particularly of a disciplinary type, and also because Mr.
Lennox had indicated that he wished to be kept advised because
the matter was receiving comment in the public press.

The plaintiff apparently having decided not to submit his
resignation, a letter, ex. 33, from the president of the
Exchange was delivered to the Daly firm on March 10th.  It
informed Mr. R.A. Daly, Jr. that by resolution dated March 1,
1961, the Board of Governors of the Exchange, "under the
provisions of section 16 of By-law No. 67, have terminated all
prior consents given by the Board for Mr. Wilfred M. Posluns to
be a director, officer, shareholder or employee of R.A. Daly
& Co. Limited.  Will you kindly take such immediate action as
may be necessary to conform to such termination of approval."
In the actual resolution of the Board, no mention had been made
of the withdrawal of any consent with respect to the plaintiff
as an employee.  In fact, approval of the Exchange is not
required for an employee of a member firm unless he is to act
as a customers' man.  At the trial, General Graham explained
that the word "employee" was inserted by him in his letter by
sheer error, but I believe that its inclusion better expresses
the full intent of the Board.

By notice dated March 10th (ex. 57) the Exchange informed all
members of the resolution in respect to Mr. Posluns and stated
that the Board had terminated all prior consents given to the
plaintiff to be "a director, officer, shareholder or employee
of R.A. Daly & Co. Limited".  It is to be noted that again the
plaintiff's position as an employee was said to have been
within the range of the resolution.  This notice was available
to the newspapers which occupy space in the Exchange building.
Communications to members such as that one can be perused by
the men of the press and, in fact, ordinarily are.

On March 13th the plaintiff was removed as a director of the
Daly company and was discharged as an employee.  As already
mentioned, he was not an officer of the company.  Pursuant to
the relevant provisions in the shareholders' agreement to which
the plaintiff was a party, he subsequently sold his shares to
the other shareholders for a negotiated price which was
satisfactory to him.

On the same day, articles appeared in the Toronto Telegram
and the Toronto Star disclosing that the Exchange had withdrawn
its approval of Mr. Posluns acting as a director of the Daly
firm.  At the trial he stated that those articles caused
embarrassment to Lido and that he received personal comments
from friends and acquaintances.  He also testified that in the
period which followed, broker members of the Exchange
telephoned to say that they no longer wished to deal with
options or stock held by Lido and its business came to an end
during the next few weeks.

Dr. Shulman swore that the business died because brokers
refused to trade any longer in options.  He qualified this
statement, however, by saying that with respect to American
options, while a put and call dealer such as Filer Schmidt in
New York did not refuse to continue doing business with Lido,
it had been impossible to obtain an endorsement by a member
firm of the New York Stock Exchange of the stock options of
Lido.  He further qualified the last assertion by admitting
that the Lido firm could have gone to any member of the New
York Stock Exchange and deposited stock as margin, but stated
that the deposit of such stock would have caused Lido's trading
position to be less fluid and that it was not practical to
attempt such a procedure.  He did say that the discontinuance
of business in puts and calls by Lido was not attributable to
the fact that Mr. Lynch had gone out of business, pointing out
that the Lido firm had been active in that field prior to the
appearance of Mr. Lynch.  I do not accept his statement to that
effect.

One other matter should be mentioned.  Shortly after March
10th, Mr. Somerville became aware of the existence of the
Toronto Option Account which had not been referred to at either
of the hearings held on February 28th or March 2nd. Mr.
Lavender was accordingly asked to look into this aspect of the
matter and he made another extensive examination of the Daly
books.  At about this time Mr. Robb was relieved of his
responsibility as the vice-president in charge of the Daly
stock department and Mr. Wiley resigned as a director although
he was to continue as a customers' man.  Those changes were
approved by the Exchange on March 31st.

During the period of Mr. Lavender's last-mentioned
examination of the Daly books, that firm learned that Mr. Robb
had, in the month of August, 1960, opened the new account to
serve the same functions as those performed by the New York
joint account.  That was the Toronto office Option Account.  It
was also discovered that improper spreads had been taken
against Mr. Lynch and Lido in that account in the same manner
as had been done in the New York joint account.  In the light
of those facts it becomes quite clear that Mr. Robb's
explanation that he was unaware of the fact that spreads were
being taken was not true.

In the first week of April, the Board of Governors of the
Exchange, acting upon this new information, decided to reopen
its enquiry with respect to the Daly trading in puts and calls,
and at the Daly company Mr. Robb was requested to resign as a
director.  He did so, but at a meeting of the Board of
Governors on April 11th it was decided to advise the Daly firm
that the Board did not wish to accept notice of Mr. Robb's
resignation as a director at that time.  That position was
taken because the investigation into the matter had not been
completed and the governors did not know whether further
charges would be laid. The investigation was fully carried out
and on May 4th General Graham and Mr. Somerville discussed the
additional spreads that had been found in the Toronto office
Option Account with Mr. R.A. Daly, Jr. and Mr. Robb.  At a
meeting of the Board held on May 9th, General Graham reported
on this discussion and recommended that no further action be
taken in the matter.  The Board adopted that recommendation and
accepted the resignation of Mr. Robb as a shareholder and
director of the firm.  General Graham testified that his reason
for making the foregoing recommendation was that he had
concluded that the additional spreads taken by Dalys were part
of the misdemeanours which Dalys had committed and for which
the firm already had been punished.  Accordingly, he felt that
there was no necessity of taking furhter action.  So far as Mr.
Robb was concerned, the General thought, as apparently did the
governors, that since Mr. Posluns had been given an opportunity
to resign (although he had not availed himself of that
opportunity), rather than withdrawing his approvals Mr. Robb
should also be given the same opportunity.  His resignation was
thereupon approved.

The Exchange bulletin to its members, dated May 9th, stated
that its enquiry into the put and call transactions carried out
by the Daly firm had been completed, and that after examination
of the evidence of Board had concluded that no further action
against the company would be justified.  By another bulletin of
the same date the heading "Change in a Member Corporation"
appears and beneath it there was reported that the Board of
Governors had approved the resignation of Mr. Robb as an
officer, director and shareholder of the Daly company.

Four or five months later, Mr. Robb obtained employment with
another firm as a customers' man and the Board, after some
discussion and considering the fact that he had no occupation
other than the brokerage buisness, approved his application to
be so engaged.

So much for the history of the events giving rise to this
action.  In my view, it must be dismissed.

XII THE PLAINTIFF'S CLAIM AGAINST THE STOCK EXCHANGE FOR
WRONGFULLY INDUCING A BREACH OF HIS EMPLOYMENT CONTRACT WITH
DALYS

(a) General principles

I propose first to examine the plaintiff's claim against the
Exchange for damages for having procured a breach of his
contract with the Daly company.

While a contract cannot impose the burden of an obligation on
one who is not a party to it, a duty is undoubtedly cast upon
any person, although extraneous to the obligation, to refrain
from interfering with its due performance unless he has a duty
or a right in law to so act.  Thus, if a person without lawful
justification knowingly and intentionally procures the breach
by a party to a contract which is valid and enforceable and
thereby causes damage to another party to the contract, the
person who has induced the breach commits an actionable wrong.
That wrong does not rest upon the fact that the intervenor has
acted in order to harm his victim, for a bad motive does not
per se convert an otherwise lawful act into an unlawful one,
but rather because there has been an unlawful invasion of legal
relations existing between others.

This has been established in our jurisprudence by an ever-
developing body of authority which had its origin in the
great case of Lumley v. Gye
(1853), 2 El. & Bl. 216, 118 E.R.
749
.  Most, if not all, of the relevant judgments following it
were cited and thoroughly discussed with me during the course
of the argument at trial, but there is no point in analyzing
them individually or collectively at this stage.  It will
surely be enough to say that while some of the judgments are
not susceptible of easy interpretation, perhaps because in many
instances they were so elaborate, and others give the
appearance or irreconcilability, there can be no doubt that our
law recognizes as tortious any unjustifiable and unlawful
violation of economic interests which causes harm.
Accordingly, if the Toronto Stock Exchange knowingly procured a
breach by the Daly company of any contract it had with the
plaintiff and so caused actual damage to be inflicted upon him,
the Exchange is liable for that damage unless it was privileged
to act as it did.

In this case it was pleaded that not only did the Stock
Exchange, acting by itself, bring about a breach of a contract
of employment between the plaintiff and Dalys, but also that it
caused his removal as a shareholder and director of that
company and induced a breach of the share agreement referred to
at the outset of these reasons.  It is to be stressed, however,
that the claim on this branch of the case is confined to
damages for the inducement by the Exchange of the alleged
breach of the plaintiff's "employment contract" with Dalys. It
is only on the conspiracy side that damages are put on a wider
base.

To sustain the cause of action now being discussed, and in
the circumstances which prevailed, it must be shown that:

1. A valid and enforceable employment contract subsisted
between the palintiff  and the Daly company; and

2. The defendant Exchange was or can be assumed to have been
aware of the existence  of that contract; and

3. A breach of that contract was procured by the Exchange; and

4. Such breach was effected by wrongful interference on the
part of the Exchange;  and

5. The plaintiff suffered damage as a result thereof.  If all
of those elements  have been proved the plaintiff is entitled
to relief.

(b) Was there a contract between the plaintiff and the Daly
firm of which the Exchange was aware?

Did the evidence at the trial establish that on March 2, 1961
there was a contract of employment between the Daly company and
Mr. Posluns?  Certainly there was no written contract to that
effect and Mr. Howard contended with much force that any claim
formulated upon the premise of even an implied contract should
fail.  He pointed to the fact, for example, that while the
plaintiff received commissions and bonuses he was paid no
salary, and that ex. 48, the approval of the plaintiff as a
salesman by the Ontario Securities Commission, was endorsed
"director" by someone at the Exchange, thus suggesting that
so far as it was concerned he was to be regarded as being at
Dalys in that capacity rather than as an employee.  I was also
reminded that when Mr. Posluns changed offices, he was not
expressly approved by the Exchange as a customers' man at
Dalys.  It was also argued that it was not shown that there was
any measure of control exercised over the plaintiff as a member
of the Daly organization.

On the whole of the evidence, however, I am convinced that
the relationship of employer and employee did exist. In the
first place, Mr. Posluns testified that he was at Dalys, inter
alia, as a commission salesman, and ex. 120, the statement as
to his earnings, gives clear indication that deductions were
made as if he were an employee.  Whatever other inference may
be drawn from the Ontario Securities Commission approval, at
least it was for the "transfer" of the plaintiff's registration
"as a salesman".  Several of those features are equivocal as
to whether he was merely a director or was a director and an
employee, but I think that the latter has greater logic for
although his position on the Board of the Daly company
influenced his rate of earnings, there was no evidence whatever
that he was to be paid or was in fact paid anything as a
director.

At the hearing on February 28th, Mr. Posluns stated that he
was a salesman and his income tax returns for the past made the
same disclosure.  Then, too, following March 10th he was
discharged by Colonel Christie expressly "as an employee" (see
Mr. Stapell's evidence, vol. 4, p. 967), and the Ontario
Securities Commission received word from the Daly firm (ex. 43)
which in turn was passed on to the Exchange and to the
plaintiff, that the latter was "no longer employed ... as a
securities salesman".  In my opinion that wording cannot be
said to be attributable solely to the fact that the Daly
company was automatically and blindly repeating the edict of
the Exchange.  Plainly, Mr. Posluns had been an employee as
well as a shareholder and a director.

As to the second requisite, the evidence proved beyond
peradventure that before reaching their decision with respect
to the plaintiff, the relevant governors were cognizant of his
position as a Daly employee (see, for example, ex. 48 and the
top line on p. 7 of ex. 15).  It is equally clear that those
gentlemen came to the conclusion that Mr. Posluns must cease to
be an employee of the Daly company.

(c) Was there a breach of contract rather than a lawful
termination?

Is it also correct to conclude that a breach of the contract
of employment rather than its lawful termination was the result
of the action by the Exchange? Admittedly, the contract of
employment could have been brought to an end by a
contemporaneous arrangement between the parties to that effect,
or by reasonable notice or compensation in lieu thereof, or for
cause, or if there were any express or implied term in the
original engagement giving either party that right.  Certainly
the plaintiff did not voluntarily retire and no notice nor
compensation was given.  Because of the extent of the knowledge
of other officers of the Daly firm and its measure of
involvement in the Lynch and Lido operations, it is my view
that the plaintiff could not, as between himself and his
employer, have been discharged for cause.  Nor was there any
express contractual term authorizing the dismissal of the
plaintiff upon notice to that effect from the Exchange.

There then comes the question of whether there was an
unexpressed understanding between the plaintiff and the firm
that his employment could be terminated whenever the Exchange
properly withdrew its approval to the continuation of the
relationship.

As to the instances when the Court will imply a term in a
contract, see The "Moorcock" (1889), 14 P.D. 64, and the
language of Bowen, L.J., at p. 68, where he indicates that a
term will be implied to give effect to the presumed intention
of the parties, in order to give such business efficacy to the
transaction as must have been intended.  MacKinnon, L.J.,
stated the test in Shirlaw v. Southern Foundries (1926), Ltd.,

[1939] 2 K.B. 206 at p. 227
:

"Prima facie that which in any contract is left to be implied
and need not be expressed is something so obvious that it
goes without saying; so that, if, while the parties were
making their bargain, an officious bystander were to suggest
some express provision for it in their agreement, they would
testily suppress him with a common 'Oh, of course!'"

I am persuaded that some term should be implied in this case,
but a difficulty is presented when one comes to determine what
the parties contemplated as sufficient action by the Exchange
to justify dismissal by Dalys.  I cannot believe on the one
hand that patently capricious action by the Exchange was
intended to provide it.  Nor would it be sensible to think that
the employer would not be entitled to despatch the plaintiff
unless and until Dalys were satisfied that it had been shown to
the Exchange that Dalys would have had proper cause in its own
right to take the step.  It seems to me, rather, that the range
of permissible discharge pursuant to instructions from the
Exchange fell somewhere between the two extremes and that it
was implicit that compliance with an order of dismissal by the
Exchange would constitute a breach of contract by the Daly
company if that order was made beyond the powers conferred upon
the Exchange by its by-laws, regulations and rulings, or was in
contravention of the principles of ordinary justice.  It may be
argued that such a term ought not to be implied for it would
have placed the Daly firm in an unenviable position.  On the
one side it might be subject to an action for breach of
contract by Mr. Posluns for obeying an invalid Exchange order,
while, on the other measure of authority wielded over any
member by the Exchange would make it unlikely from a practical
view-point that a member would pause to examine closely the
legal validity of any Exchange order, and, in fact, disobey it.
However, it is probable that the Daly firm would be entitled to
be indemnified by the Exchange if loss were incurred as a
result of complying with such an order in view of the general
principle of law that "when an act is done by one person at the
request of another which act is not in itself manifestly
tortious to the knowledge of the person doing it, and such act
turns out to be injurious to the rights of a third party, the
person doing it is entitled to an indemnity from him who
requested that it should be done", as quoted by the Earl of
Halsbury, L.C., in Sheffield Corporation v. Barclay,
[1905]
A.C. 392 at p. 397
.  Accordingly, the question of whether the
Exchange did procure a breach rather than a lawful termination
of the employment contract must depend upon whether the
Exchange followed the dictates of its own rules and the
principles of essential justice, for the failure to do either
one or the other would destroy the implied contractual right of
Dalys to validly cause its arrangements with Mr. Posluns to be
ended.  Whether there was such a failure will be discussed when
I come to consider whether justification for the action by the
Exchange was extinguished because it adopted improper means to
reach its objective.

Before turning to the next issue on this branch of the case,
there are several contentions of the Exchange which should be
mentioned and dismissed.  In the first place, I do not accept
Mr. Howard's proposition that it was the terms of the
shareholders' agreement (ex. 100) and not ex. 33 which brought
about the dismissal of the plaintiff.  Nor should the Board be
excused because it was General Graham who "inadvertently", as
it was put, included the order to oust the plaintiff as an
employee in ex. 33.  Not only would it be natural for the Daly
firm to act, as it did, upon any apparently sensible direction
contained in a letter from the president of the Exchange, one
of whose duties was to write it, but, in any event, the
governors candidly and honestly conceded that it was their
intention and decision that Dalys should dismiss Mr. Posluns
from whatever position he held with that firm.  Accordingly,
the letter was not, in fact, inaccurately worded.

(d) Was there unlawful interference on the part of the
Exchange?

I now pass to the next link in the plaintiff chain of action.
Does he show that the interference, if any, on the part of the
Exchange with his contractual rights was such as to sustain his
claim, for the law stipulates that to be tortious the
interference which is the source of damage to another must be
"unlawful" before it will be actionable.  It is unnecessary
to consider the various kinds of particular interference which
have been held to be wrongful; it will suffice to say that to
procure a breach of contract by direct intervention is
"unlawful", and will give rise to a cause of action to the
person who is thereby injured unless it is justifiable.  For
that proposition I rely, amongst others, upon D.C. Thomson
& Co. Ltd. v. Deakin,
[1952] Ch. 646, where, at pp. 677 and 681

respectively, Lord Evershed, M.R., stated:

At any rate, it is clear that, when there is such a direct
intervention by the intervener [causing a party to break his
contract], the intervention itself is thereby considered
wrongful.

And:

Dealing first with individual contractors, it seems to me
that the intervener, assuming in all cases that he knows of
the contract and acts with the aim and object of procuring
its breach to the damage of B, one of the contracting
parties, will be liable not only (1) if he directly
intervenes by persuading A to break it, but also (2) if he
intervenes by the commission of some act wrongful in itself
so as to prevent A from in fact performing his contract...

In the same case Jenkins, L.J., had this to say at p. 694:

Direct persuasion or procurement or inducement applied by the
third party to the contract breaker, with knowledge of the
contract and the intention of bringing about its breach, is
clearly to be regarded as a wrongful act in itself, and where
this is shown a case of actionable interference in its
primary form is made out:  Lumley v. Gye, 2 El. & Bl. 216.

I pause here to point out that when considering this tort,
care must be taken always to distinguish between a cause of
action based upon the procurement of a breach of a contract and
one for interference with other civil rights.  The House of
Lords in England has restricted the scope of the principle
which I have just outlined to interference with actual
contracts:  see Allen v. Flood
[1898] A.C. 1
and Sorrell v.
Smith,
[1925] A.C. 700
.  Thus, some of the observations by
Judges in cases such as Crofter Hand Woven Harris Tweed Co.,
Ltd. v. Veitch,
[1942] A.C. 435
must be interpreted in the
light of the fact that no breach of contract was involved.

Here, there was direct and deliberate interference by the
Exchange with the contractual relations between the plaintiff
and the Daly Company.  On the authorities, that interference,
unless justifiable, must be deemed to be unlawful action on the
part of the Exchange if a breach of those contractual relations
was the result.  True, it did not act for the purpose of
causing damages to Mr. Posluns or with malice or spite, but
that is immaterial, for if the Exchange intended to bring an
end to the employment contract and such was clearly its
purpsoe, that intention is sufficient and does not have to be
accompanied by a wish to do harm.  As to this, I cite further
words of Jenkins, L.J., in the Thomson case, at pp. 696-7:
Nevertheless, I think that in principle an actionable
interference with contractual relations may be committed by a
third party who, with knowledge of a contract between two other
persons and with the intention of causing its breach, or of
preventing its performance, persuades, induces or procures the
servants of one of those parties, on whose services he relies
for the performance of his contract, to break their contracts
of employment with him, either by leaving him without notice or
by refusing to do what is necessary for the performance of his
contract, provided that the breach of the contract between the
two other persons intended to be brought about by the third
party does in fact ensue as a necessary consequence of the
third party's wrongful interference with the contracts of
employment.

. . . . .

But, while admitting this form of actionable interference
in principle, I would hold it strictly confined to cases
where it is clearly shown, first, that the person charged
with actionable interference knew of the existence of the
contract and intended to procure its breach; secondly, that
the person so charged did definitely and unequivocally
persuade, induce or procure the employees concerned to break
their contracts of employment with the intent I have
mentioned; thirdly, that the employees so persuaded, induced
or procured did in fact break their contracts of employment;
and, fourthly, that breach of the contract forming the
alleged subject of interference ensued as a necessary
consequence of the breaches by the employees concerned of
their contracts of employment.

My conclusion is reinforced by the observation of Lord James in
South Wales Miners' Federation v. Glamorgan Coal Co., Ltd.,

[1905] A.C. 239 at p. 252
:

The intention of the defendants was directly to procure the
breach of contracts. The fact that their motives were good in
the interest of those they moved to action does not form any
answer to those who have suffered from the unlawful act.
During the arguments that have been addressed to your
Lordships I do not think quite sufficient distinction was
drawn between the intention and the motives of the
defendants.  Their intention clearly was that the workmen
should break their contracts.  The defendants' motives, no
doubt, were that by so doing wages should be raised.  But if
in carrying out the intention the defendants purposely
procured an unlawful act to be committed, the wrong that is
thereby inflicted cannot be obliterated by the existence of a
motive to secure a money benefit to the wrong-doers.

Similar reasoning is to be found in the judgments in British
Motor Trade Ass'n v. Salvadori,
[1949] Ch. 556
, and Exchange
Telegraph Co. v. Gregory & Co.,
[1896] 1 Q.B. 147
.

In short, therefore, it would seem that the plaintiff is
entitled to reparation from the Exchange if the latter by
direct, intentional and unjustified intervention through the
Daly company, effected a breach of a contract of which it was
or ought to have been aware. Mr. Howard argued with much force
that before the Exchange could be made liable the plaintiff had
to show that it knowingly and intentionally sought a breach of
his contract with the Daly company.  Reliance for that
proposition was logically placed upon British Industrial
Plastics, Ltd. v. Ferguson,
[1938] 4 All E.R. 504
; affd
[1940]
1 All E.R. 479
, and the Thomson case.  I concede that if a
breach of contract is effected by one who does not know of its
existence or without any intent to bring about such a
consequence, that person has not committed an actionable wrong.
In this case, however, the Exchange was aware that some
contract of employment, written or oral, existed, and in
requiring an early severance of all relations between the
employer and employee, it must be taken to have intended that
the contract was to be ended by whatever means were necessary
in the circumstances, including a breach of it by Dalys.  That
the precise terms of the contract were not known to the
governors is quite immaterial.

In somewhat the same vein, counsel for the Exchange contended
that the Daly company could have lawfully terminated its
relationship with the plaintiff by providing him with
compensation in lieu of notice.  Konski v. Peet,
[1915] 1 Ch.
530
was cited on the point.  There, Neville, J., held that as
between the contracting parties, the payment by the employer of
a week's salary in lieu of giving the week's notice provided in
the contract, was not a breach of such contract by the employer
since it was not an agreement to provide employment while
paying wages. Surely, however, the principle that an employer
does not breach his contract by paying compensation to an
employee, in lieu of giving him reasonable notice (where no
period of notice is specified in the contract), does not enable
a third party who is alleged to have procured a breach of
contract, to contend without any supporting evidence, that he
contemplated that the employer, in discharging the employee
immediately, would pay adequate compensation in lieu of notice.
Should this contention prevail, it would be applicable to every
action for wrongfully procuring the breach of an employment
contract.

There is another aspect of this particular issue which calls
for consideration. A breach of contract induced by a stranger
to it by illegal means is clearly actionable.  See, for
example, the Crofter case at pp. 447 and 451 and the judgment
of the late Mr. Justice Laidlaw in Fokuhl v. Raymond et al.,

1949 CanLII 69 (ON CA)
, [1949] 4 D.L.R. 145 at pp. 156-7, [1949] O.R. 704 at p. 714.
It is difficult to know, however, what is illegal in this
context and in particular whether conduct which is neither
criminal nor tortious in the strict sense will be so regarded.
Certainly any action which would of itself constitute a tort or
a crime such as the use of violence, intimidation, coercion,
obstruction, molestation, fraud, or misrepresentation will be
deemed to be illegal.  It is also true, however, that certain
conduct not of itself actionable as a tort, has been looked
upon as creating liability if a breach of contract between
others is its consequence.  Threats to commit torts have been
said, for example, to be illegal for the purposes of this cause
of action.  It was decided by the Supreme Court of Canada in
Orchard et al. v. Tunney,
1957 CanLII 57 (SCC)
, 8 D.L.R.(2d) 273, [1957] S.C.R. 436,
that false statements by union officers that the plaintiff had
been expelled from his union represented the use of illegal
means though not otherwise actionable as a tort.  An earlier
case in that Court, McGillivray v. Kimber (1915),
1915 CanLII 608 (SCC)
, 26 D.L.R.
164, 52 S.C.R. 146, furnishes further guidance on this point.
There a pilotage authority had revoked a pilot's licence
without observing the statutory requirements with respect to
proceedings for that purpose. It was held that the dismissed
pilot had his remedy in damages since he had been prevented
from pursuing his calling and the resolution of dismissal was
an act "without justification or excuse".  That phrase is of
special significance here for the illegality of what was done
was based upon the absence of lawful authority to act in the
way in which the governing body acted and in this case the
plaintiff suffered interference with his contractual rights by
reason of action on the part of the Exchange which may have
been beyond its powers.   If the lack of authority in the
statutory body referred to in the McGillivray case was
equivalent to the employment of illegal means as was apparently
thought, then the supposed exercise of powers which a
corporation or statutory body like the Exchange believes it
enjoys but in fact does ot possess, must be tantamount to the
use of unlawful procedures, for it does not involve the
exercise of any vested right.  In this regard the following
passage in the judgment of Simons, J., in Camden NOminees, Ltd.
v. Forcey,
[1940] Ch. 352 at p. 365,
is of interest:

The end which they sought, namely, the performance by the
landlords of their obligations, was one which could be
reached by process of law.  If the landlords broke their
contract the law gave the defendants their remedy by way of
damages, or in a proper case by way of specific performance.
There is neither reason nor authority for the suggestion that
in such circumstances a common interest can justify the
interference with contractual rights.

I am satisfied therefore that direct and deliberate
disruption of contractual rights in others is a sufficient
legal wrong to forge the tort of actionable interference.  That
being so, and since the Exchange intentionally interfered with
the plaintiff's arrangements with Dalys, it must respond in
damages unless it was privileged to act as it did.

(e) Was the Exchange justified in procuring a breach of
contract?

The limits of the doctrine of justification as it applies to
the tort under discussion have never been defined with any
degree of precision.  Perhaps the only safe guide in the matter
is to follow, and try to enlist, the words of Romer, L.J., at
p. 574 in the report of the judgments in the Court of Appeal in
Glamorgan Coal Co. Ltd. v. South Wales Miners' Federation,

[1903] 2 K.B. 545
, where this appears:

I will only add that, in analyzing or considering the
circumstances, I think that regard might be had to the nature
of the contract; the position of the parties to the contract;
the grounds for the breach; the means employed to procure the
breach; the relation of the person procuring the breach to
the person who breaks the contract; and I think also to the
object of the person in procuring the breach.

If the act of interference is in itself a lawful one, both as
to purpose and means, then no vindication is required unless it
was committed in the course of a conspiracy to injure the
victim.  If, on the other hand, unlawful intervention had been
the source of the harm, justification must be shown if the
claim is to be avoided.  The defence rarely succeeds.  Self-
interest, alone or with others, or the fulfilment of an
undertaking to protect others in the same interest, will not of
themselves amount ot justification:  South Wales Miners'
Federation v. Glamorgan Coal Co. Ltd.,
[1905] A.C. 239
; Pratt
et al. v. British Medical Ass'n
[1919] 1 K.B. 244
; nor where
there is an honest belief that there is a duty to act:  Camden
Nominees, Ltd. v. Forcey; nor where a person is induced to
break a contract because the other party to it has breached his
contract with the intervenor: Smithies v. National Ass'n of
Operative Plasterers,
[1909] 1 K.B. 310
. These are but a few of
the cases in which it was decided that pleas of justification
could not prevail.

On the other hand, in several instances the Courts have
sanctioned interference, particularly where it has been
promoted by impersonal or disinterested motives. For example,
in some of the early cases it was intimated that a defendant
might be excused from the consequences of his otherwise illegal
act if he was under the influence of some great moral or
religious force, reference being made to a father who might
induce his impressionable daughter to break a contract for the
promise of marriage with a scoundrel.  And I suppose if a
doctor were to cause a patient to end a contract of service for
health reasons, he would likewise be protected. Even in those
examples, however, the distinction between inducement and mere
advice is significant and should be heeded.

In two instances interference which otherwise would have been
illegal was held to be privileged on the ground that it was
effected in the public interest. I have in mind Stott v.
Gamble,
[1916] 2 K.B. 504
, where a licensing body banned an
objectionable film which the plaintiff had arranged to exhibit
at another theatre, and Brimelow v. Casson,
[1924] 1 Ch. 302
,
where a protective committee was held to be justified in
procuring breaches of employment contracts under which chorus
girls were so grossly underpaid as to compel them to resort to
immorality.  In the first case, however, reliance was placed
upon a condition attached to the licence, and the second is
today of doubtful authority for a contrary view expressed in
the Smithies case was apparently not considered.  Nor has the
case been applied, so far as I can find, on any other occasion,
and, in fact, was gently criticized by Simonds, J., as he then
was, in the Camden case.  In any event, those cases do not
cover the situation before me.  The Exchange was not here
primarily engaged in upholding the public interest.  That
certainly was one of the purposes in the minds of the governors
but not the predominant one.  They were disciplining the Daly
firm, Mr. Posluns and, later Mr. Robb.  I am inclinded to the
view, therefore, that the action of the Exchange, if otherwise
illegal, cannot be excused on the theory that it was acting in
the public welfare.

Lastly, a person may be justified in encroaching upon
another's civil rights because of some statutory or contractual
privilege, in which case he can be said to be acting in
accordance with a right conferred by contract or a duty imposed
upon him by competent authority as distinct from the mere
protection of his own interest.  Really, this has been already
touched upon, for if that person is under such a cloak, he is
not deemed to be acting unlawfully.  In Read v. Friendly
Society of Operative Stonemasons of England, Ireland & Wales,

[1902] 2 K.B. 88
and 732, for example, Darling, J., stated
at p. 95 that a person would be justified in causing the breach
of contract which was incapable of being carried out without
infringing his rights under another contract.  That appears to
be an illustration of a contractual privilege and, in a sense,
the Stott case exemplifies recourse to a statutory one.  Here,
the Exchange could not say that it was acting under an explicit
statutory licence, but, by reason of its relations with the
plaintiff, it enjoyed a very considerable measure of control
over him, for he submitted himself to its jurisdiction when he
applied to become, and was approved as, a customers' man at
Burns.  I think it is only reasonable to conclude that he
thereby impliedly agreed that so long as he continued under the
aegis of the Exchange, he would submit to any control properly
exerted by it. In this respect, reference might well be made to
Bonsor v. Musicians' Union,
[1956] A.C. 104
.  A correlative
obligation was, however, cast upon the Exchange to act within
its own rules and within the realm of natural justice when
exerting that control, and unless it did both when dealing with
Mr. Posluns, any implied contractual right to interfere was
lost.

Was the Board's decision justified as to purpose?  During the
course of his argument, counsel for the plaintiff emphasized
that while his client was seeking financial redress, his
foremost wish was a finding that he had done no wrong in which
case his character would be completely vindicated. Counsel
urged me to hold that the Board arrived at its decision on the
basis of a wrong principle of law and a complete
misunderstanding of the facts presented to it.  He submitted
that there was no evidence before the governors to sustain
their finding that Mr. Posluns was guilty of impropriety.  This
contention was based on the following grounds:

1. There is no fiduciary relationship between a director of a
corporation  and a person to whom that corporation stands in
a fiduciary position.

2. Mr. Posluns did not act as an agent for Mr. Lynch or in any
other confidential  capacity.

3. There could be no breach of a fiduciary duty because all
material facts  were disclosed to Mr. Lynch.

4. If there was any lack of disclosure to Mr. Lynch, the
