responsibility was  that of the Daly Company and not of the
plaintiff.

5. In any event, the degree of disclosure made to Mr. Lynch was
greater than  that which is generally required by the ethical
standards of the Exchange.

6. The Exchange was expressly put on notice of the plaintiff's
interest  in Lido and knew that Lido was buying and selling
options from the Daly firm and selling such options to Daly
clients.

7. The governors reached their decision on the basis of a wrong
principle  of law in since they were of the view that no
amount of disclosure to Mr. Lynch would affect their
decision.

This raises the question of the extent to which a Court can
examine the decision of a domestic tribunal on the merits.  The
cases generally indicate that with respect to a question of
fact, the Courts will not act as Courts of Appeal from the
decisions of such tribunals.  Provided that a domestic tribunal
has acted honestly and bona fide, and certainly that was so
with respect to the one with which I am concerned, a Court of
law will not probe the domestic tribunal's decision to see if
it would have reached a similar verdict.  If that is so, then I
must accept the decision of the Board of Governors as being
right.  However, there is language used in at least one case
which leads to the cnclusion that a Court can look into the
question of whether there is any evidence at all to support the
finding of the domestic tribunal.

I propose to examine briefly the leading cases dealing with
this point in chronological order.  In comparing them with the
case at bar, it should be noted that a specific ground or
reason is sassigned in the rules of the relevant organization
for the expulsion of members, whereas in this case By-laws
49(4) and 67(16) do not require any particular reason for the
Board of Governors to terminate approvals previously granted.

The first case with respect to a domestice tribunal that
touches this point is Wood v. Woad (1874), L.R.
9 Ex. 190
.
There, Kelly, C.B., at p. 196, stated that if the committee of
the mutual insurance society had in fact exercised their power
under the rules, their decision could not be questioned;
however unfounded the reasons for it may have been, it would
have been final and could not be reviewed by any Court.

In Dawkins v. Antrobus
(1881), 17 Ch. D. 615
, a rule of the
club provided that should the conduct of any member be, in the
opinion of the committee, injurious to the character and
interest of the club, the committee could, after taking certain
procedural steps, expel the member.  At p. 628, James, L.J.,
stated that the Court had no right to sit as a Court of Appeal
on the decision of the members of a club duly assembled.  At p.
629 this appears:

Unless we can say that their decision that such conduct would
be injurious to the character and interests of the club was
so manifestly absurd and so manifestly idle that it could
only have been a false pretence to cover something else, and
therefore was, in fact, fraudulently put forward for the
purpose of giving effect to some preconceived notion of
removing him without just cause ... we have no right to sit
in judgment on their decision.

At page 630, Brett, L.J., pointed out that there was some
danger that the Court would undertake to act as Courts of
Appeal against the decisions of members of clubs and that aside
from the question of natural justice, the sole question for the
Court was whether the decision of the club had been arrived at
bona fide.  He pointed out that the Court had no authority to
consider whether what was done was right or not, or, even as a
substantive question, whether what was decided was reasonable
or not.  At p. 634, Cotton, L.J., made certain remarks to the
same effect.

In Allinson v. General Council of Medical Education
& Registration,
[1894] 1 Q.B. 750
, Lord Esher, M.R., used
language which was somewhat different from that employed in
Leeson v. General Medical Council
(1890), 43 Ch. D. 366
, an
earlier case dealing with the power of the Courts to review the
decision of the General Medical Council.  At p. 760 he stated:

... it is admitted that, if there was no evidence upon which
the council might fairly and reasonably say that the
plaintiff had been guilty of "infamous conduct in a
professional respect," they went beyond the jurisdiction
given to them by the Act ... If there was no such evidence,
they ought to have declined to interfere.  Was there, then,
any evidence which justified the council in finding the
plaintiff guilty of "infamous conduct in a professional
respect"?

At p. 761, Lord Esher, M.R., formulated the following test
-- was the evidence, taken as a whole, reasonably capable of
being treated by the Council as bringing the plaintiff within
that defintion of "infamous conduct in a professional respect"
?  This test of Lord Esher, M.R., would not seem to square with
the views of Bowen and Cotton, L.JJ., and the  Leeson case,
that the Court could only see if a domestic tribunal had acted
honestly. Bowen, L.J., did say that if nothing was brought
before the tribunal which could raise the inference of infamous
conduct, it would go to show that the inquiry had not been a
due inquiry but otherwise the Court could not examine the
evidence at all.

In the Allinson case, Lopes, L.J., at p. 763, stated:

... if there was any evidence on which the council could
reasonably have come to the conclusion to which they did
come, their decision is final.  If, on the other hand, there
was no evidence upon which they could reasonably arrive at
that conclusion, then their decision can be reviewed by this
Court.

In Weinberger v. Inglis,
[1919] A.C. 606
, Lord Atkinson noted
at p. 624 that it was the opinion of the committee on the
"eligibility" of the member, which was the determining
factor; if that opinion was honestly formed and acted upon in
good faith, their decision could not be questioned although, in
the opinion of a Court of law, it might have been erroneous and
one which the Court would not itself have made in the same
circumstances.

In Thompson v. New South Wales Branch of the British Medical
Association,
[1924] A.C. 764
, the appellant had been expelled
from the defendant association. Lord Atkinson, in the Privy
Council, at p. 778, used rather peculiar language in expressing
the jurisdiction of the Court.  He said that if any body
rightly convened is burdened with the discharge of of some
judicial or quasi-judicial duty, and makes a decision that it
has jurisdiction to make, that decision, if legal evidence be
given in the course of the proceeding adequate to sustain it,
cannot, in the absence of some fundamental error, be impeached
or set aside, save upon the ground that the body was
interested, or biased, or influenced by malice in deciding as
it did.  The peculiarity, in my view, is the reference by Lord
Atkinson to "legal evidence", since such phrase probably raises
more questions than it answers.

In Maclean v. The Workers' Union,
[1929] 1 Ch. 602
, Maugham,
J., at p. 621, stated that the decision of a domestic tribunal
cannot be attacked on the ground that it was against the weight
of evidence, since there was no evidence in the proper sense
and since decisions of the tribunal were not open to any sort
of appeal unless the rules provided for one.  With respect to
the question whether the decision can be attacked on the ground
that there was no evidence upon which the tribunal could
possibly come to its conclusion, he stated that he preferred
the view of the Court of Appeal in the Leeson case to that put
forth in the Allinson case.

In the Canadian case of Re Cherniak and College of Physicians
& Surgeons of Ontario (1919),
1919 CanLII 501 (ON SCAD)
, 51 D.L.R. 522, 46 O.L.R. 434,
Maclaren, J.A., observed at p. 527 D.L.R., p. 440 O.L.R.:

. . . we should give to their unanimous decision at least
as much weight as we would to the verdict of a jury on a
question of fact submitted to them.

In Russell v. Duke of Norfolk,
[1949] 1 All E.R. 109
, Tucker,
L.J., in obiter at p. 118 mentioned that the fact that the
tribunal may have arrived at a totally erroneous conclusion and
the fact that it may have attached a quite mistaken value to a
certain report, was altogether beside the point.

A review of all the above cases is found in Lee v. Shomen's
Guild of Great Britain,
[1952] 1 All E.R. 1175
.  There, the
English Court of Appeal held that the Court had the power to
review the decision of a domestic tribunal in expelling a
member from the union, when the decision involved a question of
law, namely, the construction or interpretation of the rules of
the organization; the members of the Court were not sitting as
a Court of Appeal from a decision of fact reached by the
domestic tribunal, but were holding that the act committed by
the plaintiff did not constitute the offence of "unfair
competition within the meaning of the rules of the Union, and
hence the plaintiff was not subject to being expelled.  It was
held that the Court was therefore considering the meaning of
the phrase "unfair competition" as found in the rules of the
Union and hence it was a question of law.

For our purposes, the Lee case is noteworthy for the comments
made by the three Judges with respect to the authorities
mentioned above concerning the power of a Court to review a
decision of a domestic tribunal on the merits.  Somervell,
L.J., at p. 1179 observed that he preferred the statements of
Lord Esher in the Allinson case to those found in the Leeson
case.  He said that the cases show that even where the subject-
matter is as it was in the medical cases, the Courts will
interferee if there is no evidence, for if such be the case,
the domestic tribunal will have acted ultra vires. At p. 1180
is to be found his opinion that there is a distinction between
cases where the decision challenged is under the rules based on
the opinion of a committee on a matter which is primarily one
of opinion, and those cases, such as that before him, where the
decision primarily rests on the legal construction of words in
a rule.

Denning, L.J., after stating that the question in the case
before him was that of determining the extent to which the
Courts will examine the decisions of domestic tribunals on
points of law, commented as follows: that such question was not
to be solved by turning to the club cases; that in the case of
social clubs the rules usually empower the committee to expel a
member who in their opinion has been guilty of conduct
detrimental to the club and this is a matter of opinion and
nothing else; and that the Courts have no wish to sit on
appeals from their decisions on such a matter any more than
from the decisions of a family conference.  However, he thought
it was different with domestic tribunals which sit in judgment
on the members of a trade or profession since they can deprive
a man of his livelihood.  He referred to Osgood v. Nelson
(1872), L.R.
5 H.L. 636
, a case concerning

[614]]

the statutory power of a corporation to remove a clerk for
inability or misbehaviour, or for any other cause which might
appear reasonable to the Mayor, Aldermen and Commons.  Lord
Hatherley, the Lord Chancellor, stated at p. 649 that there was
power in the Courts of law to see whether there has been any
evidence given in support of the cause assigned for the removal
of the clerk so as to show that the tribunal has not acted
simply upon its own view of what is right and just without any
inquiry into the case.

Denning, L.J., also approved the statements of Lord Esher,
M.R., in the Allinson case that the facts before the tribunal
must be reasonably capable of being considered as proving the
offence.  He stated at p. 1183:

It has sometimes been said in these cases that absence of
evidence is not itself a ground for the intervention of the
court, but only goes to show had faith in the tribunal:  see
Leeson's case and Maclean v. Workers' Union; but I do not
think those statements can stand in the light of Osgood9 v.
Nelson which was not cited to the court in either case.
Those cases, it is true, concerned statutory tribunals, but I
see no reason why the power of the court to intervene should
be any less in the case of domestic tribunals.  In each case
it is a question of interpretation, in the one of a statute,
in the other of the rules, in order to see whether the
tribunal have observed the law.

Romer, L.J. [p. 1185], distinguished the club cases and the
medical cases from the Lee case.  To his mind, in the club and
medical cases there were two distinguishing features -- first,
the rules usually provided for expulsion when, in the opinion
of the club, the conduct of the individual so warranted;
secondly, the decision was a question of ethics and not of law.

In the application of the above cases (certain of which are
clearly in conflict with others) to the case at bar, a number
of important facts must be borne in mind.  The termination of
the plaintiff's approval did not depend on any construction of
the Exchange by-laws by the governors, since the termination
was based upon the express and absolute power found in By-laws
49(4) and 67(16).  That being so, the ratio of the Lee case
does not assist Mr. Williston.

The case for a review of the decision reached by the Board of
Governors is rendered even more difficult by virtue of the fact
that unlike the club and medical cases, there is no provision
in the Exchange by-laws specifying that an approval is to be
terminated in the event of the governors forming a particular
opinon as to the level of conduct of an individual.  Nor is any
reference made therein as to a particular reason as grounds for
terminating an approval.  Accordingly, the decision reached by
the governors was not controlled by any statute or rules,
requiring them to form an opinion as to the conduct of Mr.
Posluns, or to make a determination that he committed a
particular act.  The power to terminate an approval is simply
one that may be exercised at the discretion of the governors.
What is the decision, therefore, that I am now entitled to
examine or review in the limited manner described in the cases
referred to above?  Is it the finding of fact by the Board of
Governors that the plaintiff, while a director of the Daly
firm, participated in the profits of Lido, a partnership which
purchased stock options from John Lynch, a client of Dalys, and
resold them immediately after the purchase at a higher price?
(The additional fact that many options were sold off by Lido
prior to being acquired from Mr. Lynch, was probably not known
to the relevant governors at the time of the withdrawal of the
approval.) If this were the decision that the Court is asked to
examine on the merits, then I would not hesitate to say that
the evidence at the two hearings amply bore out that finding by
the governors.  However, Mr. Williston apparently put the
matter in this way:  the foregoing facts amount to an
allegation of misconduct against Mr. Posluns.  But, in view of
the fact that there was not a fiduciary relationship between
Mr. Posluns and Mr. Lynch (based on the asserted legal
proposition that there is no fiduciary relationship between a
director of a corporation and a person to whom a corporation
stands in a fiduciary position), and in light of the evidence
adduced before the Board of the disclosures made by the
plaintiff, and in view of the statements by certain of the
governors that no amount of disclosure of Mr. Lynch would have
affected their decision, that which would prima facie be
misconduct, does not constitute misconduct.  As a consequence
of these additional facts, Mr. Williston urged me to review the
decision of the governors.  In other words, he argued that the
decision was not simply a finding that Mr. Posluns participated
in Lido profits earned from Lynch option transactions, but the
assertion by the governors that his act constituted misconduct.

Before dealing with this contention, I must point out that
another argument may be raised why the Court is not entitled to
examine the action of the governors. The wording of By-laws
49(4) and 67(16), empowering the Board to terminate an approval
at their discretion, does not on their face require that any
specific reason be given therefor.  Accordingly, if no reason
were given, the Court would have no basis upon which to review
the decision.  But as the governors did assign a reason for
withdrawing the Posluns approvals, may I now consider that
reason within the limits permitted by the club and medical
cases, as explained by the English Court of Appeal in the Lee
case?  I think I may.  Some support for the proposition that if
a domestic tribunal which is empowered to take dismissal
measures without providing any reason therefor, does in fact
express a reason, the Court can look at such reason, is found
in the case of Hayman v. Governors of Rugby School (1874), L.R.
18 Eq. 28.  At pp. 68-9, Sir R. Malins V.-C., in explaining the
position of the schoolmaster, who was appointed by the trustees
to hold office and be removable at the will and pleasure of
such trustees, pursuant to statute, stated:

I think the clear result of the numerous authorities cited
... is that all arbitrary powers, such as the power of
dismissal, by exercising their pleasure, which is given to
this governing body, may be exercised without assigning any
reason, provided they are fairly and honestly exercised,
which they will always be presumed to have been until the
contrary is shewn, and that the burthen of shewing the
contrary lies upon those who object to the manner in which
the power has been exercised.  No reasons need be given, but
if they are given the Court will look at their sufficiency.

I return now to the submission of Mr. Williston, that since
the reason given by the governors is a finding of misconduct,
the Court must test that reason against a background of the
alleged non-fiduciary position of Mr. Posluns to Mr. Lynch, the
disclosures made by the plaintiff, and the statements of the
governors that any amount of disclosure by him to Mr. Lynch,
would have been immaterial. These latter facts, said Mr.
Williston, convert what would prima facie be misconduct, into
non-culpable conduct.

To evaluate this contention, one must extract from the cases
referred to earlier the precise extent of the Court's power of
review.  The Court is empowered to determine if the domestice
tribunal acted honestly and bona fide -- the Leeson and
Allinson cases.  Here, there is no doubt of that.  The major
conflict in the cases is whether the Court is limited to seeing
if there is no eivdence to support the tribunal's finding
-- the Leeson case; or if the true test of the Courts' power is
that it can scrutinize the decision to see whether the
evidence, taken as a whole, is reasonably capable of supporting
the offence charged -- Lord Esher's test in the Allinson case
(approved by both Lord Justices Denning and Somervell in the
Lee case).  It can be argued that this latter standard of
review can only be applicable in the case of offences
prescribed by the rules of an organization, or by statute, as
in the Allinson case; that here, where the power of termination
is on its face arbitrary, but the tribunal assigns a reason for
terminating, the Court should restrict itself to seeing that
there was not an absence of evidence to support the tribunal's
conclusion.

If the correct principle is that enunciated in the Leeson
case, then since there certainly was not an absence of evidence
that the plaintiff was guilty of misconduct, the Court is
precluded from proceeding any further.  On the other hand, if
the correct rule is that the Court can look at the tribunal's
decision to see if the evidence was reasonably capable of
proving the wrongdoing, then the Court must deal with Mr.
Williston's submission that the plaintiff's participation in
Lido was not wrongful when other relevant facts are considered.
However, the existence of those other material facts still
yield, in my opinion, the result that the evidence, taken as a
whole, was reasonably capable of justifying the Board of
Governors in concluding that Mr. Posluns' action, having regard
to the standards of ethics and morality required to induce
public confidence in the Toronto Stock Exchange, was such as
warranted the termination of his approvals.

I turn now to the additional material facts relied upon by
Mr. Williston:

1. In the case of Bath v. Standard Land Co., Ltd.,
[1911] 1
Ch. 618
, the defendant company arranged with the plaintiff to
manage, develop and realize his estate on certain terms as to
remuneration.  During the relevant period, the company was a
mortgagee in possession and it was not disputed that the
company stood in a fiduciary relationship to the plaintiff.
During the course of its management, the defendant company
employed one of its directors, who was a solicitor, to act as
solicitor for the estate and paid his bill of costs which
included profit items; another director, who was an estate
agent, to manage at a salary a business connected with the
estate; and another director, who was an auctioneer, to act as
auctioneer at all sales of the estate at the usual commission.
The question before the Court was whether the defendant limited
company was entitled to charge to the plaintiff the amount that
it had paid to its directors for the professional services
rendered by them in respect of the estate managed by the
defendant company on behalf of the plaintiff.  The plaintiff
argued that the defendant company was required to absorb the
charges of its directors for the services rendered by them to
the company, and that these charges could not be passed on the
the plaintiff.  In a majority decision, the Court of Appeal
held that while the directors stood in a fiduciary relationship
to the company, they were not in such position in respect to
the plaintiff, and accordingly the profit cost, salary and
commission paid to them in their professional capacity might be
allowed in taking the accounts between the plaintiff and the
company.  At p. 627, Cozens-Hardy, M.R., stated:

I base my decision upon the broad principle that directors
stand in a fiduciary position only to the company, not to
creditors of the company, not even to individual shareholders
of the company, still less to strangers dealing with the
company. This principle applies equally whether the relation
between the company and the stranger is one purely of
contract, such as principal and agent, or is one of trustee
and cestui que trust.

In reaching the decision, the Court declined to follow the
Irish case of Kavanagh v. Workingman's Benefit Building
Society, [1896] 1 Ir. R. 56, where, upon similar facts, it was
held that the defendant society was not entitled to charge
professional fees paid to certain of its directors, back to the
plaintiff mortgagor.  Mr. Williston asserted that as a
consequence of the Bath case it could not be said that the
plaintiff, a director of the Daly firm, stood in a fiduciary
position to a client of that firm, namely, Mr. Lynch.  In
answer, however, it should be noted that the existence of a
fiduciary relationship depends on the facts and circumstances
of the particular case.  In the Bath case, certain individuals
had to be engaged by the defendant company to perform the
services of a solicitor, a business manager and an auctioneer.
The defendant firm hired its own directors to perform those
services and paid them their remuneration. Those payments were
specifically made by the company for the services rendered to
it and not to the plaintiff.  Despite the very broad statement
of Cozens-Hardy, M.R., I think that while in the Bath case, the
directors may have not been in a fiduciary position to the
plaintiff, in other fact situations, directors may very well
stand in a fiduciary position to individuals who are in a
fiduciary relationship with the company.  The Daly firm was
employed specifically by Mr. Lynch as his agent to sell his
options at the best price available.  That being so, the
knowledge of a director that the purchaser, a firm in which he
personally was interested, was reselling them at a higher
price, is, in my view, sufficient to place that director in a
fiduciary position to Mr. Lynch, with a concomitant requirement
of full disclosure.  In the Bath case, had not the directors
been retained to perform their services, other persons
possessing their qualifications would have been engaged.
Accordingly, the expense would have had to be borne in any
event.  The case would have been otherwise if the expenses were
unnecessary.  In this respect I mention the following comments
of Buckley, L.J., at page 647:

As regards all of them it will be open to Mr. Bath to
contend, if the facts justify it, that the employment was
unnecessary or improper in that, for instance, it was for the
render of a service which the company were themselves bound
to render and for which they had already received payment in
the benefits coming to them under the agreement.

Here, Mr. Lynch was entitled to receive the best prices for his
options, in the absence of disclosure being made to him that
the purchaser of his options (which purchaser was partly
controlled by Mr. Posluns) was reselling them at a higher
price.

In any event, even if the statement of Cozens-Hardy, M.R., is
correct, the Board of Governors is not a Court of law bound by
the principles of decided cases.  It was entitled to adopt the
view that for purposes of broker-customer dealings, a director
of a firm is in a fiduciary relationship with a customer.

2. Mr. Williston contended that the evidence at the hearing
indicated full disclosure by the plaintiff to Dalys, the
Exchange and to Mr. Lynch.  The relevance of the disclosure to
the Daly firm of Mr. Posluns' activities, lies in the fact that
such activities were not prohibited by more senior and
experienced brokerage men in the firm.  The governors took the
view that the individual at Dalys who benefited most from the
Lido operations should receive a more serious punishment than
that meted out to the firm itself.  Therefore, the fact of the
plaintiff's disclosure to the Daly firm goes to the question
whether the Board acted too severely in depriving him of his
opportunity to work as a customers' men, but that is a matter
which is not within my jurisdiction. It would also be only
right to infer, I think, that apart from Mr. Robb, none of the
other directors had much, if any, familiarity with the
intricacies of the put and call business.  Accordingly, that
which was divulged by Mr. Posluns to his fellow directors and
officers other than Mr. Robb, did not have the cogency to cause
those men, who were and still are, in my opinion, entirely
honourable, to avoid a course which, had proper particulars
been given, would have been patently wrong. The correspondence
between the Daly firm and the Exchange in 1960 (exs. 1 to 4)
certainly does not the Exchange the type of tranctions which
occurred between Lido and Mr. Lynch.  So much for the purported
disclosure of the Posluns activities to the Exchange.

With respect to the plaintiff's disclosures to Mr. Lynch
personally, it should be noted that a number of governors
stated in testimony at the trial that no amount of disclosure
to Mr. Lynch would have satisfied them that Mr. Posluns had not
erred in his conduct, for it was their feeling that investors
such as Mr. Lynch had to be protected from themselves.  I
believe that the governors, in their proper concern for the
welfare of those of the public who deal with member firms, were
thoroughly justified in ensuring that a director of a member
broker ought not to be interested in a firm which purchases
securities from a client of the broker, and resells those
securities, either immediately before the purchase or
immediately after, at a higher price.

3. Then it was argued that the amount of disclosure made by
Mr. Posluns and Dr. Shulman to Mr. Lynch was fuller than that
which is generally required by the ethical standards practised
by the governors themselves.  This contention of Mr. Williston
was based upon the fact that member firms, in sending out
recommendation lists of stocks to clients, do not show in such
lists the fact, if it be the fact, that (a) the firm or its
directors may personally own shares in a recommended stock; or
(b) that a director of the member firm may also be a
director of the corporation whose stock is being recommended;
or (c) the fact that the firm may previously have acted as
underwriter for the stock.

To my mind, however, there is a marked distinction between
the failure to disclose the foregoing three matters and any
disclosure requirements with respect to the activities of Mr.
Polsuns and Lido.  In dispatching recommendation lists, brokers
are advising clients to purchase shares, but on any purchase by
a client, the vendor of the shares is not the firm or a
director thereof (when this occurs the evidence of Mr. Deacon,
for example, was to the effect that the firm made disclosure of
this fact).  The broker merely acts as an agent in acquiring
the shares for its client; it is not selling its own personal
shares.  Moreover, the fact that the firm, or one of its
directors, may also own shares in the corporation whose stock
is purchased by a client, does not affect the intrinsic value
of the shares.  This is also true in cases (b) and (c)
mentioned above.  But compare the situation when Mr. Lynch sold
his options through the Daly firm acting as his agent.  There,
those very options were acquired by Lido, in which the
plaintiff was a partner. Furthermore, the fact that Lido had an
immediate purchaser, usually willing to pay a higher price, was
a material factor affecting the inherent value of the options.
It was necessary, therefore, that full disclosure of those
additional circumstances be made to Mr. Lynch, assuming that
disclosure was required.  But the amount of disclosure made to
this client by Dalys, on a sale of an option to Lido, was not
as complete as it could have been for all material facts were
not revealed.  A most important fact was the price at which the
option was to be resold by Lido in New York, or at which it had
already been sold.  The non-disclosure of that act renders the
disclosure to Mr. Lynch something less than adequate.

Accordingly, I am satisfied that even with the additional
aforementioned material facts, the evidence before the
governors was reasonably and logically capable of supporting
their conclusion that Mr. Posluns had been guilty of conduct
incompatible with the ethical behaviour which they deemed
necessary to protect public investors. Whether the Leeson or
Allinson standard of review is adopted, in each case the result
remains the same; I am in full agreement with the decision of
the Board of Governors on the merits.

Mr. Williston's initial complaint in argument that "the
sentence" of the Board "was that the Daly company was tried for
an offence committed by Robb and Posluns was found guilty"
cannot be sustained.  The footing upon which the Board found
each of those two gentlemen to be at fault was not at all the
same. Manifestly from its viewpoint, the hearing of February
28th was originally primarily concerned with the manner in
which the Lynch-Daly-Lido put and call operations had been
conducted.  It is true that Mr. Robb had association with those
activities but apart from his handling of the New York joint
account and the Toronto option account, which at most was a by-
product of the Daly option business, his conduct was not
drawn into the real charge against Mr. Posluns.  On the other
hand, if Dalys were reaping unjust benefits from their Lynch-
Lido dealings, Mr. Posluns was not only a member of the Daly
personnel who had an opportunity to appreciate what was going
on, but undoubtedly was the one who stood to benefit most.
Indeed, even if Mr. Robb was as much at fault as the plaintiff,
there is this significant difference:  he was not deriving
anything directly from Lido.  The fact that Mr. Posluns was
unaware of the spreads being taken in New York and subsequently
in Toronto, would not, as was argued at both hearings, excuse
his involvement in the Daly practices with respect to Mr. Lynch
and Lido.

Mr. Williston strenuously argued that the Board was required
to accept the plaintiff's assertion that he did not know the
details of the put and call transactions being carried on at
Dalys and that he was merely a passive investor in Lido.
Despite statements to the Board to that effect, I can
appreciate why it might think otherwise. There was some
indication to the Board that Mr. Posluns had had contact with
or knowledge of the put and call option business before he
transferred to the Daly company.  For example, it was told that
Dr. Shulman originally asked him to go into friendly
competition with him from which it might well be inferred that
Mr. Posluns had least been apprised of the nature of the
business.  Then, too, it was made to appear that while he was
at Burns that firm engaged in the option business and that
"when he came to Dalys they used the same procedure"
(referring to letters such as exs. 5 and 6).  Moreover, the
Board was informed that he received Lido ledger cards showing
the business done by it on the preceding day, that apparently
he knew that Lido was more successful in its trading through
Doherty Roadhouse than it was through Dalys, that he was aware
of the dealings with Mr. Lynch, and that Mr. Lynch had been
charged a commission by Dalys.  In the face of that
information, as well as knowledge of the circumstance that Mr.
Posluns had personally, and on behalf of other members of his
family, invested or made available to Lido substantial sums of
money, the Board could have concluded that he had kept a fairly
close watch on its activities throughout.  Significantly, Mr.
Stapells was fully conscious of the inherent danger of it being
established that the plaintiff had an insight into what was
being done at Dalys in the put and call business for on
February 28th he endeavoured to meet it in all possible ways
including the presentation of an argument to the effect that if
anyone had done wrong it was Dr. Shulman and not Mr. Posluns.
Of course, I do not mean to suggest that the Board had cause to
think that Mr. Posluns studied the intricate details of each
option transaction, but I believe that its information may have
led it to decide that he was conversant generally with the
nature of the Lynch-Daly-Lido relations and operations.

For those reasons, I am satisfied that the Board of Governors
was justified in its decision that the approval of the
plaintiff should be withdrawn in order to put an end to his
association with the Daly company and that justification would
be a complete defence to this branch of the action unless the
Board resorted to illegal means to achieve its aim.  In other
words, and as already mentioned, the plea of justification will
not be available to the Board if it went beyond its powers or
failed to apply the canons of justice to accomplish its
purpose, no matter how worthy that purpose was.

I must now examine those two possibilities.

(f) Was the justification vitiated because the Exchange
exceeded its powers in procuring a breach of contract?

It is true that there have been isolated suggestions in the
past that justification, if substantiated by the circumstances,
will render inactionable interference which is either unlawful
in its objective or in the means by which it is achieved.  For
example, in the Crofter case, [1942] A.C. at pp. 495-6, Lord
Porter, in what is surely obiter (see his warning at p. 496
that his observations in that respect are not necessary to the
solution of that case), stated that:

... some proceedings are not actionable because neither the
end nor the means are wrongful but there are others in which
either the end or the means are wrongful and yet those acting
in combination are excused because they have just cause for
what they have done.  To induce the breach of a contract
which may lead to immorality (see Brimelow v. Casson,
[1924]
1 Ch. 302
), or of a contract which is an infringement of the
right of of the breaker (see Smithies v. National Association
of Operative Plasterers,
[1909] 1 K.B. 310
), has been held to
be justified.

If that passage was meant to suggest that a lawful purpose
accomplished by illegal means does not give rise to a cause of
action, then it would appear to be out of harmony with positive
authority to the contrary.  Perhaps the learned law Lord
intended it to be confined to that particular case which
involved an alleged conspiracy but no breach of contract.

I am persuaded that where the methods of intervention are in
themselves unlawful, there can be no justification even if the
end sought to be obtained is lawful and desirable.  The same is
true, in my opinion, where, in bringing about a breach of a
contract, the agency involved exceeds its given powers or
authority.  My impression in this respect appears to be appears
to be supported in the following ways:

1.  In the Read case [
[1902] 2 K.B. 732
] the Master of the
Rolls, in the Court of Appeal, after deciding that there
had been a breach of a contract achieved by illegal means,
stated at p. 739: It is, however, very desirable to guard
against the notion that if the act done be illegal "just
cause" may still be averred to purge the wrong.  For
instance, where illegal means have been used to bring about
the breach of a contract to the detriment of a party
thereto, "just cause" cannot come into the discussion at
all.  The use of the illegal means evidence malice, and in
this connection malice was not equivalent ot "without just
cause."  The cause of intervention might be just, but the
means used to enforce it might be illegal.

2.  In the Camden case [
[1940] 1 Ch. 352
] Simonds, J.,
commented at p. 362 that the Read case "... is useful as
showing (a) that what is otherwise wrong is not made better
by an honest belief that it is very much to the advantage
of the person committing the wrong, and (b) that, where
illegal means are used, 'just cause' cannot come into the
discussion at all."

3.  In Klein v. Jenoves & Varley,
1932 CanLII 110 (ON CA)
, [1932] 3 D.L.R. 571, [1932]
O.R. 504, Riddell, J.A., in his striking way, said at p.
575 D.L.R., p. 509 O.R.:

But the end does not justify the means, the excellence of
the object does not purify the conduct of those prompting it,
and no more than the apostle, can the law say that we may do
evil that good may come of it.

I read those passages as establishing that regardless to what
extent the end may be justified, the employment of unlawful or
improper means to gain that end will vitiate its validity.
That conclusion is fully borne out by the text in Winfield, The
Law of Tort, 6th ed., p. 728; Restatement of the Law of Torts,
vol. IV, para. 767, p. 64; and Fleming, The Law of Torts, 2nd
ed., p. 663.

The next question to be decided is this:  although justified
in their decision, did the governors lose the defence of
justification because the means employed to force the Daly
company to break its contract with the plaintiff was beyond the
powers vested in them?  I use the word "force" deliberately
because any other would be utterly unrealistic in view of the
relative positions of the Exchange and R.A. Daly, Jr.  In
considering this issue, I propose to treat the resolution of
the Board with resepct to the plaintiff and the subsequent
delivery of the order (ex. 33) as integral parts of its course
of action to cause the severance of all association between him
and the Daly company.

Mr. Williston argued that the notice on which Dalys acted was
clearly beyond the authority of the Exchange so far as it
purported to require Dalys to dismiss the plaintiff as an
employee.  This contention was based upon the theory that as
the Exchange could not validly withdraw its approval of the
employment of one who did not have to have any approval, and as
Mr. Posluns had not been approved in fact as anything but a
shareholder and director of the Daly company, the letter, which
was the instrument whereby the employment contract was
terminated, was unsupported by any authority given by the by-
laws.  It is quite true that only shareholders, directors,
officers and customers' men of member firms were obliged to be
approved by the Exchange and that such approval could only be
withdrawn under By-law 49, s. 4, as to customers' men, and
under By-law 67, s. 16, as to the others.  The plaintiff was
never an officer of the Daly company and had not been
explicitly sanctioned as a customers' man of that firm.  If,
therefore, he enjoyed some other type of employment by what
right, it was argued, did the Exchange order Dalys to take away
that employment?  I have searched the Exchange's by-laws,
regulations and ruling, and can find no such power.  The only
prerogative that the Exchange had to correct supposed
misconduct on the part of an employee of a member other than a
customers' man and for whom that member was, by By-law 11, s.
2, responsible, was to expel, suspend or fine the member
himself under By-law 11, s. 1. Indeed, the Daly company was
subjected to that form of penalty in this case.  But there is
no authority in the Exchange to simply notify the member to
dismiss an offending employee who is not a customers' man.  If
that is what was done here with respect ot Mr. Posluns, and if,
in fact, he was an employee other than a customers' man, and
the notice brought an end to his employment, then the Exchange
procured a breach of his contract of employment by the supposed
exercise of a power which it did not possess.

While the evidence did not explain the difference, if any,
between a sales man and a customers' man, I am inclined to the
view for the reasons already mentioned, that in the
circumstances Mr. Posluns was employed as a customers' man
rather than as a mere salesman.  That being so, the Exchange
was entitled to withdraw its approval of him as such under By-
law 49, s. 4, so long as it acted within its own rules and
under the conventions of natural justice.

At the trial, much argument was directed to the nature of the
proceedings which resulted in the withdrawal of the plaintiff's
approvals.  It is unnecessary, however, to outline the various
submissions which were put forward in that respect for the
matter can be resolved very shortly.

Clearly, the Board commenced its investigation against the
Daly firm under By-laws 10 and 11.  In that particular
investigation, the Board had no authority, as already stated,
to inflict punishment upon the plaintiff personally.  In my
opinion, it did not do so for those proceedings were finished
when R.A. Daly, Jr. was fined.  Thus, any disposition of a
complaint against Mr. Posluns as a distinct individual could
not have been the result of the investigation taken pursuant to
By-laws 10 and 11.  What right, then, did the Board have to
cause him to be expelled? Such a right was undoubtedly provided
by By-law 49, s.4, and By-law 67, s. 16, and it is quite
obvious that in dealing with him personally, perhaps on
February 28th, but certainly on March 2nd, the Board must have
had recourse to the powers contained in the last-mentioned by-
laws, for while the Board did not do so explicitly, it must
be assumed that it was attempting to proceed within its
jurisdiction.

There is one other matter to be mentioned in connection with
this issue.  It was contended on behalf of the plaintiff that
if the Board did proceed under By-law 49, s. 4, it erred in
stipulating that his employment as a customers' man was to be
ended at once, since the by-law itself contemplated that the
member affected should have "a reasonable period" within which
to "discontinue" the employment of the customers' man
concerned.  I do not agree that the Board mis-applied that by-
law.  In the first place, while the member, R.A. Daly, Jr.,
was aware on February 28th that a resolution for the dismissal
of Mr. Posluns had been passed, he was not actually required to
act until after March 10th when ex. 33 was delivered to him.
During the interval, the plaintiff was given the opportunity to
resign.  Thus, I think it can rightly be said that R.A. Daly,
Jr. had a reasonable time within which to implement the Board's
decision and that Mr. Posluns had at least from March 3rd when
Mr. Goodman was informed of the decision of March 2nd until
some time after March 10th to ponder upon the effect of the
Board's decision, if he did not resign.

In the second place, the condition in the by-law as to when
the withdrawal of the approval was to be acted upon existed
initially at least for the benefit of the employer and not the
employee, and here R.A. Daly, Jr. did not object to form of the
notice, ex. 33.  It might also be argued that the order, "Will
you kindly take such immediate action as may be necessary to
conform to such termination of approval", did not effect
instant dismissal buty only required Mr. Daly to immediately
take proper steps to bring that about.

For those reasons, I have come to the conclusion that on
March 2nd the Board of Governors acted within their by-laws and
regulations when withdrawing the approvals which had been
extended earlier to the plaintiff.

(g) Was the justification vitiated because the plaintiff was
denied natural justice?

(i) Are domestic tribunals subject to the rules of natural
justice?

The problem of determining whether any particular tribunal
(in our case the governors of the Exchange) is subject to
the rules of natural justice can be simplified to some extent
by differentiating between domestic tribunals and
administrative tribunals.  For our purposes, a tribunal may be
defined as administrative if it is established and constituted
by legislation, and is in effect an arm or branch of the
Government.  The latter qualification that the Legislature
- Established tribunal is virtually an arm of the Government,
excludes from the term "administrative tribunals" such
tribunals as the Discipline Committee of the Law Society, and
the various other bodies that regulate the conduct of members
of their respective professions, such as the General Medical
Council which was the subject of litigation in the Leeson and
Allinson cases.  These professional tribunals, although
established by statute, may be classified domestic.  Maugham,
J., in Maclean v. Workers' Union,
[1929] 1 Ch. 602 at p. 620,

defined domestic tribunals as,

a phrase which may conveniently be used to include the
committees or the councils or the members of trade unions, of
members' clubs, and of professional bodies established by
statute or Royal Charter while acting in a quasi-judicial
capacity.

With reference to the term "domestic tribunal", Lord Justice
Morris, in his article in 69 L.Q. Rev. 318 (1953), entitled
"The Courts and Domestic Tribunals", states at p. 321:

I have in mind primarily the bodies or committees in whom
authority is vested in professional or trade or sporting
organisations, in various social groups or clubs or in
various guilds or trade unions.

It is to be observed that an administrative tribunal would
include not merely a number of individuals comprising a board,
but also a department of government, or even a minister.
Administrative tribunals make decisions with respect to the
rights and property of individuals and in so doing the question
frequently arises whether an individual whose rights are to be
affected by a tribunal's decision, is entitled to notice of the
proceedings being taken and an opportunity of being heard.  In
other words, do the rules of natural justice apply to the
particular tribunal?  In numerous cases the enabling
legislation expressly provides for a hearing for the individual
whose rights may be affected by a decision of the tribunal.
Where no specific provision is made in the legislation, the
question is answered by examining the nature of the power
exercised by the tribunal in order to ascertain whether the
tribunal is acting in a quasi-judicial capacity on the one
hand, or in what has been termed an "executive" or
"administrative" capacity on the other.  It is well
established that in those instances where a tribunal acts in a
judicial or quasi-judicial capacity, the rules of natural
justice prevail:  Cooper v. Wandsworth Board of Works
(1863),
14 C.B. (N.S.) 180, 143 E.R. 414
; Hopkins v. Smethwick Local
Board of Health
(1890), 24 Q.B.D. 712
; the Globe case [Re
Toronto Newspaper Guild, Local 87 and American Newspaper Guild
(C.I.O.) and Globe Printing Co.],
1951 CanLII 145 (ON HCJ)
, [1951] 3 D.L.R. 162, 100
C.C.C. 301, [1951] O.R. 435 [affd
1952 CanLII 59 (ON CA)
, [1952] 2 D.L.R. 302, 102
C.C.C. 318, [1952] O.R. 345; affd
1953 CanLII 10 (SCC)
, [1953] 3 D.L.R. 561, 106
C.C.C. 225, [1953] 2 S.C.R. 18].  Where, however, the functions
of the tribunal are held to be administrative or executive, the
tribunal is not bound by the rules of natural justice and need
not afford a hearing to an individual whose rights are touched
by its decision:  Calgary Power Ltd. and Halmrast v. Copithorne
(1958),
1958 CanLII 73 (SCC)
, 16 D.L.R. (2d) 241, 78 C.R.T.C. 31, [1959] S.C.R.
24; The King v. Inspector of Leman Street Police Station, Ex
parte Venicoff,
[1920] 3 K.B. 72
; Ontario Securities Com'n v.
Dobson et al.,
1957 CanLII 412 (ON HCJ)
, 8 D.L.R. (2d) 604, [1957] O.W.N.183, and Nakkuda
Ali v. M.F. De S. Jayaratne,
1950 CanLII 497 (UK JCPC)
, [1951] A.C. 66, [1950] 2 W.W.R.
927.  The determination of whether the function of a tribunal
is judicial or quasi-judicial as opposed to administrative or
executive is based upon the nature of the power exercised by
it:  see Lord Reid's judgment in Ridge v. Baldwin,
[1963] 2 All
E.R. 66 at pp. 78 and 79
, where he refers to the judgments of
Bankes, L.J., and of Atkin, L.J., in The King v. Electricity
Com'rs Ex p. London Electricity Joint Committee Co. (1920),
Ltd.,
[1924] 1 K.B. 171
.

Where the decision of the administrative tribunal is based in
large measure on general government policy, taking into account
the public interest, the function will generally be held to be
executive:  see Martland, J., of the Canadian Supreme Court at
p. 250 D.L.R., pp. 41-3 C.R.T.C., pp. 33-4 S.C.R. of the
Calgary Power case, supra.  In these cases, the tribunal is
accountable to Parliament for its decisions and the interest of
the individual is not paramount. Viscount Haldane, L.C.,
expressed this most aptly in Local Government Board v. Arlidge,

[1915] A.C. 120 at p. 130,
where he stated: There is no
doubt that the question is one affecting property and the
liberty of a man to do what he chooses with what is his own.
Such rights are not to be affected unless Parliament has said
so.  But Parliament, in what it considers higher interests than
those of the individual, has so often interfered with such
rights on other occasions, that it is dangerous for judges to
lay much stress on what a hundred years ago would have been a
presumption considerably stronger than it is to-day.

In the context of statutory administrative tribunals, Lord
Reid in Ridge v. Baldwin, supra, pointed out at p. 75 of the
report that one of the distinguishing characteristics between a
judicial or quasi-judicial function on the one hand and an
executive or administrative function on the other hand, is that
in the former, the tribunal is concerned largely with the
treatment to be accorded to a particular individual; whereas in
the executive type of function, the tribunal is confronted with
a situation where more than one individual's rights are
affected in as much as the problem is one of executing policy
decisions that affect the public interest.  His Lordship also
observed that wartime legislation creating tribunals was
generally interpreted on the basis that the intention of the
Legislature must have been to exclude the principles of natural
justice.

Despite Mr. Pattillo's argument to the contrary, it is quite
clear that the Board of Governors is not an administrative or
executive body to which the rules of natural justice do not
extend.

So much for the moment for non-domestic tribunals.  Turning
now to domestic tribunals, which term refers mainly to clubs,
trade unions and professional groups, and committees thereof,
the cases invariably relate to the expulsion or suspension of a
member from one of those organizations.  It can broadly be
stated that all of the cases hold that before a member of a
social club, trade union, trade or professional association,
can be expelled or suspended therefrom, he must be given notice
of the charges against him and be afforded an opportunity of
answering those charges.

Possibly the earliest case holding that the rules of natural
justice are applicable to the expulsion of a member from a club
is Innes v. Wylie
(1844), 1 Car. & K. 257, 174 E.R. 800
, where
Lord Denman, C.J., in his address to the jury, stated that
while the majority of the members of a society could by
resolution remove any one member in the event of the latter's
misconduct, such a resolution would be rendered invalid by the
lack of notice to the plaintiff of the intention to remove him
from the society, who should have been told what the charge
was, and called on to answer it, and told that it was meant to
remove him if he did not make his defence.  He stated at p.
263:

No proceeding in the nature of a judicial proceeding can be
valid unless the party charged is told that he is so charged,
is called on to answer the charge, and is warned of the
consequences of refusing to do so.  As no such noitce was
given here, I think that the removal is altogether a void
act, and I am therefore of opinion that the plaintiff is
still a member of the society.

The cases I am about to refer to now are noteworthy for the
following reasons: in each case the rules of the organization
stipulated certain grounds upon which a member could be
expelled therefrom, in certain of them the rules provided
specifically for an inquiry, and in others no mention of a
hearing or inquiry was made.  While the by-laws of the Exchange
do not refer to any specific ground for the withdrawal of the
approval granted to an applicant, the cases which follow
involve rules containing specific grounds upon which an
expulsion could be based.  This distinguishing feature will be
dealt with later.

In Wood v. Woad, L.R.
9 Ex. 190
, the rules of a mutual
insurance society provided that if the committee should at any
time deem the conduct of any member suspicious, or that such
member was for any other reason unworthy of remaining in the
society, they should have full power to exclude such member.
The plaintiff alleged that he had been expelled without being
given any opportunity of being heard in his defence or of
showing that there was no ground of suspicion against him or
anything that would make him unworthy of remaining a member.
Kelly, C.B., stated at p. 196:

... was the alleged act of expulsion void?  It is contended
for the plaintiff that the language of the rules gives an
unconditional and absolute power to the committee to expel a
member from the society, and I agree that if the committee in
fact exercised their power under the rules, their decision
could not be questioned; however unfounded the reasons for it
may have been, it would have been final and could not be
reviewed by any Court.  But they are bound in the exercise of
their funcitons by the rule expressed in the maxim audi
alteram partem, that no man shall be condemned to
consequences resulting from alleged misconduct unheard and
without having the opportunity of making his defence.  This
rule is not confined to the conduct of strictly legal
tribunals, but is applicable to every tribunal or body of
person invested with authority to adjudicate upon matters
involving civil consequences to individuals.

In Fisher v. Keane
(1879), 11 Ch. D. 353
, the rules of the
club provided that in case the conduct of any member should in
the opinion of the committee be injurious to the character and
interests of the club, the committee could, upon taking certain
steps, require the member to resign.  At p. 362 Jessel, M.R.,
after having referred to the committee as a judicial or quasi-
judicial tribunal, stated:

... in my opinion a committee, acting under such a rule as
this, are bound to act ... according to the ordinary
principles of justice, and are not to convict a man of a
grave offence which shall warrant his expulsion from the
club, without fair, adequate, and sufficient  notice, and an
opportunity of meeting the accusations brought against him.

In Dawkins v. Antrobus,
17 Ch. D. 615
, the expulsion rule was
similar to that in the Fisher case.  The members of the English
Court of Appeal in the course of their judgment mentioned that
the committee was obliged to grant natural justice to any
member whom they proposed to expel.

Turning now to cases dealing with expulsion from a union,
Burn v. National Amalgamated Labourers' Union of Great Britain
& Ireland,
[1920] 2 Ch. 364
, was concerned with a resolution by
an executive committee removing the plaintiff from any office
then held by him.  Lawrence, J., held, firstly, that the rules
of the union did not warrant the resolution passed by the
executive committee, but, secondly, even if such resolution
were within the powers granted to the executive committee by
the rules, the resolution was invalid because the plaintiff had
not been given an opportunity of being heard before it was
passed.

In Maclean v. Workers' Union,
[1929] 1 Ch. 602
, Maugham, J.,
stated at p. 624 that if the rules postulate an inquiry the
accused must be given a reasonable opportunity of being heard.

Two recent English cases also affirm the right of a member to
natural justice in the event of his expulsion from a union, or
an organization in the nature of a union.  In Abbott v.
Sullivan,
[1952] 1 K.B. 189
, the plaintiff was a cornporter,
being one of those employed in removing grain from ships in
London docks, and the cornporters had long had a committee to
safeguard their interests and exercise considerable
disciplinary powers over them.  This committee removed the
plaintiff's name from the register of cornporters, thereby
depriving him of his opportunity to work in that capacity, on
the ground that he had committed an assault on a trade union
officer, after leaving an earlier meeting of the committee.
All three Judges of the English Court of Appeal were in
agreement that the jurisdiction of the cornporters' committee
did not extend to expelling a cornporter on the grounds of an
assault committed away from his employment. They also
recognized that the rules of natural justice applied to the
action of the cornporters' committee in removing the plaintiff
from the register and that, accordingly, prior to taking such
steps the committee ought to have given the plaintiff notice of
the charge and an opportunity to appear to defend himself
against the accusations made against him.  Evershed, M.R., and
Morris, L.J., declined to reach any conclusion as to whether in
fact the plaintiff had received notice of the charge, but
Denning L.J., held that even assuming the committee to have
jurisdiction to deal with an assault on the street, it had no
jurisdiction in that instance because no proper notice had been
given to the plaintiff of the charge.

In Lee v. Showmen's Guild of Great Britain
[1952] 1 All E.R.
1175
, Denning, L.J., in obiter, stated at p. 1180 that a
domestic tribunal such as the committee of the defendant Guild,
were obliged to observe the principles of natural justice.
Such tribunal must give a man notice of a charge and a
reasonable opportunity of meeting it.  Any stipulation to the
contrary in the rules of the Guild would be invalid.  They
cannot stipulate for a power to condemn a man unheard.

In Bimson v. Johnston,
1957 CanLII 131 (ON HCJ)
, 10 D.L.R. (2d) 11, [1957] O.R. 519,
[1957] O.W.N. 439, the defendant Johnston, as president of a
trade untion, purported to suspend the plaintiff pursuant to
the rules of the constitution of the union.  My brother
Thompson, after deciding that the defendant had no such power
under the rules, and that the act with which the plaintiff was
charged was not an offence for which he could expelled under
the rules, also held that the plaintiff had not been given
notice of any charge brought against him and was not granted an
opportunity to be heard.  He concluded, therefore, that the
plaintiff's suspension was illegal as contrary to the
principles of essential and natural justice.  The decision was
affirmed by the Ontario Court of Appeal,
1958 CanLII 345 (ON CA)
, 12 D.L.R. (2d) 379,
[1958] O.W.N. 217.

A third class of domestic tribunal, other than social clubs
and trade unions discussed above, to which the Court has held
the rules of natural justice applicable, is the tribunal
created by statute to regulate the activities and conduct of a
profession such as in the Leeson case
(1889), 43 Ch. D. 366
.
Particular attention should be paid to the language of the
governing statute in that case.  It provided that if any
registered medical practitioner should, after due inquiry, be
adjudged by the General Council to have been guilty of infamous
conduct in any professional respect, the General Council might
direct the Registrar to erase the name of such practitioner
from the register.  At p. 383, Bowen, L.J., stated:

The jurisdiction is defined by the statute.  There must be an
allegation before the General Medical Council of infamous
conduct in some professional respect, and adjudication must
be arrived after due inquiry. The statute says nothing more,
but in saying so much it certainly imports that the
substantial elements of natural justice must be found to have
been present at the inquiry.  There must be due inquiry.  The
accused person must have notice of what he is accused.  He
must have an opportunity of being heard, and the decision
must be honetly arrived at after he has had a full
opportunity of being heard.

Accordingly, the fact that the tribunal was required to act in
accordance with the dictates of natural justice could be
readily inferred form the language "after due inquiry".

There are two stock exchange cases to be commented upon.  In
Kemerer v. Standard Stock & Mining Exchange
(1927), 32 O.W.N.
295
, a by-law of the Exchange provided for the forfeiture of
the seat of a member and for his suspension and the imposition
of a fine for certain defined misconduct.  The plaintiff was
suspended and fined by the Board of Directors for certain
conduct, and in speaking of their actions.  Middleton, J.A.,
who presided at the trial, stated at p. 297:

... but in carrying out this intention they failed to realise
that in conducting such an inquiry they occupied a quasi-
judicial position and were bound to give reasonable notice
to the member whose conduct was attacked of the precise
nature of the charge upon which he was to be tried; they
failed to give him a reasonable opportunity of defending
himself and meeting the accusations brought against him; and
they failed to realise the importance of having the charges
duly substantiated before acting upon them.

In the case of Silver v. New York Stock Exchange (1963), 83a
Sup. Ct. Rep. 1246, the United States Supreme Court, in a
majority decision, held that the United States anti-trust laws
were applicable to condemn the actions of the New York Stock
Exchange in ordering a number of its member firms to withdraw
their private wire connections to the non-member Silver.  The
New York Stock Exchange defended the action on the basis that
the anti-trust laws were not applicable to it in view of the
fact that the Securities Exchange Act required the Exchange to
regulate transactions of member firms and also transactions of
member firms with non-member firms.

Delivering the majority judgment, Mr. Justice Goldberg stated
at p. 1259:

The final question here is, therefore, whether the act of
self-regulation in this case was so justified.  The answer to
that question is that it was not, because the collective
refusal to continue the private wires occurred under totally
unjustificable circumstances.  Notwithstanding their prompt
and repeated requests, petitioners were not informed of the
charges underlying the decision to invoke the Exchange rules
and were not afforded an appropriate opportunity to explain
or refute the charges against them. Given the principle that
exchange self-regulation is to be regarded as justified in
response to anti-trust charges only to the extent necessary
to protect the achievement of the aims of the Securities
Exchange Act, it is clear that no justification can be
offered for self-regulation conducted without provision for
some method of telling a protesting non-member why a rule is
being invoked so as to harm him and allowing him to reply in
explanation of his position.  No policy reflected in the
Securities Exchange Act is, to begin with, served by denial
of notice and an opportunity for hearing.  Indeed, the aims
of the statutory scheme of self-policing -- to protect
investors and promote fair dealing -- are defeated when an
exchange exercises its tremendous economic power without
explaining its basis for acting, for the absence of an
obligation to give some form of notice and, if timely
requested, a hearing creates a great danger of perpetration
of injury that will damage public confidence in the
exchanges.

The case of Byrne v. Kinematograph Renters Society Ltd.,

[1958] 1 W.L.R. 762
, is also of interest.  There the
plaintiff owned a cinema where he exhibited films distributed
to him by the defendant company.  The consideration paid by him
took the form of a percentage of the receipts.  The defendant
company ascertained that there were discrepancies in certain
reports made to it by the plaintiff and informed the plaintiff
that he could attend a meeting of a general investigation
committee of the defendant company and the C.E.A., a trade
union to protect exhibitors of films and their employees, for
the purpose of making representations on the matter. The
defendant, following the meeting of the general investigation
committee, recommended its members not to supply films to the
plaintiff.  The plaintiff sued for a declaration that the
recommendation for the general investigation committee was null
and void on the ground that it was the result of proceedings
conducted contrary to natural justice.  Harman, J., stated that
in order that a declaration could be rendered on the grounds of
non-compliance with the principle of natural justice, some form
of contractual nexus between the plaintiff and the defendant
was required.  At p. 783 he stated that any contract, if there
be one, between the two parties must have come into existence
when the plaintiff was invited to attend the inquiry and agreed
to do so. The contract would then be that the inquiry should be
fairly conducted. It was his opinion that in a case such as
that before him, it was right to imply such a contract.  He
quoted the extract from Lord Parmoor at p. 636 of Weinberger v.
Inglis,
[1919] A.C. 606
, which I will refer to later, and
continued, at pp. 738-4:

It seems to me that bodies like K.R.S., who exercise
monopolistic powers and may ruin a man by their
recommendations, ought not to act in an arbitrary manner, or
at the least that if they do, as this body did, set up an
investigation committee which is a quasi-judicial body, they
must be taken to hold out to those over whom they claim to
exercise jurisdiction the assurance that the proceedings will
be fair.

Applying the Byrne case to the case at bar, it can be argued
that if the Toronto Stock Exchange by-laws do not specifically
provide for a hearing in the circumstances, then at least when
it agreed to grant a hearing to Mr. Posluns on March 1st, an
implied contract arose that the hearing should be conducted in
accordance with the principles of natural justice.

Perhaps the sole exception to the line of cases which hold
that a member of an organization can only be expelled or
suspended therefrom upon notice and after being afforded an
opportunity to be heard, is the judgment of Lord Justice Tucker
in Russell v. Duke of Norfolk,
[1949] 1 All E.R. 109
, which
concerned the withdrawal of a trainer's licence by the Jockey
Club, pursuant to rules providing for withdrawal on the ground
of misconduct, thereby disqualifying him from any further
participation in the sport of horse racing. The Jockey Club
must be considered to be a domestic tribunal on the basis that
it is somewhat analogous to the other organizations described
in that some form of consensual arrangement is derived from the
rules whereby members agree to be bound by their provisions.
It certainly does not appear to be a government tribunal.  In
the Russell case, although a notice was given and a hearing
conducted, Tucker, L.J., held that on the basis of the rules of
the club, a trainer's licence could be withdrawn without his
being afforded a hearing.  The other two Judges construed the
rules as requiring a hearing for withdrawal of a licence on
grounds of misconduct, and on the facts held that there had
been no denial of natural justice.  This judgment will be
referred to later in greater detail for the purpose of
determining whether appropriate language found in the rules of
a voluntary association, such as we are dealing with here, can
exclude the rules of natural justice.

In the result, and despite Lord Tucker's views on the Russell
case, it would appear that with respect to all domestic
tribunals whose constitution or rules provide for expulsion of
a member for a stipulated cause, the rules of natural justice
apply.

(ii) Need a hearing be granted where dismissal is in the
discretion of a  tribunal?

I am of the opinion, too, that a hearing must be granted
where the power of dismissal is exercisable in the discretion
of a domestic tribunal. Ridge v. Baldwin,
[1963] 2 All E.R. 66
,
is certainly one of the most important cases on this whole
subject.  In it the watch committee, a police authority,
established by statute, was empowered by s.191(4) of the
Municipal Corporations Act, 1882, to "dismiss any borough
constable whom they think negligent in the discharge of his
duty, or otherwise unfit for the same".

In determining whether the watch committee in exercising its
power of dismissal was obliged to follow the rules of natural
justice, Lord Reid, at p. 71, divided cases of dismissal into
three categories:  dismissal of a servant by his master,
dismissal from an office held during pleasure, and dismissal
from an office when there must be something against a man to
warrant dismissal.  With respect to a case where a man holds an
office at pleasure, the law is that an officer has no right to
be heard before he is dismissed.  Since the person having the
power of dismissal need not have anything against the officer,
he need not give any reason.  While agreeing that the decision
was doubted in Dean v. Bennett (1870), L.R. 6 Ch. 489 at p.
496, and distinguished on narrow grounds in Willis v. Childe

(1851), 13 Beav. 117, 51 E.R. 46
, Lord Reid states that the
leading case on this point is The Queen v. Governors of
Darlington Free Grammar School
(1844), 6 Q.B. 682, 115 E.R.
257
.  This triumvirate of cases is interesting from the point
of view of the language employed in the authorizing charters
empowering the governing officials of the respective
institutions to dismiss a particular officer.  There is a
distinct similarity in the language used in the charter in the
Darlington case, where the officer was held to be holding
office at pleasure, and the language found in By-law 67, s. 16
of the Exchange by-laws.  Mr. Pattillo argued that the position
held by Mr. Posluns was akin to that of an officer at pleasure
and hence he could be removed, in the sense of having his
approval terminated, without any hearing being granted to him
by the Board of Governors.  I propose therefore to examine the
three cases cited by Lord Reid, but it should be remembered
that in each of the three the person dismissed was holding an
office and was dismissed by his superior.  In the case at bar,
the plaintiff had his licence approval terminated not, by his
immediate superior, but by a body that governed, inter alia,
the actions of himself and of his immediate superior, the Daly
firm.

In The Queen v. Governors of Darlington Free Grammar School,
the school charter empowered the governors to remove a master
according to their sound discretion.  It was held by both Lord
Denman, C.J., and by the Court of Exchequer Chamber that the
governors might in their discretion remove a master without
summons or hearing.  The dismissed master argued that as the
governors had in fact specified certain grounds as a reason for
dismissing him, and that as the jury had found that he had not
in fact done the acts complained of, their order of dismissal
was without justification.  In answer to that Lord Denman said
that the governors might be reasonably satisfied of the truth
of the charges without presenting any means of proving them by
evidence and, even if they had no charge before them, they
might still, in the exercise of their discretion, remove him
for reasonable cause.  Tindal, C.J., at p. 715, stated that the
governors would be guilty of misconduct if they exercised their
discretion of removal in an oppressive manner, or from any
corrupt or indirect motive, but that there was nothing to
restrain them from exercising such discretionary power whenever
they honestly thought it proper so to do.

In Willis v. Childe, Lord Langdale, M.R., held that the power
vested in the trustees of the grammar school to remove the
master at their discretion, was in the nature of a trust in
view of the following language found in the scheme of
regulation:  "... in the due exercise and execution of the
powers and trusts reposed in them ...."  Accordingly, it was
decided that the provision did not confer upon the trustees an
arbitrary power to dismiss the master upon any grounds which
they might deem just, free from any control of the Court, and
an injunction was granted since he had not been given a proper
hearing.

Finally, in Dean v. Bennett, where the deed of settlement of
a Baptist chapel provided that every minister of the church
should be liable to removal by the decision, order or direction
of the church, made and declared at one meeting, and confirmed
at a second meeting called for that purpose, Lord Hatherley,
L.C. held that since the discretion was oppressively exercised,
the principle of the Darlington case did not apply.
Furthermore, the notice calling the second meeting was
defective.  Accordingly, the resolution of dismissal was held
void.

The importance of the Darlington case and the Dean v. Bennett
case for our purposes is this:  the Exchange can point to the
language of the Charter in the Darlington case as being quite
similar to that found in the relevant by-laws of the Exchange.
It was held in Darlington that since the power of dismissal was
in the discretion of the governors, the governors were not
obliged to prove any charge against the master and were not
required to give him a summons or hearing.  Likewise, Mr.
Pattillo argued that since the governors could in their
discretion terminate any approval, they did not need to provide
any charge or reason for so doing, and did not need to grant a
hearing.  Moreover, in the Darlington case, the governors did
in fact allege specific charges against the master, which
charges the jury found had not been proved.  Despite this fact,
it was decided that the governors were entitled to terminate
the master's position.  The Exchequer Court found that the
office of a master was an office held at pleasure only, and
that the governors could exercise their discretionary power
whenever they honestly thought it proper so to do.  The
Exchange can point to a parallel situation here inasmuch as the
language of its by-laws is couched in similar terms, and
accordingly, it was contended that the mere fact that they
charged Mr. Posluns with a specific offence, to wit,
misconduct, did not prevent the governors from falling back
upon the words of the by-law, enabling the Exchange to
terminate his approval in its discretion, and hence without a
hearing.

Mr. Posluns can argue, perhaps, that Dean v. Bennett is in
his favour inasmuch as the arbitrary power of dismissal
contained in the deed of settlement was somewhat similar to the
language of By-laws 49, s. 4 and 67, s. 16, and yet Lord
Hatherley found that the tribunal had not exercised a sound
discretion. Moreover, his Lordship criticized the church for
having held a meeting at which charges were made without first
giving notification to the minister as to what the charges
would be.

Thus, these two cases raised the following questions -- where
the rules of the organization enable the tribunal to dismiss an
individual in its discretion without qualification, if the
tribunal purports to exercise its discretion of dismissal or
removal and specifically alleges a charge of misconduct, is a
hearing required? And is a hearing in such circumstances
necessary where the order does not sever the relations between
the organization and the person condemned, but between that
person and another?

In his article on "The Disciplinary Powers of Professional
Bodies", 13 Modern Law Rev. 281 (1950), Professor Lloyd stated
at p. 285 that one of the currents of authority drawn upon by
the Court in formulating rules with respect to domestic
tribunals, was a number of Chancery decisions relating to the
expulsion of partners or directors from trading partnerships or
companies.

In Blisset v. Daniel
(1853), 10 Hare 493, 68 E.R. 1022
, the
articles of partnership provided that it should be lawful for
the holders of two-thirds or more of the partnership shares for
the time being to expel any partner by giving him notice
thereof under their hands in the form thereby prescribed. Upon
a partner being expelled, the amount of his share was to be
ascertained and his share would thereafter be disposed of to
the remaining partners.  Sir W. Page Wood, V.-C., held that the
power of expulsion of a partner might be exercisable by two-
thirds of the partners without any previous meeting of the
partners and committee upon the question, and without any cause
being assigned for such expulsion.  However, he emphasized that
the power must be exercised with good faith, and not against
the truth and honour of the contract, pointing out that such a
power must be understood to exist, not for the benefit of any
particular party holding two-thirds or more of the shares, but
for the benefit of the whole society or partnership.  It could
not be exercised merely to enable the continuing partners to
appropriate to themselves a share of the expelled partner at a
fixed value less than the true value.  At p. 530 the Vice-
Chancellor said that it was incumbent upon that partner who
was taking the initiative in the matter, to let the proposed
expelled partner have at least an equal opportunity with
himself of laying his case before the other partners, who held
the two-thirds.

That case was explained by Jessel, M.R. in Russell v. Russell

(1880), 14 Ch. D. 471
.  At p. 479 he said that the Vice-
Chancellor had decided that in a case of that kind the
partner had no right to expel merely for the purpose of buying
up the shares; to do so was not a fair and bona fide exercise
of the power.  He continued:

Then they alleged that they had grounds of dissatisfaction
with the partner, but his reply in effect was, "If you have
any ground of dissatisfaction you ought to have given me
notice to see if I had anything to answer."

There the Vice-Chancellor was of opinion that even in that
