limited case, where it was only inter se as regards the
partners themselves, yet, if the reason, as far as the other
parnters concerned, was misconduct, they ought to give the
partner sought to be expelled an opportunity of explaining
his alleged misconduct.

It should also be mentioned that Kelly, C.B., in delivering
his judgment in Wood v. Woad, strongly relied upon Blisset v.
Daniel.  He stated that the decision in that case was in point
to show that it was incumbent upon the committee in the mutual
insurance society to give any partner whom they proposed to
exclude a chance of stating his case.  One can therefore
conclude from Blisset v. Daniel that although a power of
expulsion may be worded absolutely, yet, if it is proposed to
exercise such power on the ground of misconduct, notice must be
given to the individual who it is proposed to expel.

The strongest authority to support the contention of the
Exchange that no notice was required to be given to the
plaintiff is the judgment of Tucker, L.J., in Russell v. Duke
of Norfolk, mentioned earlier.  The plaintiff was a trainer of
horses and had paid to obtain his annual licence from the
stewards of the jockey club.  A condition of the licence was
[[1949] 1 All E.R. at p. 111]:

3. A trainer's licence may be withdrawn or suspended by the
stewards of the Jockey Club in their absolute discretion, and
such withdrawal or suspension may be published in the RACING
CALENDAR, for any reason which may seem proper to them, and
they shall not be bound to state their reasons.

The licence was expressed to be subject to the provisions of
the Rules of Racing.  Rule 17 of such Rules provided [p. 113]:

The stewards of the Jockey Club have power, at their
discretion, to grant, and to withdraw, licences ... to make
inquiry into, and deal with, any matters relating to racing,
and to warn any person off Newmarket Heath...

Another rule provided that a person whose licence to train has
been withdrawn on the ground of misconduct was a disqualified
person, that is, one prohibited from having any connection with
horse racing.  Following an inquiry into the circumstances in
which one of the horses trained by him won a race, the stewards
of the Jockey Club withdrew the plaintiff's trainer licence on
the ground of negligence amounting to grave misconduct.  The
plaintiff thus became a disqualified person.  He argued that he
had not been given sufficient notice of the charges made
against him and had not been given a proper hearing. Tucker,
L.J., stated that, assuming there was a contract between the
plaintiffs and defendants based upon the licence and the Rules
of Racing, the question first to be decided was whether it was
a term or condition of that contract that he should not have
his licence withdrawn or could not be disqualified on the
ground of misconduct without an inquiry having been conducted
in accordance with the principles of natural justice.  He
construed the rules in such a way that it was impossible to
imply into the contract the term sought by the plaintiff, and
stated that such a term would have been inconsistent with the
existence of an unfettered and absolute discretion in the
stewards.  He decided, therefore, that they were entitled to
withdraw a licence without making inquiries.

Asquith, L.J., stated that reading the rules as a whole,
where what is involved is the proposed withdrawal of a licence
for misconduct, and inquiry, and an inquiry which conforms to
the principles of natural justice, is a necessary pre-
condition.  Denning, L.J., drew a distinction between the
case where the Jockey Club merely withdrew the licence as a
matter of discretion without inflicting any penalty, and the
case where the club withdrew it as a penalty for misconduct.
In the former, he said that he did not think the rules
postulated an inquiry and that the stewards had an absolute
discretion on the matter; they need hold no inquiry and need
give no reason.  However, he was of the opinion that when the
stewards were exercising the far more serious power of
withdrawing a licence under another rule on the ground of
misconduct, they must give the trainer an opportunity of
defending himself, saying at p. 119:

It [the penalty] disqualifies the trainer from taking any
part in racing and thus takes away his livelihood.  Common
justice requires that before any man is found guilty of an
offence carrying such consequences, there should be an
inquiry at which he has the opportunity of being heard.  It
might, perhaps, be possible for the stewards to stipulate
expressly for power to condemn a man unheard, but I should
doubt it.  It may be that such a stipulation would be
contrary to public policy.

After pointing out that in any event he found no stipulation in
the rules enabling the stewards to withdraw the licence on the
ground of misconduct without an inquiry, Denning, L.J., also
said:

It has been argued that the stewards need have no inquiry at
all, and that, therefore, it does not matter if they hold one
which is not a proper one. I do not agree with that.  I think
there must be an inquiry at which the person concerned has an
opportunity of being heard.  The stewards should not act on
information against him without giving him an opportunity of
answering it.

Accordingly, it is reasonably apparent that Denning, L.J.,
based his judgment on two grounds:  first, that the rules
themselves provided for an inquiry where the licence was
withdrawn on the ground of misconduct, and, secondly, common
justice required that where a person was to be disqualified
from horse racing on the ground of his misconduct, a hearing
should be afforded him.

In any event, it is of importance that all three Judges were
in agreement that the plaintiff had been accorded a fair
hearing and that the rules of natural justice had not been
denied him.

At this stage, I should deal more fully with Weinberger v.
Inglis,
[1919] A.C. 606
, a case in which it was held that the
rules of natural justice apply to the governing committee of a
stock exchange.  It is noteworthy that Tucker, L.J., in the
Russell case did not refer to the Weinberger case.  In the
latter, the facts were these:  the proprietors of a stock
exchange were a voluntary association regulated by a deed of
settlement which provided that a committee for general purposes
should be annually elected by the members, and that the
committee should admit such persons as they should "think
proper" to frequent the stock exchange, for transacting therein
the business of a stock broker for the term of one year on
payment of the entrance fee (if any) and annual subscription.
The deed empowered the committee to make rules not inconsistent
with the provisions of the deed respecting (inter alia) the
admission, expulsion and suspension of members.  By r. 21(1) of
the Rules of the Stock Exchange made under this power, "the
committee shall on the first Monday in March proceed to re-
elect such members ... as they shall deem eligible to be
members of the Stock Exchange, for one year..."

The plaintiff in the action was a naturalized British subject
of German birth and had been a member of the Stock Exchange for
many years. During the 1914-18 war the plaintiff applied for
re-election as a member, but his application was refused.  The
plaintiff ahd been informed that the committee would not re-
elect him on the ground of his German birth, and he was
invited to appear before the committee to show cause why the
fact of his German birth should not preclude him from re-
election as a member of the Exchange. The plaintiff attended
before the committee and stated numerous facts in proof of his
loyalty with a view to displacing the objection.  However, as
stated, the committee deconed to re-elect him.  The plaintiff
sued to impugn the decision of the committee on the ground that
it was arbitrary and capricious. The committee by their defence
alleged that they did not re-elect the plaintiff because they
did not deem him eligible to be a member of the Stock Exchange
for the year in question, pursuant to r. 21(1).  All the
learned law Lords held that in the circumstances there had been
no improper exercise of the discretion vested in the committee.

The House of Lords decided that the discretion of the
committee had been exercised bona fide and not arbitrarily or
capriciously, and that the proper inference from the facts was
that the refusal of the committee had proceeded solely on the
ground of enemy birth, as to which the plaintiff had been
heard.  The ratio, pure and simple, appears to be that the
committee had exercised its discretion bona fide.  However,
since five different judgments were rendered, there are a
number of dicta concerning various other aspects of the case,
including the question of whether the plaintiff was entitled to
notice and a hearing prior to the decision of the committee not
to re-elect him in view of his German birth.  Before referring
to the comments of the various Lords with respect to the
requirement of natural justice, I think that in comparing this
case with the case at bar, two important facts should be borne
in mind: (1) the language in the deed of settlement provided
that the committee should admit such persons as they should
"think proper" and the rules provided that they should re-
elect such members "as they shall deem eligible".  This
terminology is quite broad in its nature and should be compared
with the language of By-law 67, s. 16 of the Exchange by-laws,
providing that the Board of Governors may, in its discretion,
at any time, terminate any approval which it may have given
with respect to any corporation, and of By-law 49, s. 4,
permitting the Board to terminate the approval of a customers'
man at any time; (2) the law Lords in examining the nature of
the interest acquired by a member on his election for a year,
were not in precise agreement but nevertheless did indicate
that a member's right expired at the end of the year with
respect to which he was elected, and further, that he did not
possess a vested right to be elected for the subsequent year.
That should be contrasted with the position of Mr. Posluns who
would seem to have had approvals that were vested, but were
subject to being divested.

From the language used by the law Lords in the Weinberger
case, a member of the Exchange had no vested interest but was
required in each year to apply to be re-elected as a member.
On the basis that a new application was to be made each year,
one might have thought that the committee exercising its
discretion bona fide in refusing to re-elect, might have been
justified in refusing to grant a hearing since a previously
elected member had legally not been deprived of any position.
However, that was not the position taken by three of the four
law Lords who expressed an opinion on the point.  At p. 616,
Lord Birkenhead, L.C., for example, had this to say:

I may add that if I took the view that the appellant was
condemned upon grounds never brought to his notice, I should
not assent to the legality of this course, unless compelled
by authority.

The observations of Lord Parmoor at pp. 635-6 are significant:

... this finding that the consideration of the Committee was
limited to a single issue, of which the appellant had notice,
and which he had full opportunity to answer, is of critical
importance in the determination of the appeal.

As at present advised and without hearing further argument,
I am not prepared to hold that a body in the position of the
Committee of the Stock Exchange have an absolutely autocratic
power to act as they please, and without regard to
fundamental principles of just inquiry, in exercising a duty
which is judicial in this sense, that it necessarily implies
consideration and a decision which affects not only the
immediate pecuniary interests, but also the whole business
status of the member whose re-election is refused .... I know
of no decision in this House which would exempt the Committee
of the Stock Exchange from similar obligations to observe the
fundamental principles of just action in giving a decision on
the ineligibility of a member of the Stock Exchange, but, on
my interpretation of the facts, the question does not arise
for determination in the present appeal.

Ridge v. Baldwin,
[1963] 2 All E.R. 66
, also contains a
number of statements which certainly do not assist the Exchange
on this branch of the case.  At p. 75, Lord Reid, after quoting
the above statement of Lord Birkenhead in Weinberger v. Inglis,
continued on to observe:

He said this although the rule under which the committee
acted was in the widest possible terms -- that the committee
should each year re-elect such members as they should deem
eligible as members of the stock exchange.

This last statement certainly indicates the view of Lord Reid
that although a power of removal or dismissal, as in the
Weinberger case, may be worded very broadly, nevertheless, the
grounds upon which such action is being taken should be brought
to the attention of the party, and he should be granted a
hearing at which to answer such grounds as best he can.

Before referring to portions of the judgments of Lord Morris
and Lord Hodson, I draw attention again to the statutory
language empowering the watch committee to dismiss any
constable whom they thought negligent in the discharge of his
duty, or otherwise unfit.  At p. 107, Lord Morris stated:

I cannot think that the dismissal of the appellant should be
regarded as an executive or administrative act if based on a
suggestion of neglect of duty:  before it could be decided
that there had been neglect of duty it would be a pre-
requisite that the question should be considered in a
judicial spirit.  In order to give the appellant an
opportunity to defend himself against a charge of neglect of
duty he would have to be told what the alleged neglect of
duty was.

At p. 114, Lord Hodson observed that where the power to be
exercised involved a charge made against the person who is
dismissed (In other words a charge of misconduct), the
principles of natural justice have to be observed before the
power is exercised.  Those statements of Lords Morris and
Hodson must be taken in their context, which relates to a
specific statutory power to dismiss for negligence in the
discharge of duty.  With reference to the power of the watch
committee to dismiss a constable on the ground that he was
"otherwise unfit for the same", Lord Morris stated at p.
111:

I do not find it necessary to express any concluded opinion
whether, if there were no suggestion of having been negligent
in the discharge of duty, a decision to dismiss on the ground
of being "unfit" for the discharge of duty could be taken
without giving an opportunity to be heard.  Clearly it would
be desirable and reasonable to give such an opportunity even
though alleged unfitness did not involve misconduct.

On this point Lord Hodson comments at p. 114:

In one respect no doubt the watch committee were given an
absolute discretion to act as they might think, that is to
say, I agree that their residual power to dismiss for
unfitness may well be unfettered.

The immediate effect of all of those authorities is to
suggest to me that when dismissal is in the discretion of a
domestic tribunal, and certainly where misconduct is the
alleged ground for the exercise of that discretion, the person
affected must be given reasonable notice of the complaint made
against him and must have a fair hearing before being
dismissed.  If a charge of misconduct is required before it
becomes necessary to invoke those principles of natural justice
in a case where dismissal is in the discretion of the domestic
tribunal (and I doubt that a charge of misconduct is a
prerequisite), then it has been fully satisfied here, for the
Board of Governors alleged and found unethical practices on the
part of Mr. Posluns.  Indeed, that was the sole basis for the
withdrawal of his approval as a customers' man. And I think it
matters not that the plaintiff was not dismissed by the
Exchange, the organization which made the order.  I see no
reason whatever to insist upon the application of the precepts
of natural justice where a penalty is imposed directly and to
discard those salutary precepts when the penalty is to be
effectively executed by indirect means.

(iii) Can the express rules of an association validly exclude
the rules of natural justice?

Mr. Pattillo argued, however, that s. 4 of By-law 49, and s.
16 of By-law 67, had to be construed as tantamount to express
provisions excluding the principles of natural justice, and
that the plaintiff, by the terms of the application for
approval as a customers' man, had contractually bound himself
by those provisions.  Before determining whether the by-laws
can be so interpreted, I propose first to examine the validity
of an express prohibition, for if such a provision is bad in
law, then obviously the same is true for a provision whcih is
construed to have that effect. Halsbury, 3rd ed., vol. 5, with
reference to the topic "Clubs", p. 263, states that the
principles of natural justice must also be observed in
exercising a power of expulsion, unless it plainly appears, on
the true construction of the rules, that the power was intended
to be absolute.  That statement implies that the rules of
natural justice can be excluded.  However, neither of the cases
cited in support of it, Wood v. Woad and Russell v. Russell,
referred to above, would seem to bear it out.  It is difficult
to see how the judgment of Kelly, C.B. [L.R.
9 Ex. 190
], and
the extract therefrom at p. 196, can sustain this proposition
that the rules can be excluded, for he makes no reference
whatever to such a possibility.  Russell v. Russell,
14 Ch. D.
471
, concerned a partnership of two individuals where the
articles provided that if the business could not be conducted,
or the result therof should not be, to the satisfaction of B,
he should have power to give notice to A to determine the
partnership.  Jessel, M.R., held that the power to give notice
under the articles was exerciseable by B at his own will and
pleasure and that there was no obligation upon him to act as a
tribunal or to state the grounds upon which he decided for
himself.  This case of a partnership composed of two partners
was distinguished from the situation in Blisset v. Daniel where
there were a number of partners, and the case of Wood v. Woad
where there was a mutual insurance society.  He stated at p.
480:

How that case applies to the case of a single partner I do
not well understand. In the case of several partners it may
well be that it is a thing to be considered, but if it is a
single partner it is plain that neither Blisset v. Daniel nor
Wood v. Woad has any application, because the moment you give
the power to a single partner in terms which shew that he is
to be sole judge for himself, not to acquire a benefit, but
to dissolve a partnership, then he may exercise that
discretion capriciously, and there is no obligation upon him
to act as a tribunal, or to state the grounds on which he
decides for himself.

The Master of the Rolls went on to state that the partner
having this power need not make any inquiry, and need not call
upon the partners for explanation. It is open for him to say,
"I am not satisfied", and that is an end to it [p. 481].

It is true that in Maclean v. Workers' Union,
[1929] 1 Ch.
602
, Maugham, J., at p. 623, stated that the rights of a member
of a union depended simply upon contract, and that the material
terms of the contract were to be found in the rules.  He
stated:

In the case I have before me (and I may add in such a case as
a power of expulsion in a members' club) it seems to me
reasonably clear that the matter can only depend on contract
express or implied. If, for instance, there was a clearly
expressed rule stating that a member might be expelled by a
defined body without calling upon the member in question to
explain his conduct, I see no reason for supposing that the
Courts would interfere with such a rule on the ground of
public policy.

However, in Dawkins v. Antrobus, 17 Ch. D. at p. 630, Brett,
L.J., stated, with reference to a club, that the Court could
only consider whether anything had been done which was contrary
to natural justice although within the rules of the club -- in
other words, whether the rules of the club were contrary to
natural justice.  The inference, of course, is that if the
rules are contrary to natural justice, they would be invalid.

It should be noted that both of the preceding statements were
obiter in the respective cases.

There are three recent decisions of the English Court of
Appeal containing dicta by Denning, L.J., to the effect that
any provision in the rules of an association which excludes the
rules of natural justice would be invalid as being contrary to
public policy.  In Russell v. Duke of Norfolk, [1949] 1 All
E.R. at p. 119, he stated:

It might, perhaps, be possible for the stewards to stipulate
expressly for power to condemn a man unheard, but I should
doubt it.  It may be that such a stipulation would be
contrary to public policy:  see the judgment of BRETT, L.J.,
in Dawkins v. Antrobus (
17 Ch. D. 630
), the judgment of
KELLY, C.B., in Wood v. Woad (L.R. 9 Exch. 196) and of LORD
BIRKENHEAD, L.C., in Weinberger v. Inglis (
[1919] A.C. at
616
).  It is very different from a mere dismissal of a
servant or withdrawal of a licence or even expulsion from a
club, which MAUGHAM, J., had in mind in  Maclean v. Workers'
Union (
[1929] 1 Ch. at 623
].  The Jockey Club has a monopoly
in an important field of human activity.  It has great powers
with corresponding responsibilities.

It should be observed that the foregoing statement is obiter
in view of the fact the Denning, L.J., expressly finds no
stipulation in the rules of the Jockey Club enabling the
stewards to act under a specified rule (r. 102) without an
inquiry.  Moreover, as already mentioned, the statements of
Brett, L.J., and Maugham, J., which conflict with each other,
are both obiter. Thirdly, in neither of the remarks of Kelly,
C.B., or of Lord Birkenhead, L.C., is there any reference to
there being any rules ousting the principles of natural
justice.

In Abbott v. Sullivan,
[1952] 1 K.B. 189
, Denning, L.J., at
p. 198, repeated the remarks he had made in the earlier case,
and in Lee v. Showmen's Guild,
[1952] 1 All E.R. 1175, at p.
1180,
he does the same, and again refers to the cases to which
he had referred in the Russell case. He states that the
judgments of Brett, L.J., Kelly, C.B., and Lord Birkenhead,
L.C., are to be preferred to the dictum of Maugham, J.  As
before, his remarks in both those cases were obiter.

Two Canadian trial judgments have applied the language of
Denning, L.J., in the Lee case to hold that provisions in the
constitution of a union which purport to exclude the right to a
hearing, are contrary to public policy, and hence invalid.  In
Kennedy v. Gillis et al., Gillis et al. v. Smith & Kennedy,
1961 CanLII 149 (ON HCJ)
, 30
D.L.R. (2d) 82, [1961] O.R. 878, a section of the Mine, Mill
and Smelter Workers' Canadian Constitution, provided that if
any officer did any act in furtherance of the secession or
withdrawal of any local union from the international union,
that person should be deemed, upon the performance of such act,
to have automatically forfeited his right and title to his
office or position, and that the Canadian president should have
the power to so declare.  McRuer, C.J.H.C., interpreted that
provision to mean that the forfeiture to the office followed
the declaration of the president.  The Canadian president made
the declaration contemplated by the section, removing certain
members as officers of the local union, without granting to
these officers a hearing or even without making any specific
charges against them.  The Chief Justice held that natural
justice demanded that the officers be given an opportunity to
be heard with respect to any allegation made against them,
before the president exercised his power to make a declaration
affecting their rights.  Counsel for the president had argued
that the language of the constitution, read as a layman would
read it, did not contemplate a hearing by the president before
he exercised his power to make a declaration. McRuer, C.J.H.C.,
held that that contention was disposed of by the statement of
Lord Justice Denning in the Lee case.  He continued at pp. 88-9
D.L.R., pp. 884-5 O.R.:

This case goes so far as to hold that even if such a
provision was expressly made in the constitution it would be
contrary to public policy.  I do not have to deal with an
express provision but I am asked to imply that the parties
have agreed that the ordinary common law rights to a hearing
do not apply.  I am not prepared to make that implication.
There is nothing in the constitution that would warrant me in
doing so and even if I did the Lee case would be a complete
answer to this argument.

In Hughes v. Seafarers' International Union of North America,
Canadian District & Heinekey (1961),
1961 CanLII 390 (BC SC)
, 31 D.L.R. (2d) 441,
Verchere, J., of the British Columbia Supreme Court held that
the plaintiff had been wrongfully expelled from the defendant
trade union.  His first ground was that the tribunal that had
heard charges against the plaintiff had had the composition of
those sitting altered between hearings, and accordingly this
nullified the decision of the tribunal.  Secondly, the
constitution of the union required that any report of a union
tribunal should be ratified at the next regular meeting of the
union.  This in fact occurred.  However, the plaintiff was
excluded from attending at the regular union meeting held for
the purpose of ratifying the decision of the tribunal, upon the
basis that an article of the constitution provided that a
member under charges should not be permitted to enjoy
membership facilities.  Since the ratification meeting was to
take place in the union hall the plaintiff, was not permitted
to be present. Speaking with reference to that provision in the
constitution, Verchere, J., said, at p. 447, that that
interpretation of the article should not have been accepted
with its resultant denial to the plaintiff of a right to a
hearing. He quoted Denning, L.J., in the Lee case, and decided
that the action of the defendant union in ratifying the
tribunal's report in the absence of the plaintiff could not be
supported.

In an article ["Natural Justice and the 'Warned Off'
Bookmaker"] in (1963), 26 Modern Law Rev. 412, Professor Lloyd
refers to a judgment of the Supreme Court of British Guiana,
Demara Turf Club Ltd. v. Phang (1961). There, the stewards of
the Turf Club declared Mr. Phang a warned-off person, and
distributed notices to this effect to all concerned.  At p.
415, Professor Lloyd writes that the Court adopted the view,
strongly urged in the English cases by Denning, L.J., that
where the rules provide for disqualification, expulsion or some
other  serious penalty, they cannot confer an absolute
discretion on the stewards who must be made subject to due
inquiry in accordance with the rules of natural justice.  In
his opinion, the view taken by the Court in the case was either
(i) that there was no contract between the two parties, so
that the decision warning him off was nugatory, or (ii) that
there was an implied contract between the parties but that in
this event there was no power under the rules to warn him off
save after due inquiry.  The Court had a great deal to say in
rejection of the contention of the Club in favour of a
construction of the rules conferring an absolute power on the
stewards to warn any person off in their discretion.

As a consequence of the various dicta of Denning, L.J., and
their application in the two Canadian cases (in the Kennedy
case perhaps as obiter, and in the Hughes case as a secondary
ground for the decision), I think it can at least be safely
said that in the absence of an express prohibition, the Court
will not construe the rules of an association as to impliedly
exclude, where they would otherwise be applicable, the rules of
natural justice.  The question of whether an express and
absolute power of expulsion or punishment is contrary to public
policy as Denning, L.J., has suggested, or can be exercised
without regard to natural justice, must be left to be resolved
when it arises.

(iv) How are the rules of natural justice to be applied?

Having decided that the governors were bound to adhere to the
rules of natural justice, it becomes necessary to define the
rules and examine the circumstances of this case in order to
see whether those rules were observed.  They are, of course,
simple to state, but it is the manner of their application that
may yield different inferences as to whether there has been
compliance.  My reading of the authorities leads me to believe
that each case must of necessity rest on its own facts and to a
certain extent on the type of tribunal that is involved. Mr.
Williston endeavoured to distinguish between judicial, quasi-
judicial, and administrative functions.  He took the
position that while the first two were subject to the rules of
natural justice, a standard similar to that of Court of law was
required in the case of a tribunal exercising judicial
functions. In describing the nature of the business exercisable
by a tribunal that is subject to the rules of natural justice,
however, the cases appear to use the words "judicial" and
"quasi-judicial" interchangeably.  In no case have I found a
Judge drawing any real distinction between the two terms in
order to require a tribunal to abide by higher standards of
procedure in the one case than in the other.  There are cases
where the Courts have said that a higher standard is required
in view of the consequences attached to any action taken by the
tribunal (see for example Lord Atkin in General Medical Council
v. Spackman,
[1943] A.C. 627 at p. 638)
, but I return to my
earlier observation that each case must in the end rest upon
its own facts.  I believe I can demonstrate the accuracy of
that statement by citing extracts from some of the relevant
cases, in chronological order.

The case most frequently referred to with respect to the
procedure to be adopted by a tribunal established by statute
(and also approved with reference to domestic tribunals of
the nature of the case at bar), is Local Government Board v.
Arlidge,
[1915] A.C. 120
.  The Board was empowered by statute
to hear appeals by an owner of a dwelling-house against a
closing order made by a local authority with respect to a house
which such authority had decided to be unfit for human
habitation.  At pp. 132-3 Viscount Haldane, L.C., states:

My Lords, when the duty of deciding an appeal is imposed,
those whose duty is to decide it must act judicially .... I
agree with the view expressed in an analogous case by my
noble and learned friend Lord Loreburn. In Board of Education
v. Rice,
[1911] A.C. 179
, he laid down that, in disposing of
a question which was the subject of an appeal to it, the
Board of Education was under a duty to act in good faith, and
to listen fairly to both sides, inasmuch as that was a duty
which lay on every one who decided anything. But he went on
to say that he did not think it was bound to treat such a
question as though it were a trial.  The Board had no power
to administer an oath, and need not examine witnesses.  It
could, he thought, obtain information in any way it thought
best, always giving a fair opportunity to those who were
parties in the controversy to correct or contradict any
relevant statement prejudicial to their view.

Lord Shaw of Dunfermline at p. 138 of the same case, said
with reference to the procedure to be applied by such a board,
that the assumption that the methods of natural justice are ex
necessitate those of Courts of justice is wholly unfounded.
Lord Parmoor, at p. 140, stated that in determining whether the
principles of substantial justice have been complied with in
matters of procedure, regard must necessarily be had to the
nature of the issue to be determined and the constitution of
the tribunal.

In the case of De Verteuil v. Knaggs,
[1918] A.C. 557
, the
Privy Council was concerned with a Statute of Trinidad which
permitted the Governor, on sufficient grounds shown to his
satisfaction, to transfer indentured immigrants from one
employer to any other employer.  Lord Parmoor stated that the
Governor could not carry through the duty entrusted to him
without making some inquiry as to whether sufficient grounds
had been shown to his satisfaction that immigrants indentured
on an estate should be removed.  This appears at p. 560:

Their Lordships are of opinion that in making such an inquiry
there is, apart from special circumstances, a duty of giving
to any person against whom the complaint is made a fair
opportunity to make any relevant statement which he may
desire to bring forward and a fair opoortunity to correct or
controvert any relevant statement brought forward to his
prejudice.

In Weinberger v. Inglis,
[1919] A.C. 606
, Lord Parmoor, at p.
636, in speaking of the procedural duties cast upon the
Committee of the Stock Exchange, quoted with approval the
statement of Lord Loreburn in the Rice case (referred to by
Viscount Haldane, L.C., in Arlidge), holding it applicable to
the Stock Exchange Committee.

In Wilson v. E. & N.R. Co., E. & N.R. Co. v. Dunlop,
1921 CanLII 424 (UK JCPC)
, 61
D.L.R. 1, 28 C.R.C. 296, [1921] 3 W.W.R. 817, [1922] 1 A.C.
202, the Privy Council considered a statute under which the
Lieutenant-Governor of the Province of British Columbia had
authority to issue Crown grants upon "reasonable proof" of
certian facts. It was decided (see p. 8 D.L.R., pp. 304-5
C.R.C., p. 825 W.W.R., p. 211 A.C.), that the function of the
Lieutenant-Governor in Council in making a grant was judicial
in the sense that he had, to adapt the language of Lord Moulton
in the Arlidge case, to "preserve a judicial temper" and
perform his duties "conscientiously with a proper feeling of
responsibility".  However, the fact that the Lieutenant-
Governor in Council refused to direct the production of
certain individuals for cross-examination, and refused to grant
an adjournment for the purpose of enabling a party to adduce
evidence in opposition to evidence put forth by affidavit in
support of an application, was thought not to be a violation of
the rights of the party protesting such action, the Lieutenant-
Governor in Council not being bound to govern himself by the
rules of procedure regulating proceedings in a Court of
justice.

Lord Atkin in General Medical Council v. Spackman,
[1943]
A.C. 627 at p. 638,
stated:

Some analogy exists, no doubt, between the various
procedures of this and other not strictly judicial bodies,
but I cannot think that the procedure which may be very just
in deciding whether to close a school or an insanitary house
is necessarily right in deciding a charge of infamous conduct
against a professional man.  I would, therefore, demur to any
suggestion that the words of Lord Loreburn L.C. in Board of
Education v. Rice,
[1911] A.C. 179
, 182, afford a complete
guide to the General Medical Council in the exercise of their
duties.

In Russell v. Duke of Norfolk,
[1949] 1 All E.R. 109
, the
plaintiff claimed that he had been denied natural justice for
the reasons, inter alia, that he had not had sufficient
information before he attended the inquiry as to the nature of
the charge made against him; that he had not been supplied
before the hearing or even at the hearing with a copy of a
particular report; and that he had not been given sufficient
opportunity to present his case or call his witnesses.  Tucker,
L.J., found on the evidence that the plaintiff knew perfectly
well what was the nature of the matter that was going to be
investigated, as a consequence of his having received a letter
from the stewards, and in holding that the plaintiff had not
been denied natural justice, he stated that the matter was not
to be judged by the standarts applicable to a Court of law.  He
continued [p. 118]:

There are, in my view, no words which are of universal
application to every kind of inquiry and every kind of
domestic tribunal.  The requirements of natural justice must
depend on the circumstances of the case, the nature of the
inquiry, the rules under which the tribunal is acting, the
subject-matter that is being dealt with, and so forth.
Accordingly, to do not derive much assistance from the
definitions of natural justice which have been from time to
time used, but, whatever standard is adopted, one essential
is that the person concerned should have a reasonable
opportunity of presenting his case.

Tucker, L.J., and Denning, L.J., both were of the opinion
that once the facts had been found, it was a matter of law for
the Judge as to whether there had been a denial of natural
justice, and that the question involved a conclusion of law.

In Abbott v. Sullivan,
[1952] 1 K.B. 189
, Evershed, M.R., did
not at p. 194 and p. 195, distinguish between a judicial
function and a quasi -judicial function in describing the role
of the Cornporter Committee.  In view of his determination of
the case, he did not reach any conclusion as to whether the
plaintiff had been denied natural justice, although on the
facts the letter by which the plaintiff was informed of the
meeting contained no information of the nature of the charge
that was being made against him, or indeed that any charge was
being so made.  On the other hand, it was clearly shown the the
plaintiff was in fact well aware of the nature of the charge
and of the fact that the meeting was being summoned for the
purpose of considering what, if any, disciplinary measures
should be taken against him, for the plaintiff thereupon
challenged the comittee's jurisdiction, and abstained from
attending.  Denning, L.J., thought that the relevant letter was
not a charge, or notice of a charge, but merely an invitation
to a meeting to discuss an incident.  Morris, L.J., at p. 211,
said that the fact that the plaintiff believed or guessed that
a charge would be brought against him at the relevant meeting
did not mean that in fact he had been told he was to be
charged.

In Byrne v. Kinematograph Renters Society Ltd.,
[1958] 1
W.L.R. 762
, Harman, J., after quoting with approval the
comments of Tucker, L.J., in the Russell case, stated at p.
784:

What then are the requirements of natural justice in a case
of this kind? First, I think that the person accused should
know the nature of the accusation made; secondly, that he
should be given an opportunity to state his case; and,
thirdly, of course, that the tribunal should act in good
faith.  I do not myself think that there really is anything
more.

I believe that is the best short statement on the subject that
can be found. There, the plaintiff alleged denial of justice
based on the grounds that the committee conducting the inquiry
had refused to show a report compiled by its inspectors to the
plaintiff; and, secondly, the refusal of the committee to allow
him to call his wife as a witness.  The trial Judge concluded
that there was nothing in the report which was not contained in
a letter to the plaintiff from the defendant, and the plaintiff
therefore knew the complaint made against him.  The Court was
also of the opinion that the evidence of his wife would not
have assisted the tribunal.

In Universtiy of Ceylon v. Fernando,
[1960] 1 All E.R. 631
, a
decision of Privy Council, the relevant facts were as follows:
Pursuant to the provisions of a General Act of the University
of Ceylon, the vice-chancellor of such university appointed a
commission of inquiry to look into certain allegations that the
plaintiff Fernando had obtained information in advance as to
certian questions on an examination paper.  Fernando was
informed by letter of the allegation against him and of the
appointment of the commission, and was asked to attend before
the commission on two occasions.  At the outset of the first
interview, the plaintiff was informed that a named individual
had made the charge against him and the nature of the charge
was explained to him in detail.  He was not, however, present
when a number of witnesses, including the individual who made
the original complaint, testified before the commission and he
had not asked to be allowed to question any of them.  The
commission found Fernando guilty of examination offences, and
suspended him indefinitely from all university examinations.
Fernando brought action against the university for a
declaration that its action was null and void on the grounds of
failure of natural justice.  At p. 637, Lord Jerkins, giving
the opinion of the Privy Council, stated that the question
whether the requirements of natural justice had been met by the
procedure adopted in any given case must depend to a great
extent on the facts and circumstances of the case in point. He
quoted Tucker, L.J., in the Russell case and the words of Lord
Atkin in General Medical Council v. Spackman.  He continued:

With these reservations [referring here to Lord Atkin's
words] as to the utility of general defintions in this branch
of the law, it appears to their Lordships that LORD
LOREBURN'S much quoted statement in Board of Education v.
Rice, [1911] A.C. at p. 182, still affords as good a general
definition as any of the nature of and limits on the
requirements of natural justice in this kind of case.

He went on to quote the extracts from Viscount Haldane's
judgment in Arlidge, the Privy Council's opinion in the Knaggs
case, and language of Harman, J., in the Byrne case, all of
which have already been cited above.  The Privy Council
expressed their approval of the statement by Harman, J., as to
the requirements of natural justice.

It should be mentioned, perhaps, that on the appeal to the
Privy Council, the University did not dispute the fact that the
functions of the vice-chancellor were of a quasi-judicial
nature.

Since no special form of procedure was prescribed by the Act
as to the manner in which the vice-chancellor should be
satisfied that a candidate had committed an offence, the
Judicial Committee decided that it was for him to determine
what procedure was to be followed, so long as it satisfied the
requirements indicated in the passages from the cases of
Knaggs, Arlidge and Byrne. With respect to the fact that the
plaintiff was not given an opportunity to question the chief
witness against him it was suggested that this objection would
have been more formidable had the plaintiff asked to be allowed
to question such witness, and had his request been refused.
The fact that the commission did not volunteer the suggestion
that the plaintiff might wish to question this witness, or in
other words tender her unasked for cross-examination by the
plaintiff, was held as insufficient to invalidate the
proceedings.  Further, the fact that two witnesses had been
questioned by one member of the commission alone, was upheld on
the basis of Lord Loreburn's language in the Rice case, that
the commission could obtain information about the matter in any
way it thought best.  The judicial committee held that on the
facts a fair opportunity had been given to the plaintiff to
correct or contradict any relevant statements to his prejudice,
so as to comply with the directive of Lord Loreburn.

In Ridge v. Baldwin,
[1963] 2 All E.R. 66
, Lord Reid at p.
71, in discussing natural justice, states:

In modern times opinions have sometimes been expressed to the
effect that natural justice is so vague as to be pratically
meaningless.  But I would regard these as tainted by the
perennial fallacy that because something cannot be cut and
dried or nicely weighed or measured therefore it does not
exist.  The idea of negligence is equally insusceptible of
exact defintion but what a reasonable man would regard as
fair procedure in particular circumstances and what he would
regard as negligence in particular circumstances are equally
capable of serving as tests in law, and natural justice as it
had been interpreted in the courts is much more definite than
that.  It appears to me that one reason why the authorities
on natural justice have been found difficult to reconcile is
that insufficient attention has been paid to the great
difference between various kinds of cases in which it has
been sought to apply the principle.  What a minister ought to
do in considering objections to a scheme may be very
different from what a watch committee ought to do in
considering whether to dismiss a chief constable.

In that paragraph, it is not clear whether Lord Reid's
reference to a minister considering objections to a scheme is
intended as an example of an instance where the rules of
natural justice do not apply, or is intended as an example of
where the rules do apply but a high standard of procedure is
not required.  It appears to me that the former was his
intention because, at pp. 75 and 76, he indicates that a
minister considering objections to a scheme is acting in an
executive capacity.

With reference to Mr. Williston's assertion that there is a
distinction in the procedural requirements between a judicial
tasks and a quasi-judicial task, I refer to Lord Reid's
comments at p. 75, where after citing such older cases as
Cooper v. Wandsworth Board of Works; Hopkins v. Smethwick Local
Board of Health; Spackman v. Plumstead District Board of Works

(1885), 10 App. Cas. 229
; Wood v. Woad; Weinberger v. Inglis
and the club cases, he declares that since such a body is
performing a quasi-judicial task in considering and deciding
the matter, it is required to observe the essentials of all
proceedings of a judicial character, in other words, the
principles of natural justice.  Again, on p. 109, Lord Morris
says that a decision to dismiss the appellant for neglect of
duty ought only to have been taken in the exercise of a quasi-
judicial funtion which demanded an observance of the rules
of natural justice.  This latter statement also seems to
challenge Mr. Williston's argument that a dismissal on grounds
of misconduct is the performance of a judicial function.

I think that one can conclude from those cases that although
the question of whether the principles of natural justice have
been complied with in any one case is an issue of law,
nevertheless it rests in each instance on the particular facts.
It is for the Judge to draw the necessary inferences whether
adequate notice of the charges was given to the person who is
in essence accused of misconduct, and whether he has had
sufficient opportunity to present his case.

(v) Were the rules of natural justice followed on February 28,
1961?

I entertain no doubt that the principles of natural justice
were not honoured so far as the plaintiff was concerned when,
on February 28th, the Board of Governors withdrew their
approval of him as set forth in the letter, ex. 33.

It should first be noted that in determining whether an
individual has received adequate notice of the charges levied
against him, the state of his knowledge is probably the most
important factor.  In my opinion, Mr. Posluns was not given any
notice that charges were being brought which might involve him
in his personal capacity.  I agree with Mr. Pattillo's
submission that the notice of an inquiry by a domestic tribunal
need not take any particular form, and that there need not be a
formal charge as in judicial proceedings.  It is enough if, in
all the circumstances, the notice fairly conveys to a
reasonable man that, as a result of the inquiry, the tribunal
may take action prejudicial to him.  But I do not agree with
Mr. Pattillo's next contention that, on the evidence in this
case, the plaintiff had warning that his approvals by the
Exchange might be taken from him on February 28th.
Undoubtedly, he knew that the continuation of those approvals
was subject to the discretion of the Board, and that the
inquiry brought against R.A. Daly, Jr., who was the person
responsible to the Exchange, was due in part at least to his
conduct. He was also aware of Mr. Lavender's investigations,
and that he had been asked to delay his trip to Mexico.  His
presence and participation in the discussion with General
Graham, Mr. Gardiner and Mr. Stearns on February 15th
undoubtedly provided him with further information concerning
the matter. Then, too, on the evening of February 27th he asked
Mr. Stapells whether he should be separately represented at the
hearing.  But none of those circumstances, or any others,
persuade me that Mr. Posluns had reason to think that he was in
personal jeopardy in the inquiry, or, as Mr. Pattillo argued,
that the hearing, although in form a hearing of charges against
Mr. Daly, was in fact, and to his knowledge, a hearing which
might conclude with the withdrawal of his approvals.  On the
contrary, I am fully convinced that no man in his position
would, or could, believe that on the morning of February 28th
he was personally in peril, vis- a-vis the Exchange.  The
notice calling the hearing (ex. 12) was explicitly given
pursuant to By-laws 10 and 11, and so was directed only at Mr.
Daly, Jr., and I think the plaintiff could logically assume
that before he could be affected, he would have to be made
aware that the Board was acting under By-law 49, s. 4, and By-
law 67, s. 16.  This is more than confirmed by the fact that
Mr. Stapells, who could be regarded by the plaintiff as having
deep insight into the whole affair, informed the plaintiff in
answer to the latter's quest for advice as to whether he should
be separately represented, that he did not think that his
position was particularly different from the other directors.
Whatever he may have suspected theretofore, from that moment on
the plaintiff was completely justified, in my opinion, in
deciding, as he did, that he was not implicated personally; he
would have no more ground for believing that his approvals
would be disturbed than would, for example, Mr. Wiley.  And
certainly that gentleman would have had good cause to complain
had he been the object that day of a resolution similar to the
one aimed at the plaintiff.

Moreover, I think it can be fairly said that the
representations made by Mr. Posluns to the Board on February
28th were consciously directed to complaints against the firm
and not in defence of his status with the Exchange.  He had
received instructions from counsel for the Daly company to
answer only questions put to him.  Thus, it can be argued with
some force that even before the Board retired to consider the
penalties to be inflicted, the plaintiff did not have a real
opportunity to defend his personal position, for, not having
been made aware of the possibility that he might be dealt with
as an individual, his mind was not addressed to that
contingency.

Even if all else was regular and proper, there remains the
decisive fact that the plaintiff was afforded no chance
whatever to speak to the matter of the penalty.

As to this last point, Annamunthodo v. Oilfields Workers'
Trade Union,
[1961] 3 All E.R. 621
, is of interest.  There a
union member was given notice of the fact that certain charges
were to be brought against him at a hearing on a specified
date.  All the charges were punishable by fine.  The plaintiff
did not attend an adjournment of the initial hearing, and he
was expelled from the union pursuant to another rule under
which he had not been charged.  That rule provided that any
member who was proved to the satisfaction of the Council of the
union to have been guilty of conduct prejudicial to the
interests of the union could be expelled.  Lord Denning, in
delivering the opinion of the Privy Council, held that the rule
could not have been invoked for the purpose of expelling the
plaintiff unless he had been made aware of the charge under it
and had had a fair opportunity of meeting it.  He went on to
say that even if the rule only implied more severe penalties
(as opposed to specifying another offence), nevertheless,
those severe penalties could only be imposed where the conduct
was prejudicial to the interests of the union; and on that
view, the rule should not have been invoked without giving the
plaintiff notice of it. Counsel for the union had argued that
the substance of the matter lay in the facts alleged in the
letter to the plaintiff, and that the specific formulation of
charges was immaterial.  Lord Denning refused to accede to that
view, and stated that if a domestic tribunal formulates
specific charges which lead only to a fine, it cannot, without
notice, resort to other charges which lead to more severe
penalties.

For those reasons, I am of the opinion that the order made on
February 28th against the plaintiff offended the requirements
of essential justice.

(vi) Did the hearing on March 2, 1961 cure the prior defect?

When one comes to consider the effect of the second hearing
on March 2nd, one is faced with a more difficult problem.
Indeed, it is probably the most troublesome point in the whole
case.  It will be remembered that by that time the plaintiff
and his counsel had knowledge of the nature of the misconduct
alleged against him, the relevant evidence, and the punishment
which had been thought just.  They had had some time to prepare
for the new hearing in whatever way they saw fit, they were
given full scope to call evidence or otherwise to say anything
they wished to say, and, in fact, on the second occasion both
did make representations on all aspects of the matter.  Had the
atmosphere and extent of knowledge which was then available to
the plaintiff been present on February 28th, the resolution
passed on that day could not have been attacked successfully.

But was it then too late, as Mr. Williston argued, for the
Board of Governors to validly sustain or revive that
resolution, or to pass a new one which differed only in the
addition of the concession allowing Mr. Posluns to retire?

I think not.

The several judgments delivered in Ridge v. Baldwin, the
facts of which bear some similarity with those in this case,
furnish the guiding principles to be applied as to the effect
of the second hearing on March 2nd.  In that case, the
plaintiff had no prior notice of any proposal to discharge him,
or of any charges against him by the watch committee, or of its
meeting on March 7, 1958, at which he was, in his absence,
dismissed.  The House of Lords held that such dismissal was
null and void on the ground, inter alia, that the committee was
bound to observe the principles of natural justice, and that it
had failed to do so.  After that meeting the plaintiff was
informed of its outcome by letter which set forth the
considerations upon which the committee's decision was based,
including "...(f) certain statements made today by members of
the committee and the town clerk...."  Those statements
included an accusation that the plaintiff had committed perjury
when he was on trial for a criminal offence.  Despite the
gravity of such a charge, and despite an oral request by his
solicitor for such purpose, the content or nature of those
statements were never revealed to the plaintiff.  He appealed
to the Home Secretary, as he was permitted to do under the
relevant statute, but before that appeal was disposed of the
watch committee held another special meeting to hear the
plaintiff's solicitor on his request that they should
reconsider their decision as to the plaintiff's pension.  At
that second meeting, the members of the committee "listened in
courtesy and silence" while the solicitor endeavoured to
persuade them to allow his client to resign so that he might
have a pension, but a majority adhered to their previous
decision.

With reference to the position of the watch committee at the
second hearing, Lord Reid said this at pp. 80-1 of the report:

Next comes the question whether the respondents' failure to
follow the rules of natural justice on Mar. 7 was made good
by the meeting on Mar. 18. I do not doubt that if an officer
or body realises that it has acted hastily and reconsiders
the whole matter afresh after affording to the person
affected a proper opportunity to present his case then its
later decision will be valid.  An example is De Verteuil v.
Knaggs,
[1918] A.C. 557
.  But here the appellant's solicitor
was not fully informed of the charges against the appellant
and the watch committee did not annul the decision which they
had already published and proceed to make a new decision.  In
my judgment what was done on that day was a very inadequate
substitute for a full rehearing. Even so three members of the
committee changed their minds, and it is impossible to say
what the decision of the committee would have been if there
had been a full hearing after disclosure to the appellant of
the whole case against him.  I agree with those of your
lordships who hold that this meeting of Mar. 18 cannot affect
the result of this appeal.

At p. 106 of the report, Lord Morris dealt with that aspect
of the matter in this way:

The question next arises whether the events subsequent to
Mar. 7 form any bar to the appellant's claim.  I have already
referred to the meeting of Mar. 18.  That occasion afforded
an opportunity for the watch committee to tell the appellant
and his solicitor what were the allegations that he had to
meet.  The documents which the solicitor sent to the watch
committee emphasised the point that the appellant had been
given no notice of them:  mention was also made of the fact
that the appellant did not know what were the statements made
by members of the watch committee referred to in the letter
of Mar. 7. He most certainly had no hint that is was being
said of him that he had given some false evidence.  The
appellant's case is that he never had the chance -- which he
would have welcomed -- of refuting that suggestion before the
watch committee and the chance of calling such evidence as he
might desire to call to deal with the suggestion.  The oral
request for information made by the solicitor met with no
response.  Even though the watch committee had communicated
there previous decision to the press a full enquiry might
still have been possible but the watch committee neither took
the opportunity then to begin compliance with the regulations
nor even, in default of that, to give information to the
appellant as to the case that he had to meet.  In the result,
in my judgment, nothing occurred on Mar. 18 to give validity
to what the watch committee had purported to do on Mar. 7.

Lord Hodson had this to say at p. 112:

I do not find that the answer put by counsel for the watch
committee to your lordships that the case was as plain as a
pike-staff is an answer to the demand for natural justice.
The case on natural justice does not rest on the events of
Mar. 7, 1958, alone for the appellant was given a further
opportunity on Mar. 18, 1958, to address the watch committee
and of this he availed himself by his solicitor who appeared
and was allowed to address and the committee without
restriction.  I agree with PEARCE, L.J., that at that stage
the watch committee could have re-opened the matter, and
indeed three out of the twelve were in favour of so doing
(cf. De Verteuil v. Knaggs,
[1918] A.C. 557
) but the
position was then that the watch committee had given their
decision that the appellant be dismissed not only on the
ground of unfitness but also on other grounds which included
not only negligence in discharge of his duty but also
unspecified matters, which were said to be "certain
statements made today by members of the committee and the
town clerk".  It was not until Apr. 5 when the watch
committee communicated with the Home Secretary prior to the
appellant's appeal to the minister that it emerged that these
statements had reference to allegations of perjury against
the appellant.  On Mar. 18 Mr. Bosley was given not only a
full but a courteous hearing by the watch committee, but
received no indication of the nature of the charges which his
client had to answer notwithstanding his repeated statements
that he did not know what they were.  It is plain therefore
that, if there were a failure on Mar. 7 to give justice to
the appellant, this was not cured on Mar. 18, when the watch
committee confirmed there previous decision.

It is reasonably obvious, and, no matter how the other law
Lords expressed themselves, that the principle laid down by the
House of Lords on the effect of the second hearing is contained
in Lord Reid's statement that "...if an officer or body
realises that it has acted hastily and reconsiders the whole
matter afresh after affording to the person affected a proper
opportunity to present his case then its later decision will be
valid".  In that instance, and this must never be overlooked,
the House came to the conclusion that the decision reached by
the watch committee at its second hearing could neither supply
cogency to the earlier one or could itself be valid, for the
reason that Chief Constable Ridge was given no inkling whatever
of what was perhaps the most serious charge against him.

Did the Board of Governors of the Exchange bring itself
within the limits of Lord Reid's prescription in this case?  I
believe it did.

Despite evidence to the contrary from at least one of the
Exchange witnesses, I am persuaded that when Mr. Stapells and
Mr. Goodman protested the step taken against the plaintiff, the
governors in attendance on February 28th, and those for whom
they were responsible, instantly came to the realization that
that they may have acted precipitately, that he ought to have
been warned about he possibility of personal danger and that he
should be afforded an opportunity to be heard on his own
behalf.  That surely was the reason why the plaintiff, through
his solicitors, was at once given an opportunity to present his
side of the matter at another hearing.

Nor can there be any doubt that by March 2nd the plaintiff
was thoroughly familiar with the nature of the allegations
being made against him.  I base that conclusion upon his own
evidence (vol. 6, pp. 1369 and 1369A) and the evidence of Mr.
Goodman (vol. 8, pp. 1641 to 1643).  Moreover, although not
then appreciating that he was in potential peril, Mr. Posluns
was present and heard all that was discussed on February 28th.
It is also significant that the submissions advanced both by
Mr. Stapells and Mr. Goodman demonstrated that both they and he
were cognizant of the Board's complaint against him.  In this
regard, see Guinane v. Sunnyside Boating Co. of Toronto
(1893),
21 O.A.R. 49
. Mr. Posluns endeavoured to leave the impression
that on March 2nd, and even when testifying at the trial, he
did not know why the Board thought that he had been guilty of
misconduct. If that be true, then he certainly shut his eyes to
the obvious.  The plaintiff's knowledge was much more complete
than that possessed by Mr. Ridge who, it will be remembered,
was ignorant throughout of the circumstance that his dismissal
was being ordered, in part, because he was believed to have
committed perjury.

There is another feature of the matter to be mentioned.  Mr.
Williston argued that neither ex. 12 nor schedule A to ex. 24
contained a charge which, without more, amounted to misconduct
on the part of Mr. Posluns, and that in truth the members of
the Board came to their verdict, not because of what was
disclosed to the plaintiff and his solicitor, but because they
secretly believed that Mr. Lynch had been duped and defrauded
by the operation in which the plaintiff derived profit singular
to him alone.  I have already pointed out that natural justice
does not demand that a charge be formulated with precision, and
in this case Mr. Posluns, to my mind, was well aware of the
nature of the complaint which had been made against him.  That
it perhaps included an allegation of moral misconduct as
distinct from a breach of a fiduciary relationship, could well
flow from the circumstances which were shown to exist and of
which he had knowledge.

Accordingly, I hold that by the time Mr. Goodman opened his
presentation to the Board on March 2nd, both he and his client
had been sufficiently apprised of the charge which had been
made against the latter.

Passing on to the nest ingredient necessary to produce a
valid order on March 2nd, was "the person affected", in the
words of Lord Reid, "given a proper opportunity to present his
case?"  Mr. Goodman was asked to offer anything he thought
relevant, as a result of which he outlined the facts, as he
understood them, and then made careful argument.  He did not
request further time in which to prepare or for the right to
adduce further evidence.  Either concession would have been
granted had it been sought:  see the evidence of General
Graham, vol. 10, p. 1997, and that of Mr. Graydon, vol. 17, p.
2874.  Furthermore, Mr. Posluns spoke on his own behalf.  There
can be no doubt, therefore, that the plaintiff was granted, and
availed himself of, the right to present his own defence.

The sole question, therefore, is whether on that occasion the
Board properly reconsidered the matter anew.  Certainly there
was as exhaustive a rehearing as the plaintiff and his counsel
wished.  However, for the plaintiff, and borrowing Lord Reid's
criticism of the watch committee's conduct, it was argued that
the Board here did not "annul" its previous resolution and
"reconsider the whole matter afresh".  Rather, it was said,
the second hearing was in the nature of an appeal to allow Mr.
Goodman to convince the Board, if he could, that its previous
decision had been wrong, and that this was made manifest by the
evidence of several of the governors and the resolution passed
on March 2nd which decreed that the former decision should
"stand".  In this regard, reference was made to Mr. Deacon's
evidence (vol. 14, pp. 2459 and 2460) that "Mr. Goodman...
presented nothing which, to my mind, changed in any way the
evidence which we had at the first hearing and which would
cause me to change my decision.  Therefore, I concurred that
the decision stood ...", to Mr. Lailey's testimony that nothing
had been changed by Mr. Goodman's presentation (vol. 16, p.
2699), to Mr. Heavenor's observation that the Board decided not
to change its previous decision (vol. 16, pp. 2722 and 2723),
and to the evidence of Mr. Gardiner to the same effect as well
as his admission, said to be decisive, that the purpose of the
hearing was an "appeal" from the earlier decision (vol. 18, p.
3125).  Reliance was also placed upon portions of the evidence
of Messrs. Solway, Goodman, Graham and Graydon on this point,
but I do not attach to them the weight suggested by Mr.
Williston for the simple reason that none of those gentlemen
were members of the Board, and so could not speak
authoritatively as to the manner or mood in which the Board
approached and made its second decision.

If the evidence by the several governors which I have cited
and Lord Reid's statement that the watch committee did not
"annul" its previous decision are to be interpreted
literally, then probably that which occurred on March 2nd could
not be deemed to remedy the deficiencies of February 28th, but
I think both of those matters must be examined more closely.

In the first place, what meaning did Lord Reid intend to
ascribe to his assertion that "the watch committee did not
annul the decision which it had already published and proceed
to make a new decision".  In attempting to place a proper
construction upon it, regard must be had to the fact that it
was no part of the general principle enunciated by him but only
an accurate reference to what had been done in that particular
case.  It may not have been intended to have application beyond
the circumstances there being considered. Nor is it right, in
my opinion to conclude that his Lordship employed the word
"annul" in a strictly literal sense, for to do so would mean
that no matter how genuine and real was the wish of a tribunal
to accomplish a just result, a new hearing could not be the
means of attaining it unless in some way (and no formula was
suggested) the earlier decision was expressly and perhaps
formally abrogated.

I am convinced that the determining factor in ascertaining
the effect of the new hearing is the state of mind which the
tribunal brings to bear upon the problem then before it. An
open, but pretended, revocation would not produce as fair a
result as one effected with an unspoken but bona fide desire on
the part of the tribunal to do what was right.

I should like to add this:  Lord Reid must have been
cognizant of the fact that no amount of formalism will in fact
wipe from the minds of those who make a decision the memory of
that decision.  He could not, therefore, have been suggesting
the need of complete mental erasure before a new hearing could
be proper, for he also held, and this is of first importance,
that in certain circumstances the failure to give natural
justice can be corrected by a subsequent hearing.

If it was intended by Lord Reid that annulment of the prior
decision is a condition precedent to the validity of a second
one, then it is doubtful whether his view is borne out by the
De Verteuil v. Knaggs case, in as much as there is no
declaration by Lord Parmoor that in that case the Governor
reconsidered the whole matter afresh.

The facts disclosed that after the Governor had made his
order ex parte, on December 16, 1915, not having afforded any
opportunity to the plaintiff to make any answer or explanation,
the Protector of Immigrants sent a letter informing the
plaintiff of the Governor's action on December 20, 1915. The
letter set out under four heads the complaints made by the
Protector of Immigrants to the Governor.  After the receipt of
that letter, the plaintiff obtained a personal interview with
the Governor on December 23, 1915.  Lord Parmoor said that it
was material that the plaintiff and his manager had been
granted a fair opportunity of placing before the Governor their
answer to the allegations made in the letter of the Protector
of Immigrants. Certain correspondence ensued between the
plaintiff and the Colonial Secretary and finally, on March 15,
1916, the Protector of Immigrants wrote to the plaintiff's
manager that the Governor had decided that the immigrants on
his estate had to be removed therfrom and transferred to
another estate.  Apparently their Lordships thought that the
correspondence showed that the Governor did not proceed without
giving fair notice to the plaintiff of the charges made against
him or without providing a fair opportunity to answer those
charges. The opinion concludes with this statement, which
supports the principle ennunciated by Lord Reid [[1918] A.C. at
p. 563]:

It was argued on behalf of the appellant that the validity of
the order should be tested either as on December 16, 1915, or
at the latest as on January 21, 1916, but there is no reason
why the acting Governor may not at any time review or alter a
decision previously given, and it may be his duty to do so,
in the prudent exercise of his discretion, on a further
consideration of all the relevant factors after full inquiry.

But it is to be observed that the passage does not contain any
express statement that the previous decision had to be revoked
before the second one could be valid.

It is perhaps significant, too, that in the speeches of the
other law Lords in Ridge v. Baldwin there is no intimation that
an earlier decision which is invalid must be annulled before a
later one will be effective. Lord Morris spoke only of the
necessity of informing the person charged of the allegations he
had to meet and of thereafter conducting a full inquiry.  Lord
Hodson suggested that since the appellant's solicitor was given
a full hearing on the second occasion, the watch committee
could have "re-opened the matter" and "confirmed their previous
decision" (the italicizing is mine) had some indication of the
nature of the charge been passed to the solicitor, thereby
implying, as it seems to me, that a tribunal need not call for
some sort of prior abrogation of its earlier finding in order
to conduct a proper and effective rehearing.

Perhaps some guidance as to the true meaning to be ascribed
to Lord Reid's words can be found in examining opinions of the
Courts as to the state of mind that the members of a domestic
tribuanl must possess when they deal with the rights of a
member at a hearing.

In the case of a non-domestic tribunal (or administrative
tribunal as I have referred to it earlier), the general
principle is that where a member of the tribunal which is
required to act judicially, as a pecuniary interest in the
matter in dispute, however small, bias is presumed and the
tribunal is automatically disqualified from adjudicating with
respect to the subject-matter of the proceedings:  The King v.
Justices of Sunderland,
[1901] 2 K.B. 357
.  In the case where
an objection is made to a tribunal on the basis that it is
interested in the proceedings in other than a pecuniary or
proprietary respect, the rule is that the tribunal will be
disqualified from acting in a judicial or quasi-judicial
capacity if a real likelihood of bias is shown, see The Queen
v. Rand (1866), L.R.
1 Q.B. 230
; R. V. Camborne Justices, Ex p.
Pearce,
[1955] 1 Q.B. 41
, and R. v. Ontario Labour Relations
Board; Ex p. Hall,
1963 CanLII 189 (ON HCJ)
, 39 D.L.R. (2d) 113, [1963] 2 O.R. 239.  A
mere suspicion of bias does not suffice to disqualify the
tribunal, but the question is whether, in the circumstances,
there is a real probability of bias. In the case of domestic
organizations whose bias is the voluntary assoication of
members, such as unions, clubs, and stock exchange committees,
the domestic tribunal that adjudicates on the rights of members
in not subject to those disqualifying bias rules applicable to
administrative tribunals.  The reason for such distinction is
stated quite clearly by Maugham, J., in Maclean v. Workers"
Union,
[1929] 1 Ch. 602 at p. 626
:

If we consider first the case of a pecuniary interest it is
impossible in general to imply from the terms of the rules
such a disqualification as regards the members of a domestic
forum. For example, when members of a club expel another
member under their rules, generally speaking, they all have a
small pecuniary interest in the matter.  Moreover the members
of a domestic tribunal have other interests in the decision
which may well render them something less than impartial.
They have, for example, the interests of their association or
body to protect, and may properly regard these interests as a
matter of great importance.  In many cases the tribunal is
necessarily entrusted with the duty of appearing to act as
prosecutors as well as that of judges; for there is no one
else to prosecute.

In other words, frequently the tribunal that makes the decision
affecting the member's rights, is the initiating medium by
which the complaint is laid against that member.  In view of
this fact, in many instances it may be difficult to find a
tribunal that is impartial towards the member, for the very
issue before the tribunal may have arisen as a consequence of
an acrimonious dispute between the member and certain
individuals sitting on the tribunal.  However, even with
domestic tribunals, there are certain limitations as to the
degree of partiality that the members may possess.  In two
cases at least the bias has been held to be so extreme as to
warrant the disqualification of the tribunal.  I refer to
Australian Workers' Union et al. v. Bowen et al. al.
(1948), 77
C.L.R. 601
, and White et al. Kuzych,
1951 CanLII 373 (UK JCPC)
, [1951] 3 D.L.R. 641, 2
W.W.R. (N.S.) 679, [1951] A.C. 585.

I think that I should also call attention to the fact that it
has been held that a Judge may lawfully sit on an appeal in a
case over which he presided in a lower Court.  In R. v.
Lovegrove,
[1951] 1 All E.R. 804
, Chief Justice Goddard in
delivering the judgment of the Court of Criminal Appeal said
that it was not wrong for the trial Judge to sit as a member of
the Court to hear the appeal.  He observed that where the
ground of appeal is nothing but an argument by the appellant
that the verdict was wrong, there was not only no objection to
the trial Judge sitting but that it might at times be very
useful for him to do so.  It is noteworthy that the appeal was
in a criminal matter.  Lord Goddard pointed out that prior to
the Judicature Act of 1873 when there was no Court of Appeal
and appeals were heard by Judges of the three common law Courts
en banc, it was a common practice for the Judge before whom the
trial had taken place, and whose ruling might be impugned, to
sit as a member of the Court even in some case where he had
sealed the bill of exceptions.

I concede that in Cooper v. Wilson,
[1937] 2 K.B. 309
, it was
held that a chief constable who had purported to dismiss one of
his officers could not sit with the watch committee when it was
deliberating as to whether to allow the officer's appeal.
However, while a different rule may prevail with respect to
domestic tribunals in certain circumstances, I have some
difficulty in believing that before such bodies may competently
enter upon a fresh hearing they must annul their previous
decision or be found to have violated the rules of justice,
whereas a Court of law composed in part at least of one who
presided over the trial at which the first verdict was reached,
may not be obliged to go through that process in order to be
deemed to do justice.

After giving the matter much thought, I doubt that lord Reid
intended his verb "annul" to be literally and strictly
interpreted.  It seems to me, rather, that if the members of a
tribunal engaged upon a rehearing resolve conscientiously and
honestly to reconsider the matter without being influenced by
the effect or terms of their earlier decision, there has been a
sufficient disavowal of that decision to permit them to do
justice, if Lord Reid's other precepts are also honoured.  In
my opinion, no higher standard of approach ought to be exacted
from such bodies in those circumstances.

If the test which I have stated is the proper one, then I am
satisfied that the governors clearly met it on March 2nd,
despite the various ways in which they expressed themselves at
the trial.  In this respect, I think that perhaps Mr. Funston
fairly outlined their attitude as to the second hearing.  I
have in mind his evidence in vol. 16, at pp. 2737, 2738 and
2739:

Q. What is your recollection of the purpose of that
meeting?  A. My recollection is that the meeting was called
at the request of Mr. Posluns and, or his solicitor, Mr.
Goodman, and it was a further hearing, and that we had the
executive staff, and the executive committee had approved
this hearing, and we were then called into the special
meeting.  Before that, I didn't know what was going on for
the two days intervening.

.  .  .  .  .  .

Q. Do you recall what decision was made by the Board of
Governors at the conclusion of the meeting of March 2nd?  A.
Yes, sir.  I remember even an exact phrase that was stated
one member of the Board after Mr. Goodman and his assistant
and Mr. Posluns had left the room. Mr. Lailey said:  "Well,
that doesn't change anything."  By which he went on to
amplify that in his opinion that didn't change the wording
-- there was no new evidence.  Now, he was speaking of the
evidence.  But then we had all listened and I have listened
particularly carefully to Mr. Goodman"s submissions with
respect to Mr. Posluns and his family, with which I was not
acquainted up until that time, and I admit I was impressed.
As a consequence I was quite in favour of permitting Mr.
