Posluns to resign as a shareholder and director and have the
matter treated in that fashion

.  .  .  .  .

Q. Were you, in any way, motivated by a desire to injure
Mr. Posluns? A. No, sir.

Q. And prior to making that decision, did you agree with
anyone as to the decision that you personally, would make on
the occasion? A. No, sir.

The other govenors gave similar testimony, and while their
words might be thought to impute to them an intention to say
that on March 2nd they considered that their duty was merely to
reconsider the former decision and determine whether it should
"stand", those words ought not, in my opinion, to be read
too meticulously.  I am convinced that those gentlemen came to
the second hearing with open and honest minds to hear and weigh
any evidence or argument which might then be tendered, whether
it be new or old, and to reach a just conclusion upon that
evidence and argument regardless of what had been decided on
February 28th.  That is exactly what they did; after hearing
the governors as witnesses and rereading their evidence, I
cannot interpret their intentions and conduct in any other way.

Undoubtedly they made no prior decision as to what they would
do at the hearing on March 2nd, and the plaintiff was afforded
in a new hearing following which his position was carefully
reconsidered (see the evidence of Mr. Somerville, introduce by
the plaintiff, vol. A, p. 274, and the evidence of Mr. Lailey,
vol. 16, p. 2697). Moreover, the fact that the governors were
prepared to judge the matter upon what was presented to them on
March 2nd, notwithstanding their earlier decision, is supported
by the circumstance that a different disposition of it was
proposed by them and adopted.

I must emphasize, too, that the answers made by the governors
at the trial ought to be interpreted in the light of the fact
that while Mr. Goodman was invited to adduce evidence, he
accepted that which had been introduced on the former occasion,
and contented himself with argument as to the inferences which
should be drawn from that evidence with respect to his client
personally, and with a plea for mercy if the Board shold be of
the opinion that Mr. Posluns had been guilty of unethical
conduct.  Accordingly, and because of the way in which Mr.
Posluns' case was presented on that occasion, the second
hearing was, in a sense, a review of what had taken place on
February 28th.  That would cause the governors to refer to it
as they did; it would even explain Mr. Gardiner's suggestion
that the purpose of the hearing was "an appeal".  In the
absence of new evidence, it would be natural for a person who
is not a lawyer to do so.  In any event, the expressions which
they used at trial do not overcome my conclusion, based upon
the whole tenor of the evidence, that on March 2nd the Board
members were not influenced by their earlier decision, but were
prepared to do what was right and just after hearing and
examining whatever was advanced in the form of evidence and
argument by Mr. Goodman and Mr. Posluns.

Thus the situation in this case differed significantly from
that which prevailed in the Ridge case in that here the earlier
mistake of the Board was effectively and properly cured.  That
being so, in the end, and by reason of all that occurred, there
was not a failure to provide natural justice, and since I have
also held that the Exchange by-laws and rules were not
transgressed, it is my view that recourse was not had to
illegal means in carrying out the Board's legitimate object of
having the Daly company sever its relations with Mr. Posluns.
Accordingly, the plaintiff cannot succeed on his claim that the
Exchange wrongfully procured a breach of his contractual
relations with this employers, because in the first place there
was no breach as distinguished from a lawful termination of the
contract since the parties to it must be assumed to have agreed
that Dalys would have the right to act upon any valid
withdrawal of approval by the Exchange, and in the second
place, even if there had been a breach, the Exchange's defence
of justification prevails since such breach was not
accomplished by illegal means.

XIII THE CLAIM FOR A DECLARATION

In his statement of claim the plaintiff sought a declaration
that the order of the Board withdrawing his privileges by the
Exchange as a director, shareholder and employee of the Daly
company was made illegally and without power or authority.
What I have said heretofore will demonstrate that it is my view
that the Board was morally justified and legally empowered to
make the order complained of, so that the plaintiff may not
have the declaration which he asks.

XIV THE CLAIM FOR DAMAGES FOR CONSPIRACY

While his counsel did not exhibit much confidence in the
plaintiff's alleged cause of action for damages for conspiracy,
it was not abandoned and I must therefore give attention to it.

It was pleaded that the defendant George Gardiner along with
the other members of the Board who participated in the events
of February 28th and March 2nd, and the Exchange itself, all
combined together to unlawfully injure the plaintiff by sending
out the notice, ex. 33, which probably had the result, not only
of bringing about his dismissal as an employee and his removal
as a director and shareholder, but also of precluding him from
obtaining immediate employment with any other member or member
corporation of the Exchange, and of damaging his reputation to
some extent.  Both compensatory and punitive damages were asked
for on this branch of the case, and it will be observed, as
stated above, that the complaint was not confined to
interference with the plaintiff's contract of employment only.

It need hardly be said that a conspiracy consists of an
agreement of two or more to do an unlawful act or to do a
lawful act by unlawful means.  Thus, the tort of conspiracy is
committed if a person is damaged by a combination which is
formed for the purpose of harming him in his trade, business or
other interests, whether or not a breach of contract is the
result, or if that damage is caused by an unlawful act on the
part of those acting in concert.

While the plaintiff's position on this side of his action
fluctuated greatly between the delivery of the statement of
claim and the time of argument, I believe that in the latter
stage it was the contention of his counsel that the two
defendants and the other governors, for the malevolent purpose
of hurting the plaintiff and by the use of improper means,
conspired together to cause the order of his dismissal to be
issued to the Daly company with resultant damage to him.  If
all of those essential elements had been established by the
evidence, then clearly he would be entitled to be compensated
this Court.  I am of the opinion, however, that some of them
were missing. The history of the plaintiff's changing
assertions is perhaps of interest in evaluating the one which
was finally put forward in support of the conspiracy claim.
Initially, the pleadings alleged, first, that the combiners
(including a governor, Mr. Eric Scott, who was then a
defendant to the action and subsequently discarded as such) had
conspired to "wilfully" injure the reputation and good name of
the plaintiff; secondly, that the Board had acted arbitrarily,
capriciously, maliciously, unfairly, and in a discriminatory
manner; and, lastly, that the defendant Gardiner, being
interested in the put and call option business, performed as he
did to deliberately remove the Daly company as a competitor in
that phase of the business.  In his opening, counsel for the
plaintiff reiterated his contention that Mr. Gardiner was being
sued because of the duality of his position; and, indeed, while
in the witness-box, Dr. Shulman feebly tried to underscore that
notion.  At a later stage of the trial, however, Mr. Williston
disclaimed any plea of dishonesty or malice on the part of Mr.
Gardiner and, I believe, on the part of any other of the Board
of Governors, and finally stated that he did ot intend to rely
upon the "conflict of interest" theory as none had been proved.

The irresolution so displayed by and on behalf of the
plaintiff is probably of no consequence except perhaps that it
does emphasize the frailty of the stand, to which he was
eventually forced, to the effect that the participating
governors and the Exchange were parties to a technical
conspiracy which came into existence when the former voted as
they did at the meetings on February 28th and again on March
2nd. It was not argued that prior to either of those
gatherings, any two or more of the governors had agreed upon a
course of action, or that there was in fact any prior agreement
among them as to what they would do when they met.  Indeed, any
submission to that effect would have been quite inappropriate
for each of the governors involved testified most definitely
that no governor, including Mr. Gardiner specifically, made any
attempt to persuade any of his associates to do anything or to
influence the vote.  Moreover, it was made perfectly clear that
each one of those gentlemen acted in what he considered was the
best interests of the Exchange and those it served, and not out
of any wish to punish the plaintiff.

In my opinion, the claim based upon a supposed conspiracy
fails for several reasons.  To begin with, there was not any
agreement to injure the plaintiff or any agreement to do
something the doing of which would harm him.  All the governors
did was to vote in the same way, but, because they had agreed
upon nothing before voting, and were not at any time actuated
by malice or any other improper motive, they did not merely, by
so voting, enter into an agreement, express or implied, to do
something which had not yet been done, the requisite of any
conspiracy.  As Mr. Arnup said, the directors of a corporation
do not make an "agreement" in the conspiracy sense by voting
the same way. They individually make the same decision.  In the
popular sence dividually make the same decision.  IN THe
popular sense they are "in agreement", but in the sense in
which the law of conspiracy uses "agree" they were not.  Each
simply expressed an individual opinion and the majority opinion
prevailed.  A contrary view would bring extraordinary
consequences.  One of its implications would be that each time
the majority of a Board of Directors voted to have the
corporation pursue a course of action which ultimately turned
out to be illegal, those who were in favour of having the
corporation act as it did would be conspirators by reason
solely of having so voted.

The proposition that the mere taking of a decision by
directors or others at a meeting cannot constitute an agreement
to conspire unless some of them have entered into a compact in
advance of the meeting to induce others to cause the
organization on whose behalf they are acting to do something
which is wrong, is supported by authority. In De Jetley Marks
v. Greenwood (Lord) et al.,
[1936] 1 All E.R. 863
, Porter, J.,
as he then was, observed at p. 872:

... I think it is true that directors in a board meeting
could not induce or conspire to induce that meeting to break
a contract -- at any rate, not without malice.

That language does not substantiate Mr. Williston's suggestion
that there is a difference between a vote to have a company
break one of its own contracts and a vote to wrongfully procure
the breach of a contract between others. I should add that
Porter, J., was careful to qualify the quoted statement by
pointing out that some or all of the directors could conspire
before the meeting to cause the Board to wrongfully break a
contract.

The principles laid down in the De Jetley case were adopted
by our Court of Appeal in R. v. Electrical Contractors Ass'n of
Ont. & Dent,
1961 CanLII 212 (ON CA)
, 27 D.L.R. (2d) 193, 131 C.C.C. 145, 37 C.P.R. 1,
[1961] O.R. 265.  The observations made by the late Mr.
Justice Laidlaw at p. 200 D.L.R., pp. 152-3 C.C.C., pp. 29-30
C.P.R., p. 272 O.R. are particularly apt, for here no governor
was alleged to have had any personal animus towards Mr. Posluns
and the act which they were taking as to him was intended to be
and was in fact the act of the Exchange.  If it was wrongful,
it was the wrongful will and act of the Exchange, not that of
any of the governors who voted.  Reference might well be made
also to Said v. Butt,
[1920] 3 K.B. 497 at p. 506
; G. Scammell
& Nephew, Ltd. v. Hurley,
[1929] 1 K.B. 419 at pp. 429,
446 and
449, and O'Brien v. Dawson et al.
(1942), 66 C.L.R. 18 at p.
32,
where this appears:

The company, if it were guilty of a breach of its contracts
in this case, acted through its director the respondent Doyle,
but it is neither "law nor sense" (Laguanas Nitrate Co. v.
Laguanas Syndicate
(1899) 2 Ch. 392, at p. 431)
to say that
Doyle in the exercise of his functions as a director of the
company combined with it to do any unlawful act or become a
joint tortfeasor.  Again, it is equally fallacious to assert
that Doyle knowingly procured the company to break its
contract.  The acts of Doyle were the acts of the company and
not his personal acts which involved him in any liability to
the plaintiff.

Since there was no agreement in the legal sense of conspiracy
between the Exchange and Mr. Gardiner relating to Mr. Posluns,
and no such agreement between either of them and any other
governor, it is quite unnecessary to consider the further
defences raised in answer to this branch of the case.

XV DAMAGES

Although the action is to be dismissed, I believe I ought to
say something as to the amount of damages to which Mr. Posluns
might have been entitled had he succeeded.

Although the prayer for relief was changed on several
occasions as the action proceeded, by the end of the argument
there was asked (a) $500,000 damages for the conspiracy; (b)
$500,000 damages against the Exchange for inducing the Daly
company to break its employment contract with him, and (c)
$100,000 punitive damages because of the conspiracy.

At the conclusion of the argument for the plaintiff, an
attempt was made on his behalf to add to the claim by asking
for damages in respect of the factual allegations set out in
the prayer for the declaration.  Not being satisfied that the
defendant Exchange would escape prejudice if such an amendment
were made at that stage of the action, I disallowed it. (a) The
claim for punitive damages.

I propose to deal with, and dismiss very quickly, the matter
of punitive damages.

In the first place, I say most emphatically that there was
not proved to have been any conduct on the part of the
governors or officers of the Exchange calling for punishment by
the Court.  They were not actuated by a malice or a desire to
harm or punish the plaintiff and there was no element whatever
of moral turpitude on their part.  Really, that is all I need
to say on the subject except, perhaps, to refer to Mayne on
Damages,  12th ed., p. 196, para. 207, where it is stated that
punitive damages "can apply only where the conduct of the
defendant merits punishment ..."  However, perhaps I had better
mention the specific allegations relied upon as establishing a
case for exemplary damages.

I have just expressed my reaction to the assertion that the
Exchange acted maliciously for the purpose of punishing the
plaintiff.  I could add, however, that as Mr. Williston
expressly disclaimed any charge of malice on the part of Mr.
Gardiner, one can only assume that it was decided that he had
acted in good faith. Because of the discontinuance of the
action against Mr. Scott, I believe that the same assumption
can be made with respect to him.  Who, then, had the evil
incentive?  Clearly, it could not have been any of the other
governors who were not even acquainted with Mr. Posluns and
some of whom spoke well of him.

Then it was said that punitive damages should be allowed
because natural justice had not been made available to the
plaintiff.  I have decided that it was, but, had it been
otherwise, surely that simple fact would not mean, of itself,
that, in the absence of malice the person aggrieved could have
vindictive or retributory damages as well as compensation for
any loss sustained by him.

Complaint was also made that there had been discrimination
practised against Mr. Posluns in that he was the only person
who was forced to retire from Dalys.  However, as I have
already indicated, his degree of culpability was greater than
any other member of the Daly firm with the possible exception
of Mr. Robb.  I do not agree that their cases were the same,
but, in any event, they were dealt with in substantially the
same way.

The confidential letter, ex. 32, from General Graham to the
late chairman of the Ontario Securities Commission, was also
put forward as decisive evidence upon which to rest exemplary
damages. But the General certainly was not incited by any bad
motive; he was simply reporting, as he honestly thought he
should, to the authority to whom was entrusted the care and
supervision of matters relating generally to the brokerage
business.

Nor would the circulation of notice of the withdrawal of Mr.
Posluns' approval to the members of the Exchange, or the fact
that such information was made available to the press, give
reason for punitive damages.  Each was done in the normal
course and the plaintiff was treated no differently than any
other person whose approval might have been withdrawn.  I add,
too, that we do not know how the matter would have been treated
had Mr. Posluns accepted the offer to resign.

It was said that apart from all other motives, the members of
the Board of Governors, or some of them, intended to punish the
plaintiff, reference being made in that regard to what one of
the governors, Marshall Stearns, said in his evidence at vol.
16 from p. 2671 to p. 2672.  Those answers, however, must be
interpreted by reference to the sense in which they were given.
Unquestionably, the withdrawal of Mr. Posluns' approvals and
the decision to force him to sever his connections with the
Daly company was a form of punishment; but it is quite wrong to
construe those matters in such a way as to suggest that the
governors acted simply for the purpose of inflicting
punishment.  What they were trying to do was to protect the
other members of the Exchange and the investing public, and in
the process Mr. Posluns had to be hurt. They did not use the
hearing as a vehicle for punishment; that was the result only.

Mr. Williston lastly took the position that because the
defendants had persisted in the untenable plea that the
plaintiff's actions were unethical right up to and during the
course of the trial, punitive damages ought to be awarded.  I
can see no merit whatever in that submission.  The defendants
and each of them were, in my opinion, entirely justified in
resisting as vigorously as they could within the bounds of
propriety the substantial claims for damages made against them
by the plaintiff.

For those reasons, I have no hesitation in holding that the
plaintiff did not make out a case for punitive damages.

(b) The claim for general damages.

So far as general damages are concerned, I think it is clear
that in an action of this kind the plaintiff is not limited to
recovery of his actual pecuniary loss, but may also have a sum
appropriate to the circumstances of the wrong inflicted upon
him once financial loss has been proved:  see for example
Exchange Telegraph Co. Ltd. v. Gregory & Co.,
[1896] 1 Q.B. 147

per Lord Esher, M.R., at p. 153, and the Pratt case, [1919] 1
K.B. at p. 281.  It was argued on behalf of the plaintiff that
he had not only shown actual monetary loss as a result of the
Exchange's order of dismissal, but had established other
circumstances which would merit greater compensation.

In the years from 1955 to 1959, Mr. Posluns' earnings at the
Burns company via salary and commissions had gone from
something in excess of $10,00 to $72,267.31. In 1960, at Dalys,
the salary and commissions paid to him amounted to $61,746.94,
and in that part of the following year during which he was with
the firm, his earnings were proportionately somewhat greater.

During that same period from 1955 to 1961, however, the
plaintiff had many, many outside interests which, though not
putting him in receipt of much actual income, steadily
increased his net worth.  That process has continued, so that
it was conceded by his counsel that today his capital position
is considerably better than it was when he was at Dalys.  In
the last two years, he has been more actively engaged in the
operations of family firms, has handled investments for his
brothers and others, and has continued his personal contact
with a huge real estate venture in Quebec city.

The first matter to be examined it the potential loss of
salary and commissions said to have been incurred as a result
of the dismissal.  On his behalf, it was argued that he would
have continued to receive in that respect an annual sum of at
least $60,000 for an indefinite period had he been permitted to
remain with the Daly firm. In this regard Mr. Posluns told us
that in addition to ordinary commissions, he was earning
commissions on underwritings and that his special type of
operations only required his presence at the Daly office for
about two to three hours a day, his clients being served mainly
by other employees of the firm.  It was therefore contended
that because he lost a source of earnings which was not
replaceable, the fact that his net worth had increased was
quite immaterial because he could also have done most of the
new work upon which he has since been engaged had he been
allowed to remain at Dalys.  He also told us, and the evidence
would seem to bear him out, that his commissions, especially
from underwritings, were becoming greater.  At first glance, it
might be thought, therefore, that he suffered an actual
pecuniary loss of at least $60,000 per annum for as many years
as he cared to stay with the Daly firm.  It was also asserted
that he was deprived of the opportunity to increase his
shareholdings in that company from 5% to 10% under the oral
agreement which was made to that effect before he came into the
Daly office.

There are, however, several factors which detract from such a
conclusion.  I have already alluded to the fact that to some
extent the release from his work at Dalys has permitted him to
devote more time to other interests, most, if not all, of which
have prospered.  His accretions in that respect are represented
by undistributed profits left with the corporations with which
he has been associated.

Then, too, an undetermined but substantial portion of the
commissions which came to the plaintiff while at Burns and
Dalys was derived from the put and call option business
generally, and from the Lynch-Lido account in particular.  Dr.
Shulman emphasized, for instance, that although by June of 1960
he had many sellers of American options (and they were the key
to the success of the business), his activities with them were
not of the magnitude of Mr. Lynch's.  By reason of what
happened in January of 1961 that source of revenue to the
plaintiff was bound to be seriously depleted if not completely
wiped out, for not only did the Lynch business come to an
abrupt halt through no action on the part of the Exchange, but
the Daly firm almost simultaneously decided, with good reason,
to withdraw from the option business entirely.  Again, I think
it is reasonable to conclude that such decision was quite
unrelated to the resolution of the Exchange with respect to Mr.
Posluns.  Accordingly, the plaintiff was due to lose his
greatest source of Daly income regardless of what the Exchange
did.  And any claim to loss of income from Lido would be
influenced by the same circumstance.  It is perfectly obvious,
therefore, that had Mr. Posluns remained with the Daly firm his
level of income would have dropped sharply not long after the
middle of March, 1961.

It is true that the plaintiff was removed, temporarily at
least, from a chance to develop an underwriting business but
the evidence also indicated that any commissions earned from
that source were relatively small and that the value of his
shares in the Daly company reflected his success in that field,
he participated in that success by being paid the book value of
his shares upon his departure. There are several other
considerations which tend to reduce the amount of damages which
might have been assessed in favour of the plaintiff.  In the
first place, and while the matter is not free from doubt, I am
inclined to the view that such part of any award of damages
which would represent loss of earnings would have had to be
reduced by the amount of income tax payable on those earnings.
According to exs. 135 and 136, the plaintiff's income taxes
amounted to about one-third of his gross income for each of the
years 1960 and 1961, a circumstance which would suggest that if
the quantum were to be diminished because of a potential tax
liability, a substantial reduction would be the consequence.

In the case of British Transport Com'n. v. Gourley,
[1956]
A.C. 185
, the House of Lords held that in assessing the damages
with  reference to the loss of earnings actual and prospective
in a personal injury action, regard should be had to the income
tax and surtax that the plaintiff would have had to pay on the
amount of such earnings had he not been injured.  Accordingly,
it was decided that in determining the amount of damages that a
defendant should be adjudged liable to pay to a plaintiff,
there should be deducted from the total loss of earnings
computed, the amount of income tax that would have been paid
thereon, namely, the actual amount up to the date of trial and
the estimated amount thereafter. The justification for making
such a deduction was placed upon the fact that in the
assessment of damages in personal injury actions, the tribunal
endeavoured to award the injured party such a sum of money as
would put him in the same position as he would have been in had
he not sustained the injury; while the plaintiff should be
compensated, he should not profit as a consequence of his
injury.

The principle in the Gourley case rested upon the admission
by all counsel that the plaintiff would incur no tax liability
on the amount of damages awarded to him in respect of his lost
earnings.  Had the award been subject to taxation, then, of
course, no deduction in respect of the income taxes otherwise
payable by the plaintiff could have been made, for such a
deduction would result in double taxation -- the deduction made
by the Judge, and the subsequent tax payable on the damages by
the Crown.  In that case, the agreement by all counsel that the
award would not be subject to taxation relieved the Court from
making any determination as to the laibility to tax of such
award. It is by no means clear, however, that damages for
temporary loss of earnings are tax free in England or Canada,
even though in practice taxes on them have apparently not been
exacted by the Crown.  In Renfrew Town Council v. Commissioners
of Inland Revenue (1934), 19 Tax Cas. 13 at pp. 18-9, Clyde,
L.P., observed that in a personal injury action, if the
individual is permanently disabled the damages would appear to
be a capital increment in so far as he is concerned, but if he
is only rendered inactive for a limited period during which
time he loses income, the damages are akin to a revenue receipt
just as the income, if earned, would have been.  These remarks
of Clyde, L.P., were obiter but since no specific exemption is
granted by the Canadian Income Tax Act [R.S.C. 1952, c. 148] to
damage awards for personal injuries, a strong case may be made
for the contention that in Canada damages in lieu of earnings
are taxable even though, by administrative tolerance, the tax
is never levied in practice.

This question of the incidence of taxation to damages awarded
in respect of lost earnings, both past and future, arises not
only in personal injury actions, but also in actions for breach
of a contract of employment, or wrongful dismissal.  While the
non-taxability of damages granted for loss of earnings in
personal injury actions may be based in both England and Canada
more on administrative policy than on a strict interpretation
of the law, the same is not true in the case of wrongful
dismissal actions.  In this type of action there is abundant
authority in both countries that the damages are not taxable
because they are not granted in lieu of income that would
otherwise have been earned, but are awarded as compensation for
the destruction of a capital right, the right to serve and
receive remuneration to the end of a contractual term.  In vol.
2 of Simon's Income Tax, 2nd ed., p. 589, the author says that
a payment, whether by agreement or by way of damages, made not
by virtue of the service agreement but as consideration for
release from that agreement is treated as not having the nature
of emoluments.  One of the early leading cases is Chibbett v.
Joseph Robinson & Sons, Com'rs of Inland Revenue v. Joseph
Robinson & Sons (1924), 9 Tax Cas. 48, where Rowlatt, J.,
stated at p. 61, in referring to a sum paid:

If it was a payment in respect of the termination of their
employment I do not think that is taxable ... It seems to me
that a payment to make up for the cessation for the future of
annual taxable profits is not itself an annual profit at all.
This rule was followed in Henley v. Murray,
[1950] 1 All E.R.
908 where, at p. 911,
Jenkins, L.J., says:

... the question in each case is whether, on the facts of the
case, the lump sum paid is in the nature of remuneration or
profits in respect of the office, or is in the nature of a
sum paid in consideration of the surrender by the recipient
of his rights in respect of the office.

His Lordship found that an amount paid to a taxpayer by way of
compensation for loss of office, although equal to the balance
of the salary to the end of the employee's period of service,
was payable in consideration of the abrogation of the contract,
and was not taxable, being received for the surrender of the
taxpayer's right to serve and receive remuneration to the end
of his contractual engagement, a capital right.

The Canadian Tax Appeal Board has arrived at the same
conclusion on several occasions.  For example, in the Hafezi
case [Hafezi v. Minister of National Revenue],
61 D.T.C. 357
,
the taxpayer had been dishcharged from his position as a
physician and surgeon with the medical staff of a clinic.  He
brought action but before the case came on for trial a
settlement was reached.  The Tax Appeal Board held that the
amount received represented nothing more than damages for the
deprivation of an enduring right, a source of income having
been destroyed and, accordingly, that it was not taxable.

In 1960 the English Parliament enacted the Finance Act, 1960
[c. 44], providing for the taxability of sums received as
damages for the breach of a service agreement.  Section 38(3)
of such Act exempted amounts not exceeding (STERLING)5,000.

In Parsons v. B.N.M. Laboratories, Ltd.,
[1963] 2 All E.R.
658
, the English Court of Appeal, in a two to one majority
decision, held that the principle in the Gourley case applied
to an action for breach of a contract of service, and
accordingly, income tax had to be taken into account by way of
deduction from the plaintiff's loss of earnings, in view of the
fact that the damages awarded to him as compensation for that
loss were not taxable in his hands, as being below the
(STERLING)5,000 taxable figure.

In Walker v. Copp Clark Publishing Co. Ltd.,
1962 CanLII 224 (ON HCJ)
, 33 D.L.R. (2d)
338, [1962] O.R. 622, an action for wrongful dismissal, Spence,
J., followed the Gourley case.  At p. 350 D.L.R., p. 634 O.R.,
in computing the damages, he stated that from the income which
would have been earned, there ought to be deducted (1) the
income tax that the plaintiff would have had to pay if he
remained in the employ of the defendant company, and (2) the
salary received elsewhere less the income tax paid on such
salary.

The Gourley case has also been followed by Winter, J., of the
Newfoundland Supreme Court in Power v. Stoyles (1958),
1958 CanLII 303 (NL SC)
, 17
D.L.R. (2d) 239, and by the Alberta Appeal Court in Widrig v.
Strazer & Gardiner et al. (1963),
1963 CanLII 492 (AB SCAD)
, 37 D.L.R. (2d) 629, 41 W.W.R.
257.  However, in Soltys v. Middup Moving & Storage Ltd.,
Stanley v. Middup Moving & Storage Ltd., (1963),
1963 CanLII 527 (MB QB)
, 41 D.L.R. (2d)
576, 44 W.W.R. 522, an action for personal injuries, where the
amount of earnings lost by the plaintiff from the date of the
accident to the date of trial was $8,570.50, which, in the
normal course, would have been subjected to income tax of
$698.45, the trial Judge held that the liability to income tax
of any award of damages was a matter res inter alios acta, a
matter between the plaintiff and the Crown, and did not concern
the defendant.

In the case at bar, any damages awarded would have included
an amount to represent whatever loss of earnings came from the
breach of contract.  It really matters not whether such a
recovery would be closer to a personal injury action, or to an
action for wrongful dismissal in view of the fact that in both
classes of action the Courts (except for the Manitoba decision)
make a deduction in respect of income taxes that would
otherwise have been paid on the earnings that have been lost.
The distinction may be important only because there are, as
yet, no cases dealing with the taxability of damages granted
for lost earnings in a personal injury action, since the
authorities have not seen fit to tax the same.  This does not
mean, of course, that some time in the future the authorities
could not take it upon themselves to make an assessment on such
damages.  However, there have been, as stated above, numerous
cases holding tht damages granted in wrongful dismissal actions
are not taxable, and I think that an action for procuring a
breach of contract, although the damages are payable not by the
contracting party, as is the case in a wrongful dismissal
action, but by a third party, is closer in its nature to the
breach of contract action than to a personal injury action.

Accordingly, in view of the decision of the English Court of
Appeal in the Parsons case and the judgment of Spence, J., in
the Walker case, I must consider the fact that had the
plaintiff actually earned his commissions by way of employment,
he would have been subjected to income tax liability with
respect thereto, whereas an award of damages would not have
been exigible to tax since such award would have been given for
the the destruction of his capital right to serve as a
customers' man with the Daly firm.  Therefore, I would have had
to reduce the damages otherwise recoverable by an amount
roughly equivalent to the income taxes which would have been
payable on that part of the award which would represent
earnings.

There is another circumstance which must be taken into
consideration in arriving at a proper assessment of damages.
It cannot be assumed that but for the action by the Exchange
Mr. Posluns would have remained indefinitely in the employ of
the Daly company.  Indeed, it seems to me that because of what
occurred the latter might well have terminated its relations
with the plaintiff by giving reasonable notice for such
purpose, in which event he would certainly not have been
entitled to more than one year's notice.

That leads me into another aspect of the plaintiff's claim.
It was asserted that because of the wrongful act of the
Exchange, he was forced out of the brokerage business "which
was his chosen profession".  I do not think that such a claim
is entirely accurate.  Even if it were, the evidence does not
support the notion that Mr. Posluns was expelled from it by the
Exchange. When asked about this, he candidly stated that after
being discharged from Dalys he did not attempt to obtain
employment with any other member of the Exchange (see the
evidence, vol. 5, p. 1214, line 20, to p. 1215, line 6). While
adding that it would have been impossible to procure a position
elsewhere, he did not say why that would be so.  All that Mr.
Gardiner, the only other witness on the subject, would say was
that he would not have employed Mr. Posluns immediately after
his discharge by Dalys, and that while he did not know whether
the plaintiff would have had a chance of becoming a customers'
man with another member at that time, at least his application
to become a commission salesman would have to go before the
customers' man committee of the Exchange (see the evidence,
vol. 5, p. 1111, line 3, to p. 1112, line 21). However, on all
the evidence I would not have been prepared to act upon the
suggestion that Mr. Posluns was forever excluded from the
brokerage business, even in Toronto.  It is impossible to
believe that a man of his standing and who was as large a
producer as he was, would not have been able to find another
place in the business if he had made any real and serious
effort in that direction. In the light of all of those facts, I
am persuaded that the plaintiff's pecuniary loss was not nearly
as substantial as first appeared.

Of course, had he been entitled to damages, the plaintiff
would have been awarded some amount to compensate him for the
embarrassment which he undoubtedly suffered as a result of the
publication of his dismissal to the members of the Exchange,
and subsequently by the press.  In the Pratt case McCardie, J.,
recognized that once actual financial loss has been proved in
an action such as this, the Court can, and probably should,
award a sum appropriate to the whole circumstances of the
tortious wrong inflicted.  One of the circumstances he bore in
mind was the humiliation to which the plaintiff was subjected.

I have arrived at the conclusion that had I been called upon
to grant damages, I would have done justice between the parties
concerned had I assessed them at $25,000.

XVI RESULT

I have endorsed the Record in this way:  "Action dismissed
with costs."

Action dismissed.
